The Prophetic Biography (Seerah): A Way of Life and a Project for Salvation

Introduction: The Urgent Need to Reread the Seerah in a Changing World

Amidst the crashing waves storming the Islamic Ummah, and in light of the rapid changes witnessed by the modern world, the need emerges—more urgent than ever before—to return to the pure source and fresh spring: the biography of the Chosen One, peace and blessings be upon him (المصطفى صلى الله عليه وسلم). Talking about the Prophetic Biography (Seerah) today is not an intellectual luxury, nor is it merely summoning the past to sing the praises of ancestors. Rather, it is a vital necessity, a religious obligation, and a psychological and intellectual need without which the state of the contemporary Muslim cannot be rectified.

When we propose the project of studying the Prophetic Biography at this specific time, we realize the magnitude of the challenges facing Muslim youth: identity crises, currents of atheism, material pressure, and intellectual distortion, not to mention the psychological frustration resulting from the reality of the Ummah. Here, the Seerah comes not as stories told for entertainment, but to be a "project for salvation" and a practical "roadmap" out of this wilderness.

1. The Seerah: A New Reading for a Renewed Reality

Limiting oneself to narrating the events of the Seerah as a historical record (he was born, lived, fought, died) is a defective reduction of this great legacy. The Prophetic Biography is the practical embodiment of Divine Revelation and the applied interpretation of the Holy Quran. Allah the Almighty says: {There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often.} [Al-Ahzab: 21]. This divine command to emulate necessarily implies the existence of a continuous methodology for reading the Seerah that suits the developments of every age.

The problems of the Muslim youth today differ from the problems of previous generations. Today, the youth faces an intellectual invasion within his own home through phone screens, facing doubts about his constants, and immense economic and social pressure. Therefore, presenting the Seerah must move from the square of "historical narration" to the square of "realistic remediation." We need to ask: How did the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) deal with the economic siege in the Glen of Abu Talib (شعب أبي طالب) so we can draw inspiration for patience in our financial crises? How did the first generation build their creed in Mecca amidst a hostile disbelieving environment so we know how to preserve our religion in a time of alienation? The Seerah is valid for every time because it is "Revelation," and Revelation does not wear out; rather, its meanings are renewed with renewed calamities.

2. The Seerah: A Comprehensive Educational and Creedal Methodology

The Prophetic Biography is the "catalog" that explains how to operate the human soul according to the will of its Creator. It is not just battles and invasions, but an integrated school in education, creed, politics, economics, and sociology.

  • Building Creed (Aqeedah): The Seerah teaches us Monotheism (Tawheed) not as theoretical information, but as a lived reality. We see Tawheed in his saying to his companion in the cave: {Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.} [At-Tawbah: 40], and we see it in his trust in Allah's victory on the Day of the Confederates (Al-Ahzab) when hearts reached the throats.
  • Education and Purification (Tazkiyah): Allah bestowed favor upon the believers by sending the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) to teach and purify them. Allah says: {Certainly did Allah confer [great] favor upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and wisdom.} [Ali 'Imran: 164]. The Seerah is the laboratory where shepherds were transformed into leaders of nations, and it is the methodology that transformed Omar bin Al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) from deep ignorance (Jahiliyyah) into the inspired Farooq (الفاروق).
  • Intellectual Building: The Seerah protects the Muslim mind from deviation; it regulates the balance between emotion and reason, clarifying when there is peace and when there is war, when there is patience and when there is action. It is the moderate methodology that protects youth from extremism and excess, and from dilution and melting away at the same time.

3. Extracting the Greatest Practical Benefit (From Theory to Application)

The goal of this in-depth study of the Seerah is to transform texts into movement in life. We do not want to exit the study of the Seerah merely memorizing the dates of battles; we want to exit carrying a "methodology of thinking."

  • Projecting Seerah onto Reality: We must learn how to measure our reality against the reality of the Seerah with caution and understanding. We must realize Allah’s laws (Sunan) in change, knowing that victory does not come by chance but has laws (faith, work, and preparation), and that defeat has causes (disobedience, dispute, and failure).
  • Inspiring Solutions: The Seerah offers solutions to our social problems (in the Prophet’s dealing with his family and companions), solutions to our psychological problems (in his dealing with grief, loss, and worry), and solutions to our advocacy problems (in the jurisprudence of gradualism and stages).

The Prophetic Biography is the practical application of Islam. If the Quran is the theoretical constitution, then the life of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) is the applied model of this constitution. Aisha (عائشة رضي الله عنها) said when asked about the character of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): "His character was the Quran" (Narrated by Muslim). Therefore, any attempt to understand Islam away from the Seerah is a deficient and incomplete attempt.

Summary of this Introduction: We are about to embark on a journey to explore "Life" in the biography of the "Master of the Living" (سيد الأحياء), peace and blessings be upon him. We search for "Salvation" in a time of trials, and there is no salvation except by boarding the ship of the Sunnah and following the traces of the one who does not speak from his own desire. It is a call to the youth specifically, and the Ummah generally, to rediscover their Prophet, not only as lovers but as followers, emulators, bearers of his banner, and completers of his path in reforming the earth and populating the universe with Monotheism (Tawheed).

Axis One: The Seerah is Applied Religion (The Model and Example)

The greatest advantage of studying the Prophetic Biography lies in moving the Muslim from the space of abstract theory to the ground of practical application. The Islamic religion is not a set of philosophical theories soaring in the imagination, nor is it a "Utopia" impossible to achieve. Rather, it is a way of life designed to be lived by humans with their weaknesses and strengths, their hopes and pains. Here, the Seerah comes to be the "Practical Application" of the Quran and Sunnah, offering us the "Complete Model" that Allah intended for humanity.

First: Practical Application: Transforming Texts into Tangible Reality

When we read the Holy Quran, we find commands for patience, reliance on Allah (Tawakkul), Jihad, forgiveness, and justice. Theoretically, these concepts may seem easy to understand, but upon application, the human soul is beset by doubts: "Is this possible? Can a human forgive someone who wronged him? Can a human stand firm against massive armies while alone?" The Seerah comes to answer "Yes," providing practical proof.

  • The Seerah is the Living Interpretation: The Seerah is the practical translation of the verses of the Wise Book. When the Mother of the Believers, Aisha (عائشة رضي الله عنها), was asked about the character of the Messenger of Allah (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم), she summarized thousands of details in one comprehensive sentence: "His character was the Quran" (Narrated by Muslim). He was not merely a copy of the Quran recited, but a Quran walking among people. People saw the verses transformed into behavior, commands transformed into obedience, and prohibitions transformed into piety.
  • The Good Example: Allah Almighty did not reveal the Quran to a mountain or an angel; He revealed it to the heart of a human and made this human the standard and the scale. Allah says: {There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allah often.} [Al-Ahzab: 21]. This verse confirms that Islam is a religion applicable to reality. If the religion were angelic, people would say, "We have no capacity for it." But the Prophet was a human; he hungered, fell ill, grieved, and rejoiced, yet he applied the religion in its entirety, negating the excuse of the incapable.
  • Countless Models: The matter does not stop at the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) alone but extends to the generation of Companions who were raised in his school. The Seerah offers us hundreds of applied models; we see Al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr) in his certainty, Al-Farooq (Omar) in his justice, Uthman (عثمان) in his modesty, and Ali (علي) in his courage. This frequency in practical application proves that this religion is valid for every time and place and that change is not impossible.

Second: Comprehensiveness: The Prophet (PBUH) Combines All Human Roles

Among the greatness of Divine planning in choosing the Seal of the Prophets is that his life (PBUH) was not one-dimensional like the life of a monk in his hermitage or a king in his ivory tower. Rather, it was a comprehensive life wherein he underwent the full human experience in all its dimensions, allowing every human being—whoever they may be—to find in the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) a role model for their specific situation.

  • Diversity of Social and Leadership Roles:
    • The Father and Husband: You find in him the example in dealing with his nine wives: how he was just, how he loved, how he was patient with human jealousy, how he consoled, and how he played. You find him a merciful father whose eyes shed tears at the loss of his son Ibrahim (إبراهيم), saying: "The eye tears, the heart grieves, and we say nothing except what pleases our Lord" (Agreed upon), teaching us patience and contentment.
    • The Political and Military Leader: You find him managing the state, concluding treaties (like the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah), sending envoys to kings, planning battles, digging the trench with his own hands, wearing armor, and enduring the pain of wounds in "Uhud."
    • The Caller (Da'iyah) and Educator: You find him teaching the ignorant, being patient with the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque, and raising the youth like Ibn Abbas (ابن عباس) and Mu'adh bin Jabal (معاذ بن جبل).
    • The Friend and Neighbor: You find him the best companion to Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) in the cave, the best neighbor, and the best upholder of kinship ties.
  • Fluctuation of Worldly Conditions:
    • He experienced states of wealth and poverty; he died while his armor was pawned to a Jew, lived days tying a stone to his stomach from hunger, and when spoils came to him, he distributed them, keeping nothing for himself.
    • He experienced states of victory and defeat; he was victorious in Badr and the Conquest of Mecca, yet was tested in Uhud and suffered in Ta'if.
    • He experienced states of health and sickness, safety and fear, stability and migration.

Therefore, there is no human on the face of the earth who does not find in the biography of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) a scene that mimics their life, inspiring them on how to act and how to please Allah in that specific situation.

Third: True Heroism: The Illusion of the "Superhero" vs. The Reality of the "Master of Humans"

In our current era, concepts of heroism have been distorted among the youth. The "role model" has become the soccer player, the actor, or the fictional character in "Superhero" movies and novels. Here, the Seerah presents the true concept of heroism.

  • Paper Hero vs. Real Hero: Heroes in movies and novels (like Superman, Batman, or detective novel heroes) are imaginary heroes with supernatural abilities, and their victories are written in the script beforehand. Emulating them breeds frustration because you will not fly, nor will you break iron. As for the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) and the Companions, their heroism was "human." They were humans of flesh and blood, with limited capabilities, but they connected with Allah and possessed an iron will and unyielding determination.
  • Psychological and Moral Heroism: The Seerah teaches us that the real hero is not the one who kills villains with magical powers, but:
    • The one who controls himself when angry.
    • The one who pardons while capable of revenge (as the Prophet did on the day of the Conquest of Mecca: "Go, for you are the free ones").
    • The one who stands firm on principle alone (as the Prophet stood firm in Ta'if and Mecca).
    • The one who endures hunger and pain for a noble goal (as in the siege of the Glen and the Battle of the Trench).
  • Testimonies of Fair-Minded People: This great realistic heroism dazzled even non-Muslims. When thinkers like Michael Hart (in his book "The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History"), Tolstoy, Gandhi, Bernard Shaw, or Lamartine read the Prophet's biography, they did not look at him as a mythical figure but as the greatest human achievement in history. They saw a man who started alone in a barren desert and, in less than a quarter of a century, changed the face of history, established a state, built a civilization, reformed souls, united hearts, and left an indelible mark.

Summary: Studying the Seerah resets the "Compass of Role Models" for the human being. It takes them out of the darkness of illusions and heart-attachment to fake heroes, linking them to the greatest man to walk the earth, and to a unique generation (the Companions) who achieved miracles by human laws and with the aid of the Lord of humans. It makes us realize that we are capable of change and making glory if we walk the same path walked by the {Excellent Pattern}.

Axis Two: Hope and Treating Frustration (Psychological Support)

Under the pressuring reality the Ummah lives in, with nations gathering against it and weakness prevailing, despair sneaks into the hearts of many youths, turning into a state of crippling frustration. Here, the Prophetic Biography stands out as the "Psychological Clinic" and the "Capsule of Hope" that treats this chronic disease. Studying the Seerah is not merely a historical review; it is a continuous process of "charging" the battery of certainty in the hearts of believers, confirming to them that no matter how long the night, the dawn must break, and that with hardship comes ease.

First: The Capsule of Hope: How Does the Seerah Give Us the Antidote Against Despair?

When we contemplate the pivotal moments of the Prophetic Biography, we find that the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) and the Companions went through circumstances far harsher and darker than what we go through today by light-years, yet despair did not seep into their hearts for a single moment. The Seerah presents living scenes that tell you: "Do not despair, for the best of humans went through what is harder."

  • The Cave Scene (Peak Certainty in Peak Weakness): During the migration journey, the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) and his companion Abu Bakr (أبو بكر رضي الله عنه) were chased, their blood wanted, hiding in the Cave of Thawr. The polytheists stood at the mouth of the cave; if one of them had looked under his feet, he would have seen them. In the language of material calculations: it was over, and the Call (Da'wah) was finished in its cradle. Here, Abu Bakr trembled with fear for the Messenger of Allah, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looked under his feet, he would see us." The reply came, taught in the institutes of building certainty: "O Abu Bakr, what is your thought of two, of whom Allah is the third?" The Quran descended immortalizing this moment: {When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."} [At-Tawbah: 40]. The Seerah teaches us here that "Divine Company" flips the balance of power and that earthly causes vanish before the power of Heaven.
  • The Confederates Scene (Hope Amidst Siege): In the Battle of the Trench (Al-Khandaq), the Arab armies gathered (ten thousand fighters) to eradicate the Muslims. The Jews (Banu Qurayzah - بنو قريظة) betrayed the covenant from within, and the cold, hunger, and fear intensified until Allah described the situation: {[Remember] when they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted [in fear], and hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah [various] assumptions.} [Al-Ahzab: 10]. In this bleak moment, a rock obstructed the Companions which they could not break. The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) came, while people tied stones to their stomachs from hunger, to strike the rock and give them glad tidings of possessing the palaces of Khosrow and Caesar! It was not imagination, but hope built on Divine Promise. Indeed, the clouds cleared, the Muslims won by wind and terror, and the glad tidings were realized a few years later.
  • The Ta'if Scene (The Gift within the Ordeal): When Mecca closed its doors, the Prophet went to Ta'if seeking support. They met him with the worst reception, inciting their fools against him, throwing stones at him until his noble feet bled. This situation represents the peak of psychological and physical brokenness for a human. But did he despair? Did he pray against them when the Angel of the Mountains came offering to crush them between the two mountains (Al-Akhshabayn)? No, he said: "Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him" (Agreed upon). The Seerah teaches us here "Long Patience," that losing a round does not mean the end of the battle, and that the caller does not take revenge for himself but lives for his message.

Second: Rules of Victory and Defeat (Jurisprudence of Divine Laws)

The Prophetic Biography is not a series of supernatural miracles that do not recur; rather, it is a human movement governed by strict "Divine Laws" (Sunan) that favor no one, even if the Master of Creation (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) is among them. Understanding these rules removes the frustration resulting from questions like: "Why are we defeated when we are Muslims?"

  • Laws Know No Favoritism (The Lesson of Uhud): In the Battle of Uhud, the army included the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم), Abu Bakr, Omar, Ali, and Hamzah (حمزة). Yet, the Muslims were defeated, the Prophet’s face was wounded, his incisor was broken, and 70 of the best Companions were killed. Why? Because the archers violated a military and tactical order of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) and descended to collect spoils. The lesson here is harsh but pivotal: Victory is not free, nor does it come by supplications and wishes alone; it comes by obeying Allah and taking material causes. When the Companions asked in astonishment: {When a disaster struck you, although you had struck [the enemy in Badr] with one twice as great, you said, "From where is this?"}, the shocking and clear Divine response came: {Say, "It is from yourselves."} [Ali 'Imran: 165]. The Seerah teaches us that disobeying the leader's order and seeking the world (spoils) inevitably leads to defeat, and this is a law applicable to everyone.
  • The Law of Merit (The Rule of Khadija): At the beginning of Revelation, when the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) came down from the Cave of Hira trembling, saying: "Cover me, cover me," Khadija (خديجة رضي الله عنها) reassured him with a golden rule in the "Laws of Hope and Victory." She did not tell him "Allah will not disgrace you because you are a Prophet" (as she did not know the details of the message yet). Instead, she reasoned with his social and moral practice, saying: "Nay! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you; for you uphold the ties of kinship, bear the burden of the weak, earn for the poor, entertain the guest, and help in the calamities of truth" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari). This is the law of safety: Whoever is in the aid of people, Allah is in his aid. Hope, victory, and protection from Allah do not come to the isolated, but to those active in society, people of white hands (charity), and high morals. This rule dispels the youth's frustration, telling them: "Do good, and you will never be lost."

Third: Comparing Reality (Between Yesterday's Jahiliyyah and Today's Reality)

One of the most important treatments for frustration offered by the Seerah is placing our current reality in its natural size compared to the reality in which the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) started.

  • Pitch Darkness Before the Mission: The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) describes the state of the earth before his mission in a Hadith Qudsi: "Allah looked at the people of the earth and hated them, Arabs and non-Arabs, except for remnants of the People of the Book" (Narrated by Muslim). Humanity was drowning in a swamp of polytheism, injustice, burying daughters alive, grinding tribal wars, and worshipping idols, stones, and fire. Superpowers (Persians and Romans) enslaved nations. The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) started alone, as an individual, in the desert of Mecca, with no money, no army, no media, and no supporter except Allah.
  • The Miraculous Achievement: Within just 23 years, this "Lone Man" transformed into the leader of a nation that changed the course of history, toppled empires of injustice, and spread Monotheism and justice from the borders of China to Southern France (shortly after his death due to the blessing of his call).
  • Our Reality Today: Today – despite all tragedies – we possess:
    • More than 1.5 billion Muslims (Numbers).
    • The Holy Quran preserved among us without a single letter changed (Methodology).
    • The Purified Sunnah recorded and preserved (Application).
    • Mosques filling the earth, and scholars, callers, and reformers exist. We do not start from zero as the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) did; rather, we start from a massive foundation.

Therapeutic Summary: If one man (PBUH) could change that dark reality with zero capabilities, how can we despair when we possess all these elements? Frustration in our time is an "illusion" resulting from weak resolve and misunderstanding, not from the impossibility of change. The Seerah tells you: "The path is trodden, the methodology is preserved, and the result is guaranteed for those who walk the path."

Axis Three: Awareness and Understanding Reality (Intellectual Building)

One of the most important goals of studying the Prophetic Biography is building a Muslim mind capable of understanding what is happening around it deeply, not superficially. The Seerah is not just tales; it is a "lens" through which we see the world, understand the laws of history, the nature of conflicts, and the objectives of the Quran. It grants the Muslim "intellectual immunity" and "political and social awareness" that protects them from being deceived by glittering slogans or falling into the trap of purely materialistic interpretations of events.

First: The Nature of Conflict: The Permanent Ideological Conflict

In today's world, many try to limit conflicts and wars to economic reasons (oil, gas, water) or geopolitical ones (borders, influence). Although these reasons might be tools or catalysts, the Seerah reveals to us the true essence of the conflict between Truth and Falsehood: it is primarily an "ideological" conflict and a permanent "existential" conflict that ends only with the Hour.

  • The Reality of Enmity: The Holy Quran and the Seerah clarify that hostility towards Islam is not born of chance or changing interests, but is hostility towards "Religion" and "Tawheed." Allah Almighty says, revealing this truth: {And they will continue to fight you until they turn you back from your religion if they are able.} [Al-Baqarah: 217]. The phrase "continue to" implies continuity and permanence, and the ultimate goal is "apostasy from religion," not merely occupying land.
  • Examples from the Seerah:
    • The Prophet's conflict with the Jews of Medina (Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, Banu Qurayzah) was not due to commercial disputes, but due to their breaking of covenants, their hatred for the Truth he brought, and their desperate attempts to kill him and eliminate his call.
    • The Prophet's conflict with Quraysh was not a competition for tribal leadership; they offered him kingship, money, and status in exchange for abandoning the Creed. They said: "If you want money with what you brought, we will collect for you... and if you want kingship, we will make you our king." He refused because the issue was an issue of "Tawheed."
  • Tolerance Does Not Cancel Conflict: The Seerah teaches us that the Muslim is required to be just and equitable even with enemies, but this does not mean naivety and ignoring their plotting. Conflict is a cosmic law: {And if it were not for Allah checking [some] people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted.} [Al-Baqarah: 251]. Understanding this truth frees the youth from the illusion of "absolute world peace" promoted by some to dilute the creed, making them realize that steadfastness on Truth has a tax, and that spiritual and material preparation is a necessity for survival.

Second: Understanding the Quran: The Seerah is the "Context" for the Text

The Holy Quran is a book of guidance, but its verses were revealed piecemeal over 23 years, keeping pace with the events of the Seerah. Therefore, it is impossible to understand many verses and Surahs deeply and correctly in isolation from the "Reasons for Revelation" (Asbab al-Nuzul) and the historical circumstances in which they were revealed (the Seerah).

  • The Quran Documents the Seerah: Many Surahs of the Quran are, in reality, "Divine Commentary" on the events of the Seerah.
    • Surah Al-Fath: Whoever reads it without knowing about the "Treaty of Hudaybiyyah" may not understand anything. His saying: {Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest} was revealed following the Treaty which some Companions (like Omar bin Al-Khattab initially) saw as "humiliating," while Allah called it a "Conquest." The verses speak about the Pledge under the Tree, restraining people's hands from them, and preventing fighting in Mecca... all these details are only understood by reading the story of Hudaybiyyah.
    • Surah At-Tawbah (Bara'ah): It is the Surah that "Exposed" the hypocrites. One cannot understand its verses about {Those who said, "Do not go forth in the heat"} or {And among them are some who criticize you concerning the [distribution of] charities} or the story of "Masjid Al-Dirar" except by knowing the events of the "Battle of Tabuk," the conditions of hardship, and the conspiracies of the hypocrites in Medina.
    • Surah Al-Hashr: Revealed entirely regarding the Jews of "Banu Nadir." His saying: {It is He who expelled the ones who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering}, and the details of cutting palm trees and distributing spoils (Fai'), do not become clear without reading the story of the expulsion of Banu Nadir in the Seerah.
    • Surah Ali 'Imran: A large part of it (from verse 121 onwards) deals with a precise analysis of the "Battle of Uhud," causes of defeat, consoling the believers, and exposing the hypocrites who returned with a third of the army.
  • Correcting Concepts: Understanding the Seerah prevents "twisting the necks of texts." For example, verses of "Sword" and fighting are only understood in the context of repelling aggression or securing the Da'wah, and verses of "Pardon and Forgiveness" have their context. This leads us to the next point.

Third: Jurisprudence of Gradualism and Stages of Da'wah (Adjusting the Kinetic Compass)

One of the most dangerous intellectual errors falling upon some enthusiastic youth is the "Wrong Projection" of Seerah events onto reality, such as taking a verse revealed in the stage of "Weakness" and applying it in the stage of "Empowerment," or vice versa. The Seerah teaches us the "Jurisprudence of Gradualism" and "Stages" in Da'wah and Jihad.

  • Stages of Da'wah:
    1. Secret Stage (Building the Core): Lasted 3 years, in which the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) focused on "Selection" and intensive spiritual upbringing of individuals in "Dar Al-Arqam." The lesson here: Change begins with building the human, not with media noise.
    2. Public Stage (Proclaiming the Truth): Started with His saying: {Then declare what you are commanded} [Al-Hijr: 94]. Here, it moved to open conflict and enduring harm, while maintaining restraint from fighting.
  • Stages of Legislating Jihad (Wise Gradualism):
    1. Stage of Restraint (Patience): In Mecca, Muslims were tortured and killed (like the family of Yasir), and the Divine Command was: {Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands and establish prayer..."} [An-Nisa: 77]. Why? Because fighting at that stage meant "suicide" and extermination of the small believing group. The lesson: Wisdom sometimes requires patience and not being dragged into unequal battles that might end the Da'wah.
    2. Stage of Permission to Fight (Defense): After migration and establishing the state, permission came: {Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged.} [Al-Hajj: 39]. The Muslims now had an entity to defend itself.
    3. Stage of Fighting Those Who Fight You: {Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress.} [Al-Baqarah: 190].
    4. Stage of General Fighting (Empowerment and Removing Tyrants): To ensure freedom of Da'wah and lack of Fitnah (persecution): {And fight them until there is no fitnah and [until] the religion, all of it, is for Allah.} [Al-Anfal: 39].
  • Importance of Awareness of Stages: Understanding these stages makes the Muslim realize "Where do I stand now?" and what is the legitimate duty suitable for their reality? Are they in a stage of weakness requiring patience, preparation, and wise Da'wah? Or in a stage of empowerment requiring establishing limits (Hudud) and Jihad? This jurisprudence protects the youth from recklessness that harms the Ummah (rushing into confrontation prematurely), and also protects them from dilution and submission (canceling Jihad entirely under the pretext of tolerance). The Seerah puts everything in its place: "For every situation, there is a saying, and for every stage, there are men and actions."

Axis Four: Education and Nation Building (The Practical Methodology)

The Prophetic Biography is not just a record of military victories; in its essence, it is the greatest human experience in "Human Building" and "Social Engineering." The true miracle of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) was not only splitting the moon or water flowing from between his fingers, but it was in "Manufacturing the Unique Generation" that carried this religion. How did an unlettered man in a primitive tribal environment bring forth to humanity the greatest leaders history has known? And how did he build a state from nothing? This axis reveals the secrets of the Prophetic "Factory of Men."

First: The Industry of Men: From Shepherds to Leaders of Nations

When the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) was sent, the Arabs were a torn nation, having no weight among nations, the strong eating the weak, worshipping stones and trees. The "raw material" of humans existed, but it was lost in the darkness of Jahiliyyah. The Prophetic methodology came to reshape these personalities, not by erasing their identity, but by directing their energies towards the Truth.

  • Omar bin Al-Khattab (Transforming Strength): In Jahiliyyah, Omar was tyrannical and hard-hearted, to the point it was said: "If Al-Khattab's donkey embraced Islam, Omar would not." But the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) saw the latent "Leadership Energy" in him, so he prayed: "O Allah, strengthen Islam with one of these two men beloved to You..." When Omar embraced Islam, the Prophet did not ask him to abandon his strength to become a secluded dervish; rather, he employed that strength for Truth. He became "Al-Farooq" from whose path Satan flees, and who humiliated Khosrow and Caesar. The Seerah teaches us: Education is not suppressing energies, but directing them.
  • Abu Dharr Al-Ghifari (Refining Revolutionism): Abu Dharr (أبو ذر الغفاري) came from the tribe of Ghifar (highway robbers), carrying a sharp revolutionary soul. Islam refined him and made his revolution against falsehood and hoarding wealth. However, the Prophet directed him gently when he knew his nature, saying: "O Abu Dharr, indeed you are a man in whom is Jahiliyyah" (in the story of him shaming Bilal), and told him: "I see you are weak... do not lead two people" (Narrated by Muslim). The Seerah teaches us: Considering individual differences and placing every human in their appropriate place.
  • Mus'ab bin Umair (Sacrificing Luxury): He was "Mecca's pampered youth," wearing the most expensive clothes and wearing the most expensive perfumes. The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) made him "The First Ambassador in Islam." Mus'ab (مصعب بن عمير) left all luxury, migrated to Medina as a teacher, and died in Uhud wearing a Namirah (short piece of cloth); if they covered his head, his feet appeared. The Seerah teaches us: How the creed creates men who sell the fleeing world for the everlasting Hereafter.

Second: The Art of Da'wah and State Building (From Individual to Nation)

The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) did not begin by declaring the state immediately, but followed a gradual methodology and solid construction.

  • Individual Da'wah (The Secret of Change): The first focus was on "Selection." The Prophet did not rely on mass speeches in the beginning, but on "Individual Da'wah" (One-to-One). He was looking for "keys to hearts," sitting with Abu Bakr, Ali, and Uthman, one by one.
    • Dar Al-Arqam bin Abi Al-Arqam: It was the first "Educational Incubator." A closed university to intensify spiritual and educational doses away from the noise of Quraysh. Here, the "Solid Core" that would carry the entire structure later was manufactured. The lesson for us: Real change is not by noise, but by quiet, deep work in building individuals.
  • Political Wisdom in State Management (Constitution of Medina): When he migrated to Medina, he found a complex society (Muhajireen, Ansar, Aws, Khazraj, Jews, Polytheists, then Hypocrites). How did he manage this mix?
    • Brotherhood (Mu'akhaat): He dissolved class and tribal differences between Muhajireen and Ansar, creating a solid faithful "National Unity."
    • The Constitution of Medina (Al-Sahifah): He drafted the first civil constitution regulating relationships with non-Muslims (Jews), guaranteeing them freedom of belief, rights of citizenship, and the right of mutual defense, on the condition of no betrayal.
    • Dealing with Hypocrites: He dealt with them by the "apparent" and left their secrets to Allah, to preserve the cohesion of the internal front, saying: "Let the people not talk that Muhammad kills his companions." This is the peak of political wisdom in prioritizing higher interests.

Third: Effort and Giving: The Tax of Carrying the Message

The Seerah presents us the role model in "Selflessness" and "Sacrifice." The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) was not a pampered king ordering people from his palace; he was at the forefront in effort and fatigue.

  • A Life of Toil and Hardship: Allah says: {We have certainly created man into hardship.} The Prophet had the fullest share of this hardship. He lived his entire life in continuous Jihad; Da'wah by day, standing in prayer by night until his feet swelled, fighting enemies, patience with the harm of hypocrites, teaching the ignorant, and solving people's family and social problems.
  • "No More Distress for Your Father After Today": It is narrated that Lady Fatimah (فاطمة رضي الله عنها), when she saw her father (PBUH) in the throes of death, sweating profusely from intense pain, said with a burning heart: "Oh, the distress of my father!" He replied with a word summarizing his entire life: "There is no distress for your father after today" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari). Meaning: The time of fatigue, hardship, Jihad, hunger, and pain has ended. Today begins eternal rest with the Highest Companion. This phrase makes you feel the magnitude of the "Heavy Load" he carried on his shoulders for 23 years without resting a moment from the concern of the Ummah.
  • Message to the Generation: The Seerah says to every young person wanting to serve their religion: This religion did not reach us on a gold platter. Rather, the road was paved with the skulls of martyrs, the blood of the wounded, the tears of those praying at night, and the sweat of the Mujahideen. Do not think you will support the religion while reclining on your couch or by some posts on social media. The tax of empowerment is effort, and whoever wants rest leaves rest. As one of the predecessors said: "The bliss of the Hereafter is not attained by the bliss of this world."

Axis Five: Love and Glorification (The Heart Aspect)

After touring the intellectual, practical, and educational aspects of the Seerah, we arrive at the supreme goal and greatest fruit of studying the Seerah: "Heart Attachment." The Muslim's relationship with their Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) is not a dry "informational" relationship; it is a relationship of "Love and Infatuation," and a relationship of "Reverence and Glorification." Studying the Seerah is the fuel that ignites the flame of this love in the heart, for a servant's faith is not complete unless the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) is more beloved to him than his father, his child, and all people.

First: Increasing Love: The Path to Accompanying the Beloved

Love does not come from a void; it comes from knowledge. The rule says: "Whoever knows, loves." Many people claim to love the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم), but it is superficial emotional love because they ignore the details of his life and sacrifices.

  • The Seerah Generates Love: When you read how he used to weep in his prostration saying: "My Ummah, my Ummah," how his face was wounded for your sake, how he went hungry to feed his companions, and how he endured the harm of polytheists to deliver the Light to you; you cannot help but love him.
  • The Grand Prize (A Person is With Whom They Love): A Bedouin came to the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) asking about the Hour. The Prophet asked him: "And what have you prepared for it?" The Bedouin said spontaneously with love: "Nothing (meaning of much prayer or fasting), except that I love Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet (PBUH) gave him the glad tidings that made the Companions' hearts fly with joy: "You are with whom you loved." Anas bin Malik (أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه) comments: "We never rejoiced at anything as we rejoiced at the Prophet's saying: 'You are with whom you loved.' So I love the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Omar, and I hope to be with them because of my love for them, even if I did not work with deeds like theirs" (Agreed upon). Studying the Seerah is an "investment" in the Hereafter; every tear you shed in longing for him, and every feeling of love that stirs you while reading his stance, is a ticket to accompany him in Al-Firdaus Al-A'la (The Highest Paradise).

Second: Increasing Awe through Proximity: The Divine Secret in the Muhammadan Personality

It is human nature that "Awe drops with mixing." The closer you get to a great person (scholar, leader, manager), and see them in their daily life details (eating, sleeping, getting sick, getting angry), the halo of greatness fades, and you see human weakness and imperfection, and you might get bored of them. Except for one person in human history who broke this rule; it is Muhammad (صلى الله عليه وسلم).

  • The Closer You Get... The More Dazzled You Become: The Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) is the only one whom the closer you got to him, and viewed the secrets of his home and details of his sleep and wakefulness, the more you increased in love, glorification, and reverence for him. His wives (closest people to him) were the most intense in love and reverence for him. His servant Anas bin Malik, who lived with him for 10 years inside the house, conveys the minutest details while melting in love, saying: "I have never touched brocade or silk softer than the palm of the Messenger of Allah, nor did I smell musk or ambergris better than the scent of the Messenger of Allah" (Agreed upon).
  • Testimony of Enemies and Friends:
    • Amr bin Al-Aas (Before and After): He was the cunning man of the Arabs and one of the most hostile people to the Prophet. When he embraced Islam, he says on his deathbed describing the Prophet's status in his heart: "No one was more beloved to me than the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم), nor more majestic in my eyes than him. I could not bear to fill my eyes with him out of reverence for him, and if I were asked to describe him, I could not have done so because I did not fill my eyes with him" (Narrated by Muslim). The awe of love and reverence prevented him from staring, even though he lived with him and mixed with him.
    • Urwah bin Mas'ud Al-Thaqafi (Envoy of Quraysh): He returned to Quraysh after the negotiations of Hudaybiyyah astonished, saying: "O people, by Allah I have visited kings, and I visited Caesar, Khosrow, and Negus. By Allah, I have never seen a king whose companions glorify him as the companions of Muhammad glorify Muhammad" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari). This glorification was not out of fear or oppression, but was glorification of "Love and Ransom," such that they would not let his wudu water fall on the ground, seeking blessings from it.

Third: The Best of Allah’s Creation: Number (1) in the Universe

Human instinct is predisposed to love perfection and search for "The Best." When we talk about the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم), we are not talking about the "best leader" or "best reformer" only, but we are talking about the "Master of the Sons of Adam" and the "Best of Allah’s Creation" absolutely, among humans, Jinn, and Angels.

  • Human Perfection: Allah beautified His Prophet outwardly and inwardly, so he was "the most beautiful of people in face, and the best of them in character." Allah gathered in him all noble morals; he was the most truthful, the bravest, the most generous, and the most forbearing. Studying the Seerah is a journey to explore this "Absolute Beauty" that satisfies the soul's hunger for the perfect role model.
  • The World's Fascination with Him (Western Testimonies): This Muhammadan greatness was so bright that it forced fair-minded non-Muslims to bow in respect to it. They read the Seerah with abstract minds and were dazzled:
    • Michael H. Hart: In his book "The 100," he placed Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) as number (1) at the top of the list, saying: "My choice of Muhammad to lead the list of the world's most influential persons... he was the only man in history who was supremely successful on both the religious and secular levels."
    • George Bernard Shaw: Said: "The world is in dire need of a man with the mind of Muhammad... if he were to undertake the command of the modern world, he would succeed in solving its problems in a way that would bring it the much-needed peace and happiness."
    • Mahatma Gandhi: Said after reading the Seerah: "I wanted to know the best of one who holds today's undisputed sway over the hearts of millions of mankind... I became more than convinced that it was not the sword that won a place for Islam... It was the rigid simplicity, the utter self-effacement of the Prophet, the scrupulous regard for his pledges, his intense devotion to his friends and followers."
    • Leo Tolstoy: The Russian novelist, was dazzled by the sayings of the Prophet and his Sharia, seeing that they agree with reason and sound nature.

Summary: If these people (non-Muslims) glorified him just by reading about him, how about us, his followers and believers in him? Are we not more deserving of this love? Studying the Seerah is the only way to transform this "innate love" into "conscious love," and to fill our hearts and minds with his morals and attributes, so we live with him in this world by emulation and are gathered with him in the Hereafter by loyalty.

Conclusion: Sources of the Seerah and How to Start the Journey?

After this enjoyable tour of the reasons and importance of studying the Prophetic Biography, the most important practical question remains: "Where do I start? And what are the reliable sources from which I draw this knowledge?" The Islamic library abounds with thousands of volumes written about the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم), and this diversity might cause confusion for the beginner. Therefore, we will draw here a clear roadmap for sources, graded from the most authentic to the most comprehensive, and from the brief to the detailed, so that every seeker of truth can drink from this pure spring according to their determination and level.

First: Basic Sources (Origins)

One cannot understand the Seerah correctly without referring to the "First Sources" that documented the life of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) through Divine Revelation and authentic concurrent transmission.

  1. The Holy Quran (The First and Most Authentic Source): It is the "Record of Immortality" for Seerah events. The Quran did not narrate the Seerah as a sequential historical narrative but addressed its major junctures with analysis and guidance.
    • Examples: Surah (Ali 'Imran) is the most important reference for the Battle of Uhud, Surah (Al-Anfal) for the Battle of Badr, Surah (Al-Ahzab) for the Battle of the Trench and the Prophet's marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh, Surah (Al-Fath) for the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, Surah (At-Tawbah) for the Battle of Tabuk and exposing hypocrites, and Surah (Al-Hashr) for the Battle of Banu Nadir.
    • Value: The Quran gives you the "Divine Interpretation" of the event, reveals what is in the chests, and clarifies the lessons and Lordly morals that human historians do not perceive.
  2. The Prophetic Sunnah and Explanations of Hadith (Sahih and Sunan Books): It is the second source, detailing what the Quran summarized. Hadith books (like Sahih Al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawood, Al-Tirmidhi, and Al-Nasa'i) are full of complete books and chapters on "Maghazi" (Campaigns), "Siyar" (Biographies), "Jihad," and "Manaqib" (Virtues).
    • Explanations of Hadith: Like the book "Fath al-Bari Sharh Sahih Al-Bukhari" by Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar Al-Asqalani, and "Sharh Al-Nawawi on Sahih Muslim." These explanations are considered a strategic treasure because they collect narrations, verify chains of transmission, deduce jurisprudence from the event, and reconcile narrations that might seem contradictory.

Second: Specialized Books (Variety of Perspectives)

Over time, scholars specialized in specific aspects of the Prophet's life (PBUH), so different types of classification appeared:

  1. Books of Shamail Muhammadiyah (Characteristics): These books focus on "Description" not "Events." They describe his physical appearance (shape, height, skin color) and his character (forbearance, generosity, humility), and describe his daily life (how he eats, drinks, sleeps, laughs, dresses).
    • Most famous: The book "Al-Shamail Al-Muhammadiyah" by Imam Al-Tirmidhi. Reading this type of book breeds "Love" and psychological "Proximity," as you feel you are seeing the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) with your own eyes.
  2. Books of Dalail (Proofs of Prophethood): Focus on proving his Prophethood (PBUH) through sensory miracles (like water springing from his fingers, increasing food, weeping of the trunk), previous prophecies, and unseen news that came true.
    • Most famous: The book "Dalail Al-Nubuwwah" by Al-Bayhaqi, and "Dalail Al-Nubuwwah" by Abu Nu'aym Al-Asbahani. These books increase "Certainty" and stabilize the believer's heart.
  3. Books of Tabaqat and Biographies: Encyclopedic books translating the lives of Companions and Followers, usually starting with the biography of the Prophet (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم) as an introduction.
    • Most famous: The book "Al-Tabaqat Al-Kubra" by Ibn Sa'd, "Usd Al-Ghabah" by Ibn Al-Athir, and "Al-Isabah" by Ibn Hajar. These books are useful for knowing the biographies of the men made by the Prophet.
  4. Books of Maghazi and Siyar (Chronology of Events): These are concerned with the chronological sequence of events from birth to death, focusing on invasions and expeditions. The predecessors used to teach them to their children just as they taught them a Surah from the Quran.

Third: Proposed Reading Roadmap (Ladder of Progression)

So that the reader does not get distracted, we advise gradual reading based on scientific level and available time:

Level One: For Beginners (The Facilitated Entry)

For those who want to know the general structure of the Seerah, arranging events chronologically, in an easy and concise style without entering into the details of complex differences and narrations.

  • "Al-Khulasah Al-Bahiyyah fi Tartib Ahdath Al-Sirah Al-Nabawiyyah" (The Beautiful Summary in Arranging Events of the Prophetic Biography) by Sheikh Waheed Abdussalam Bali: An excellent book, consisting of specific points arranged historically (in the first year, such and such happened...). It gives you the "Skeleton" of the Seerah.
  • "Rawdat Al-Anwar fi Sirat Al-Nabi Al-Mukhtar" (The Garden of Lights in the Biography of the Chosen Prophet) by Safiur Rahman Mubarakpuri: It is a summary of his larger book "The Sealed Nectar," characterized by a modern easy style, presenting basic information in a focused manner.

Level Two: For Intermediates (Analytical Reading)

For those who want to expand a little, know details, and enjoy the literary style, with some scientific verification.

  • "Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum" (The Sealed Nectar) by Safiur Rahman Mubarakpuri: Perhaps the most famous contemporary book on Seerah, winner of the Muslim World League prize. It is characterized by historical accuracy, strong phrasing, and comprehensive presentation.
  • "Hadha Al-Habib Ya Muhib" (This is the Beloved, O Lover) by Sheikh Abu Bakr Al-Jazaery: A book characterized by "Spirituality" and touching preaching style. It focuses on provoking emotions and love, ending each chapter with a paragraph "What is learned from the Hadith," making it a first-class educational book. (One can combine it with The Sealed Nectar; the former for historical accuracy and the latter for the educational dose).

Level Three: For Advanced and Researchers (Deep Dive and Investigation)

For those who want to dive into depths, read original texts, and understand jurisprudential rulings deduced from the Seerah.

  • "Sirat Ibn Hisham" (Refinement of Ibn Ishaq's Seerah): It is the "Mother of Seerah Books." Ibn Ishaq is the Imam of Maghazi, and Ibn Hisham refined his book. The book is characterized by high Arabic language, poetry, and supported narrations. Reading it gives you the flavor of heritage and authenticity.
  • "Zad al-Ma'ad fi Hadyi Khayr al-'Ibad" (Provision of the Afterlife in the Guidance of the Best of Servants) by Ibn al-Qayyim al-Jawziyya: This is not just a Seerah book, but an encyclopedia in Fiqh (Jurisprudence), Prophetic Medicine, Creed, and Behavior, built upon the Seerah. Ibn al-Qayyim does not just narrate the event but extracts treasures of Fiqh and rulings (like Fiqh of divorce, sales, Jihad, medicine) based on the Prophet's action. It is a book for those who want to live the Prophetic "Methodology" in all their life affairs.
  • "Jawami' al-Sirah" by Ibn Hazm Al-Andalusi: A focused book characterized by Ibn Hazm's precise Zahiri style and his keenness on brevity without defect.

Finally:

Start from where you are, and do not postpone. Choose a book that suits you and start today. Make for yourself a daily portion (Wird) of the Seerah, even if only a few pages. Remember that you are not reading past history, but you are reading the "Operation Manual" for your life, and reading the story of the man who will take your hand—God willing—to cross the Sirat (Bridge) and enter Paradise. This journey will inevitably change you, so prepare for takeoff towards the sky of Prophethood.

Studying the Biography of the Prophet (PBUH): The Fourth Session

The State of the World Before the Muhammadan Mission (An Extensive and Detailed Explanation)

Expanded and Detailed Introduction

All praise is due to Allah Who created and proportioned, Who destined and guided, Who brought forth the pasture, and then made it dark stubble. All praise is due to Allah Who sent His messengers with clear proofs and guidance, to bring people out of darkness into light by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy. All praise is due to Allah Who sealed the messages with the message of His beloved and chosen one, our Prophet Muhammad (صلى الله عليه وسلم - Peace and blessings be upon him), a comprehensive and conclusive message, suitable for every time and place, guiding all of humanity to what brings صلاح (righteousness) and فلاح (success) in this world and the Hereafter. We send our prayers and peace upon this noble Prophet, his pure family, his excellent companions, and those who follow them in excellence until the Day of Judgment.

Dear respected brothers and sisters, we continue our blessed journey in the realm of the Seerah (biography) of the Chosen One (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH), a biography that is an inexhaustible source of wisdom and lessons, and a light by which we illuminate the paths of our lives. In this fourth session, we pause for reflection and contemplation before a decisive stage in human history, a stage that preceded the dawn of the Muhammadan prophethood. We will explore together the conditions of the world in that era, to realize the extent of the darkness that enveloped the corners of the earth, and the urgent need for the light of revelation to dispel these darknesses.

Understanding the historical, social, and religious context that preceded the mission of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH) is not merely an intellectual luxury or a display of information. Rather, it is a methodological necessity for understanding the depth of the Muhammadan message and realizing the magnitude of the change it brought about in people's lives. Just as a doctor does not diagnose a disease except after a careful examination of the patient, likewise, we cannot appreciate the value of the divine cure that Islam brought except after we become acquainted with the diseases that were ravaging human societies at that time.

In our previous session, dear loved ones, we delved into the lineage of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH), that noble lineage which is like a good tree, whose root is firm and its branches are in the sky. We explained how this lineage was not just a series of names, but reflected a prestigious social status, and clarified for us the complex map of tribal relations that governed Meccan and Arab society in general. Knowing these minute details, such as the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH) belonging to Banu Hashim (بنو هاشم), the relationship of Banu Hashim with the rest of the clans of Quraysh (قريش), and the relationship of Quraysh with other Arab tribes, all contribute to our understanding of many of the events and situations that accompanied the Islamic call. For example, when we talk about Abu Talib's (أبو طالب) protection of the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH), we realize that this protection was not merely an avuncular affection, but was also based on tribal customs that obligated the chief of the tribe to protect the members of his clan. When we reflect on the conflict that took place between the Muslims and Quraysh (قريش), we find that tribal affiliations played an important role in determining the loyalties of individuals and groups. The same applies when we study the events that followed the death of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH), such as the issue of the Caliphate and the conflicts that arose among the Companions; understanding the tribal structure helps us to analyze these events more deeply and objectively.

Transition to Today's Topic: The World on the Cusp of Transformation

After shedding light on the lineage of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH) and his status among his people, we move today, by the permission and guidance of Allah, to a panoramic exploration of the state of the world just before the moment Allah Almighty chose to send His final Prophet and Messenger. We will try to paint a comprehensive picture of the religious, moral, social, and economic reality that humanity was living in during that period, with a special focus on the Arabian Peninsula, as it is the land that Allah chose to be the cradle of the last heavenly messages. This review is not merely aimed at enumerating a list of vices and shortcomings. Rather, it is an attempt to understand the divine wisdom in choosing this time and place for the mission of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH), and to realize the magnitude of the challenges faced by the Islamic call in its beginnings, and the greatness manifested in Islam's ability to bring about this radical transformation in people's lives.

Key Concept: The Pre-Islamic World

This session explores the global conditions—religious, moral, social, and economic—especially in Arabia, before Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) mission, highlighting the need for divine guidance.

Quranic and Prophetic Depiction of the World Before Islam

The Quran and the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH) have depicted the state of the world before Islam in eloquent and impactful ways. Allah the Almighty says in His decisive Book, describing the state of the Arabs in particular:

"And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers. And you were on the edge of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may be guided." (Quran, Al 'Imran آل عمران: 103)

This noble verse depicts how they were on the brink of an abyss, about to fall into the fire of misery and destruction, had not the mercy of Allah reached them with the mission of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH).

As for the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH), he summarized this bitter reality for us in his noble Hadith, narrated by Imam Muslim from 'Iyad ibn Himar al-Mujashi'i (عيَاض بن حِمَار المُجَاشِعِي - May Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH) said one day in his sermon:

"Behold, my Lord commanded me to teach you what you were ignorant of, from what He taught me this day of mine... (until he said) And indeed, Allah looked at the people of the earth and despised them (مَقَتَهُمْ - maqatahum), their Arabs and their non-Arabs, except for remnants of the People of the Book..."

"Al-Maqt" (المقت) means the most severe hatred and wrath. This Hadith indicates that the anger of Allah Almighty had encompassed most of the people of the earth, their Arabs and their non-Arabs, due to their state of polytheism (الشرك - ash-Shirk), corruption, and deviation. Only a very few of the People of the Book were saved from this wrath, those who still adhered to remnants of the monotheistic religion (دين التوحيد - din at-Tawhid) brought by their prophets, even though their religion had also been subjected to much distortion and alteration.

Humanity, O brothers, was living in one of the darkest periods of its history. Noble human values had vanished or were on the verge of vanishing, and injustice, ignorance, and corruption had spread everywhere. There was no voice of truth to be heard, nor a beacon of guidance to be followed. The previous heavenly religions had been subjected to distortion and corruption, and had lost much of their original essence. Christianity, which Jesus (عيسى - 'Isa, peace be upon him) brought as a message of love, peace, and monotheism, had deviated from its course, and doctrines of the Trinity, worship of saints and images, had entered it, and it had moved away from the simplicity of monotheism to which Christ had called. Judaism, which Allah revealed to Moses (موسى - Musa, peace be upon him) as a law and guidance, had turned into a closed, racial religion, and its scholars and rabbis had distorted the words of Allah, and sold them for a paltry price. As for the rest of the nations, they had drowned in the mires of paganism, worshipping idols, planets, animals, and even humans.

Humanity yearned for a savior and looked forward to a light that would dispel this oppressive darkness. The human فطرة (fitrah - innate disposition), which Allah created upon monotheism, was suffering under the weight of this polytheism and misguidance. Thus, the mission of Prophet Muhammad (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH) was a response to this urgent need, and a mercy from Allah to the worlds.

The Conditions of the Arabs Before Islam: Detail and Expansion

Now, let us delve into the details of the conditions of the Arabs before Islam, to paint a clearer picture of the society that witnessed the dawn of prophethood.

First: The Economic Aspect and Prevailing Livelihoods (Detail and Analysis)

Economic life in the Arabian Peninsula, that vast land whose topography varies between arid deserts, towering mountains, and green oases, was characterized by diversity and contrast, but overall, it was a simple life, dependent on limited natural resources, and greatly affected by harsh climatic conditions.

Desert Dwellers and the Life of Pastoralism and Nomadism (The Dominant Lifestyle)

Bedouin pastoralists constituted the vast majority of the population of the Arabian Peninsula. Their lives revolved around herds of camels, sheep, and goats, which were their primary source of livelihood. Theirs was not a life of stability, but one of constant wandering, moving from place to place in search of "الربع" (ar-Raba' - areas of pasture and water) for their livestock. This lifestyle imposed upon them a certain harshness and toughness of character, and the ability to endure hardships and difficulties. They lived in simple tents made of goat hair or camel-hair, which were easy to transport, dismantle, and set up. Their food depended heavily on the milk and meat of their livestock, in addition to dates obtained from oases, and some wild plants that grew in the desert. They did not have organized agriculture, except in some scattered oases, nor did they have advanced industries; their industries were simple handicrafts to meet their daily needs, such as making tents, leather goods, and some simple weapons.

Trade among them was limited, confined to the exchange of some basic goods. This lifestyle, although it endowed them with some positive qualities such as courage, generosity, and patience, also made them live in a state of relative poverty and lack of many of the components of civilization and material progress. Their lives were subject to the vagaries of nature, such as drought and famine, and raids by other tribes.

Urban Centers and Trading Hubs: Mecca (مكة المكرمة) as an Economic and Religious Center (Case Study)

In contrast to the Bedouin life of nomadism, some cities and urban centers in the Arabian Peninsula witnessed a degree of stability and economic prosperity. The most prominent of these cities, undoubtedly, was Mecca (مكة المكرمة - Makkah al-Mukarramah). Mecca gained its economic importance from several factors:

  • Strategic Location: Mecca was located at the crossroads of ancient trade routes, connecting the south of the Arabian Peninsula (Yemen - اليمن and Abyssinia - الحبشة) with its north (the Levant - بلاد الشام, Persia - فارس, and Egypt - مصر). This location made it an important station for trade caravans and a transit point for various goods and commodities.
  • Religious Status (The Biggest Attraction): Mecca housed the Kaaba (الكعبة المشرفة - al-Ka'bah al-Musharrafah), the Sacred House of Allah, built by Abraham (إبراهيم - Ibrahim) and Ishmael (إسماعيل - Isma'il, peace be upon them). Despite the spread of paganism and idol worship, the Arabs still venerated the Kaaba and performed Hajj (pilgrimage) to it from various parts of the Peninsula. This annual religious influx represented an important commercial season for the people of Mecca, where they would set up markets, and buy and sell with the pilgrims and those performing 'Umrah (عمرة - lesser pilgrimage).
  • Organization of Trade (The Role of Banu Hashim - بنو هاشم): Some prominent figures from Quraysh (قريش) played an important role in organizing and expanding trade. Among the most prominent of these was Hashim ibn Abd Manaf (هاشم بن عبد مناف), the grandfather of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم - PBUH). Hashim was a man of insight and wisdom. He was the one who established the "الإيلاف" (al-Ilaf) for Quraysh, which involved concluding commercial treaties and pacts with tribes and kings of neighboring regions (like the Levant, Yemen, Abyssinia, and Persia) to secure the trade routes for Quraysh's caravans. He also organized the two famous trade journeys: the winter journey (رحلة الشتاء - rihlat ash-shita') which headed south to Yemen and Abyssinia, laden with goods brought from the Levant and Persia, and the summer journey (رحلة الصيف - rihlat as-saif) which headed north to the Levant, laden with products from Yemen and India. The Quran refers to these two journeys in Surah Quraysh (سورة قريش), reminding Quraysh of this great blessing:
    "For the accustomed security of Quraysh – Their accustomed security [in] the caravan of winter and summer – Let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them, [saving them] from hunger and made them safe, [saving them] from fear." (Quran, Quraysh قريش: 1-4)

These factors combined made Mecca a prosperous economic center and gave Quraysh (قريش) a prestigious position among the Arab tribes. They enjoyed security and stability in their sanctuary, while the rest of the regions lived in a state of chaos and turmoil. The Quran pointed to this blessing, saying:

"Have they not seen that We made [Makkah] a safe sanctuary, while people are being snatched away all around them? Then do they believe in falsehood and deny the favor of Allah?" (Quran, Al-'Ankabut العنكبوت: 67)
Yemen (اليمن) and its Vanished Agricultural Civilization (Reasons for Decline)

Yemen (اليمن), located in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, had a rich civilizational history and was known in ancient times as "Arabia Felix" (العربية السعيدة) for its fertile land, abundant water, and flourishing agriculture. The great Ma'rib Dam (سد مأرب - Sadd Ma'rib), considered one of the wonders of ancient engineering, played a vital role in irrigating vast areas of agricultural land, contributing to the establishment of an advanced and prosperous agricultural civilization. However, this prosperity did not last. The Ma'rib Dam (سد مأرب) suffered cracks and gradual collapse due to neglect, internal conflicts, and possibly other natural factors. This deterioration culminated in the "Flood of the 'Arim" (سيل العرم - Sayl al-'Arim), a massive flood that destroyed the dam, inundated agricultural lands, and led to significant economic and social decline in Yemen. The Quran narrates this incident in Surah Saba' (سورة سبأ) as a lesson and admonition for those who would take heed:

"There was for [the tribe of] Saba' in their dwelling place a sign: two [fields of] gardens on the right and on the left. [They were told], 'Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land [have you], and a forgiving Lord.' But they turned away [refusing], so We sent upon them the flood of the dam, and We replaced their two [fields of] gardens with gardens of bitter fruit, tamarisks and something of sparse lote trees. That We recompensed them for what they denied, and do We recompense except the ungrateful?" (Quran, Saba' سبأ: 15-17)

This catastrophic event led to the dispersal of the people of Yemen to various parts of the Arabian Peninsula and beyond, and the migration of many Yemeni tribes northward, weakening Yemen's economic and political strength.

Yathrib (يثرب - Medina المنورة) as an Agricultural Oasis (The Role of the Ansar - الأنصار)

Yathrib (يثرب), which later became the first capital of the Islamic state and Medina (المدينة المنورة - al-Madinah al-Munawwarah), was located in a fertile area north of Mecca. It was famous for its abundant water and fertile soil, making it an important agricultural oasis. Its people, especially the tribes of Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج) (later known as the Ansar - الأنصار), relied heavily on agriculture, particularly date palm cultivation, which was an important source of food and income. They also grew some grains and vegetables. The Ansar (الأنصار) were known for their skill in agriculture and were people of hard work and diligence.

Summary of the General Economic Situation

In general, it can be said that economic life in the Arabian Peninsula before Islam was characterized by stark contrasts. While some areas, such as Mecca (مكة), Yathrib (يثرب), and Yemen (اليمن) (in its prosperous eras), enjoyed a degree of stability and relative prosperity, the vast majority of the population, especially in the deserts, lived a harsh and difficult life, dependent on limited resources, and greatly affected by the fluctuations of nature. There was no unified currency; trade was conducted through barter or by using foreign currencies like the Persian Dirham (الدرهم الفارسي) and the Roman Dinar (الدينار الروماني). There were no developed financial or economic institutions. This fragile economic situation had its repercussions on social and moral life, as we shall see.

Recap: Economic Landscape

  • Bedouins: Pastoral nomadism, harsh life, limited trade.
  • Mecca: Trade hub (Ilaf, winter/summer caravans), religious center (Kaaba).
  • Yemen: Past agricultural glory (Ma'rib Dam), decline due to dam collapse.
  • Yathrib (Medina): Agricultural oasis (dates, grains), home to Aws & Khazraj.
  • Overall: Contrasting conditions, resource scarcity, lack of unified economy.

Second: The Social and Moral Aspect: A Mosaic of Contradictions (Detailed and In-depth Analysis)

The social and moral fabric in the pre-Islamic Arabian Peninsula was a complex mosaic, where the dark colors of vices and deviations intertwined with some bright glimmers of noble values and ethical virtues. Social life did not follow a single pattern but was influenced by many factors, such as the geographical environment, tribal structure, religious beliefs, and inherited customs and traditions.

The Most Prominent Social and Moral Vices that Were Rampant (Critical Analysis)

The Jahiliyyah (الجاهلية - pre-Islamic) society suffered from many social and moral diseases that led to its deterioration and decline. Among the most prominent of these vices were:

Spread of Prohibitions and the Trade of Vice (Reflection of a Spiritual Crisis)

Prohibitions were not just isolated individual practices but were often part of the prevailing culture. Wine (الخمر - al-Khamr) was drunk in their gatherings, they boasted about it, and held festivals for it. Much mention of wine and its gatherings is found in their poetry. The wine trade was thriving, and there were no restrictions to prevent it. Allah Almighty said, describing Islam's view of wine and gambling:

"O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful." (Quran, Al-Ma'idah المائدة: 90)

Gambling (الميسر - al-Maysir) was also a common practice. They would gamble on everything, sometimes even on themselves and their families. They saw it as a kind of generosity and munificence, as the winner in gambling would distribute his winnings to the poor and needy. However, Islam forbade gambling because it involved unjustly consuming people's wealth and led to enmity and hatred. Prostitution existed in various forms and was not condemned in all circles to the same degree. This reflects the extent of moral degradation the society had reached.

The Issue of Rebuilding the Kaaba and Illicit Money (Deep Implications)

The story of rebuilding the Kaaba (الكعبة), which we mentioned earlier, carries deep implications about the moral consciousness of Quraysh (قريش). Despite their veneration for the Kaaba, they were aware that much of their wealth was acquired through illicit means. This indicates a kind of duality in their moral standards. They venerated sacred things but, at the same time, did not hesitate to earn unlawful money. When they stipulated that only "طيب" (tayyib - pure/good) money should be used in building the Kaaba, this condition in itself reflects an implicit admission of the existence of "خبيث" (khabeeth - impure/evil) money in their possessions. When the pure money was insufficient to complete the building on the foundations of Abraham (إبراهيم), this reveals the extent of illicit money circulating among them. This incident, while indicating remnants of religious scruples, also exposes the pervasiveness of financial corruption in their lives.

Adultery (الزنا - az-Zina) and its Various Forms (Collapse of Family Values)

Adultery, in its various forms, represented a serious threat to family and social values. Books of Seerah (السيرة) and historical accounts mention several types of Nikah (النكاح - marriage) that were prevalent in Jahiliyyah (الجاهلية), which can only be described as forms of institutionalized or concealed adultery.

  • Taking Akhdan (الأخدان - Secret and Forbidden Relationships): This type of relationship was common, where a man would take a woman as his secret lover (خليلة - khaleelah), or a woman would take a man as her secret lover, without a legitimate marriage contract. These relationships were often conducted in secret, but were sometimes known. Islam forbade this type of relationship and considered it explicit adultery.
  • Nikah al-Istibda' (نكاح الاستبضاع - Seeking Offspring from Someone Other Than the Husband to Improve Lineage): This was one of the strangest and most heinous types of pre-Islamic "marriage." If a man wanted to have a child with certain qualities (like courage, generosity, or eloquence) that he did not find in himself, he would ask his wife to go to another man known for these qualities and ask him to have intercourse with her. If she conceived from him, her husband would stay away from her until she delivered, and then the child would be attributed to him. This type of "marriage" reflects a demeaning view of women, considering them mere vessels for procreation, and also reflects ignorance of the laws of heredity and a disregard for honor and chastity.
  • Public Prostitution (Nikah ar-Rayat - نكاح الرايات, and Brothels): Some women, especially slave girls or those without tribal protection, practiced prostitution openly. They would plant red flags (رايات - rayat) at their doors as a sign by which their houses were known. Men would come to them from all directions and satisfy their desires for a known fee. This indicates the extent of moral degradation the society had reached, where prostitution became a declared profession in some places.
  • Nikah ar-Raht (نكاح الرهط - A Group Sharing One Woman): This was another type of pre-Islamic "marriage" where a group (رهط - raht) of men, not exceeding ten, would all have intercourse with one woman. If she conceived and gave birth, she would send for all of them, and none could refuse. When they gathered, she would say: "You know what happened, and I have given birth. He is your son, O so-and-so," naming whomever she wished among them. Her child would then be attributed to him, and the man could not refuse.
  • Nikah al-Badal (نكاح البدل - Wife Swapping): This is when a man would say to another man: "Give up your wife to me, and I will give up my wife to you," and they would exchange wives. This is one of the ugliest forms of violating honor and confusing lineage.

These types of "marriage," and others, indicate the extent of sexual chaos that prevailed in pre-Islamic society, and the absence of moral and legal controls governing relations between men and women.

Female Infanticide (وأد البنات - Wa'd al-Banat - The Crime of Killing Innocence Due to Shame or Poverty)

The custom of female infanticide (وأد البنات) is considered one of the most heinous crimes known to humanity. This custom was widespread in some Arab tribes before Islam. If a man was given the news of the birth of a daughter, his face would darken, and his heart would fill with anxiety and grief. He saw the birth of a daughter as a shame and a deficiency. Some would bury their daughters alive, either for fear of the shame she might bring upon her family if she grew up and was captured or taken prisoner, or for fear of poverty and inability to provide for her. The Quran depicted this miserable psychological state experienced by some pre-Islamic fathers:

"And when one of them is informed of [the birth of] a female, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief. He hides himself from the people because of the ill of which he has been informed. Should he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they decide." (Quran, An-Nahl النحل: 58-59)

Islam came to eradicate this barbaric custom, to honor women, and to elevate their status. Allah Almighty threatened those who commit this crime with severe punishment, saying:

"And when the girl [who was] buried alive is asked, For what sin was she killed?" (Quran, At-Takwir التكوير: 8-9)
Killing Children for Fear of Poverty (الفقر والخوف من المستقبل - Poverty and Fear of the Future)

The crime of killing children was not limited to girls. Some Arabs would kill their children, whether male or female, for fear of poverty and inability to provide them with a livelihood. This reflects the extent of despair and despondency that controlled some souls, and lack of trust in Allah's provision and power. Islam forbade this crime and affirmed that Allah Almighty is the Provider, the Possessor of Power, the Strong, and that He has undertaken to provide for all creatures. Allah Almighty said:

"And do not kill your children out of poverty; We will provide for you and them." (Quran, Al-An'am الأنعام: 151)

And He also said:

"And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin." (Quran, Al-Isra' الإسراء: 31)
Contempt for Women and Denial of Their Basic Rights (A Demeaning View)

Women in pre-Islamic society suffered from a demeaning view and did not enjoy many of the rights that Islam granted them. They were considered inferior to men, and their opinions were often unheard.

  • Deprivation of Inheritance: Women were mostly deprived of inheritance, which was usually restricted to men capable of bearing arms and defending the tribe.
