And so it was; Ka'b bin Malik became one of the three "Poets of the Messenger" (along with Hassan bin Thabit [حسان بن ثابت] and Abdullah bin Rawahah [عبد الله بن رواحة]) who supported Islam with their tongues as they supported it with their swords.

Thus, the threads were integrated; a security plan utilizing the "license of hastening" and the chaos of the "Day of Departure" to secure the meeting, a "transient" place raising no suspicions, and preliminary meetings that "comforted hearts" and consolidated human relationships before political ones, so that everyone would be ready for the zero hour in the darkness of the night at Al-Aqaba.

Political Reliability and the Prestige of Negotiation: The Opening of Al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib

In that dark night, and when the assembly of Ansar was complete in the Ravine of Aqaba waiting for the arrival of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ appeared but was not alone. He was accompanied by only one man, a man who was not Muslim at that time, but followed the religion of his people: his uncle "Al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib" [العباس بن عبد المطلب]. Accompanying Al-Abbas was not merely family companionship; it was a political "masterstroke" and an extremely important diplomatic message sent by the Prophet ﷺ to the Ansar before beginning any negotiation.

First: The Paradox of Presence (The Polytheist Authenticating the Contract of Islam)

A question might come to mind: How does the Prophet ﷺ bring a polytheist man to the most dangerous secret meeting establishing the state of Islam? The answer lies in understanding the nature of Arab society at that time and understanding the "Jurisprudence of Seeking Assistance." Al-Abbas, although a disbeliever then, was:

  1. Head of Banu Hashim: Representing the tribal weight and family protection for the Prophet ﷺ.
  2. The Eye of the Prophet and His Protector: He loved his nephew immensely and saw his responsibility in protecting him and ensuring his future.
  3. The Guarantor and Authenticator: His presence gives the meeting a stamp of seriousness and documentation; the Ansar realize they are not negotiating with a homeless man, but with a man who has "backing" and a clan that fears for him and guarantees the agreement.

Second: Analyzing the Historical Speech (Exoneration and Raising the Ceiling)

The meeting began, and the first speaker was not the Prophet ﷺ, but Al-Abbas. Al-Abbas spoke with the tongue of the solicitous "guardian" and with the logic of the seasoned politician who wants to dot the i's and cross the t's. Al-Abbas said addressing the Ansar (whom he called Khazraj, generalizing):

"O assembly of Khazraj, indeed Muhammad is from us as you have known, and we have protected him from our people who are of the same opinion as us regarding him. He is in honor among his people and protection in his land. And he has refused but to side with you and join you..."

Analyzing the Speech Messages:

  1. Message of Dignity (We are not weak): Al-Abbas wanted to negate the description of "Political Refugee" or "Weak Fugitive" from the Prophet ﷺ. He told them clearly: Muhammad is not homeless; he is in "honor and protection," and we (Banu Hashim) protect him with our lives despite our difference with him in religion. So if he comes to you, he comes "by choice" not "by force," he comes as a "leader" not a "follower."
  2. Message of Testing (Filtering): Al-Abbas continued saying: "So if you see that you will be fulfilling to him what you have invited him to, and protecting him from those who oppose him, then you are responsible for what you have undertaken... But if you see that you will surrender him and betray him after he goes out to you, then leave him from now, for he is in honor and protection among his people and land." Al-Abbas placed the Ansar before a "real responsibility" and a terrifying one. He is telling them: This matter is not a picnic, nor just hosting a guest. It is war, enmity, and a heavy cost. If you will betray him at the first confrontation, or hand him over to his enemies when the battle intensifies, then leave him now while he is safe among us. This speech served as a "sieve" to filter intentions and ensure that these people fully realized the magnitude of the burden they were about to lift.

Third: The Jurisprudence of "Honoring the Elder" and Utilizing Social Prestige

One of the great educational and Da'wah lessons in this situation is how the Prophet ﷺ dealt with the "Elder" and the possessor of prestige, even if he was not on the same methodology or creed.

  1. Introduction and Respect: The Prophet ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah, and he is the obeyed leader, but in this council, he presented his uncle Al-Abbas to speak first. This presentation is an acknowledgment of the uncle's status, respect for age, and preservation of ranks. This refined Prophetic behavior "captured Al-Abbas's heart" and increased his love and respect for his nephew, making him feel he was a partner in the decision and not just a follower. The Lesson Learned: in Da'wah and reform work, elders (the father, grandfather, clan chief, manager) should not be marginalized on the pretext that they are "not committed" or "do not understand." Rather, they must be brought to the forefront in situations that require their prestige, and made to feel their value. A word spoken by a "social symbol" might open closed doors that a thousand speeches from an enthusiastic youth cannot open.
  2. Investing Zeal to Serve Religion: The Prophet ﷺ invested the "Jahiliyyah zeal" in Al-Abbas (zeal of lineage and tribe) and utilized it with precise Sharia utilization to serve the "protection of the Da'wah." Islam does not abolish tribal partisanships or family ties entirely, but refines them and directs them to be servants of the truth. As he ﷺ said: "The best of you in Jahiliyyah are the best of you in Islam if they comprehend." Social prestige, money, position, and connections are all "tools of power" that the caller must strive to win their people over, because supporting the religion requires "power" (Showkah) and immunity, not just texts and sermons.
  3. Relieving the Caller from the Embarrassment of "Asking Support for Himself": Al-Abbas's speech lifted the embarrassment from the Prophet ﷺ. Instead of the Prophet saying: "Protect me and support me," Al-Abbas said it with the tongue of power: "We protect him, so will you protect him?" This preserved the station of Prophethood and made the negotiations revolve between "peers" (Quraysh and the Ansar) regarding supporting the religion, which increased the prestige of the situation and the seriousness of the pledge.

Al-Abbas's opening was the "Political Document" that paved the way for the Religious Pledge and confirmed to the Ansar that they were about to conclude a historic deal in which there was no room for retreat or betrayal.

The Constitution of the Great Sacrifice: Clauses of the "Second Pledge of Aqaba" (The Pledge of War)

After Al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib finished his political speech putting dots on letters, the eyes of the Ansar turned with eagerness and longing to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying with the tongue of the stripped giver: "We have heard what you said, so speak, O Messenger of Allah, and take for yourself and for your Lord whatever you like." Here, the Prophet ﷺ pronounced the clauses of the "Historic Contract" that would change the face of the earth. They were not just conditions for joining a new religion, but a "constitution for building a fighting nation," and a solemn covenant accepting no half-measures. The pledge included five main clauses, concluding with the most dangerous clause that gave this pledge its historical title "The Pledge of War."

First: Hearing and Obedience (In Activity and Dislike)

The first clause is "Total Discipline." He ﷺ said: "You pledge allegiance to me on hearing and obeying in activity and laziness" (and in a narration: in ease and hardship/what you like and dislike). This clause addresses the human soul in its fluctuations. Humans by nature may be active for obedience and working for religion when matters are easy, psychological state is high, and conditions are favorable (activity). But the real test of loyalty lies in the "dislike" and "laziness"; when costs are heavy, resolve slackens, and orders contradict the desires of the self or the comfort of the body. The pledge here establishes a principle: Religion is not a "hobby" you practice in free time and good mood, but it is the "job of a lifetime" that you do not detach from even when you are in the most severe states of exhaustion or distress. It is a strict military commitment that cuts off the path to "selective religiosity" which takes from religion what agrees with its desire and leaves what is difficult for it.

Second: Spending (In Hardship and Ease)... Philosophy of "Financial Jihad"

The second clause, which is the nerve of state-building and the pillar of the call: "And on spending in hardship and ease." Here we pause long before a pivotal concept absent from the minds of many, which is that supporting religion does not stand on good intentions alone but needs "funding."

  1. Priority of Money in the Quran: Allah Almighty did not prioritize Jihad with wealth over Jihad with the self in the Quran in vain in most places, such as His saying: “And strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah” [At-Tawbah: 41]. Money is the nerve of equipment; it buys weapons, equips armies, sponsors callers, and builds institutions. A call cannot spread globally, nor can a state rise, without strong financial cover.
  2. The Test in "Hardship": Spending in "Ease" (when wealthy) is easy and manageable, and might be just "surplus money." But the real criterion for truthfulness is "spending in hardship"; meaning when resources narrow, income becomes scarce, and economic crises occur. In times of financial crises, humans instinctively tend to cut expenses, and the first thing usually sacrificed is "Allah's share" (charities and supporting Da'wah), keeping personal expenses and luxuries. The pledge comes to flip this equation: even in the severest states of hardship, religion must have a share of your money, even if little. This trains the soul that the "Da'wah share" is among the basic constants like food and drink, not a luxury item deleted upon deficit.
  3. Integration of Roles (The Businessman Da'i): This clause sends a message to every Muslim whom Allah provided with money but did not provide time for seeking knowledge or Da'wah with his tongue: You are not on the margin, but you are in the heart of the battle. Uthman bin Affan [عثمان بن عفان] may Allah be pleased with him, equipped the "Army of Hardship" with his money when the Muslims were unable, so he bought Paradise with his money, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Nothing Uthman does after today will harm him." Da'wah today needs sincere "financiers" who adopt Da'wah projects, sponsor students of knowledge, print books, establish media platforms, and support Muslim causes. This is the "Jihad of Money" that the Ansar pledged allegiance upon, and it is no less in reward than the Jihad of the word and the sword.

Third: Enjoining Good and Forbidding Evil

The third clause: "And on enjoining the good and forbidding the evil." Here the Prophet ﷺ moves the Muslim from the category of "Righteous" in himself, to the category of "Reformer" for others. The Muslim society is not a passive society where the individual says "myself, myself," but it is a morally mutually responsible society. This function is the safety valve preventing the destruction of the nation, and it is the feature by which this nation attained goodness: “You were the best nation produced for mankind, you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong” [Al Imran: 110]. The pledge here means you will be a guard of values, not accepting baseness in your religion, nor remaining silent about falsehood under the pretext of safety.

Fourth: Standing for Allah (Not Fearing the Blame of a Blamer)

The fourth clause: "And that you stand for Allah, not fearing in Allah the blame of a blamer." This clause is the "Shield of the Soul" against social and psychological pressures. The Ansar were approaching a step that would put them in confrontation with all Arabs, and they would be subjected to smear campaigns, mockery, boycott, and blame from near and far (How do you leave the religion of your fathers? How do you antagonize people for the sake of one man?). The Prophet ﷺ establishes here the personality of the "Solid Believer" who possesses complete psychological independence; he does not derive his value from people's satisfaction, nor does he shake at their anger. As long as he is on the truth, let people say what they wish. It is liberation from the "prison of others' looks" and from the "terror of social ostracism."

Fifth: Support and Prevention (The Condition of Blood)

The fifth and final clause, which is the substantial difference from the First Pledge of Aqaba: "And that you support me if I come to you, and prevent (protect) me from what you prevent (protect) yourselves, your wives, and your children from, and for you is Paradise." This is the crux of the matter. The Prophet ﷺ is not asking for ordinary "guest protection," but asking for "protection of cohesion and destiny."

  • Analogy of Protection: His saying "from what you prevent yourselves, your wives, and your children from" means desperate defense that has no ceiling. An Arab fights for his honor and child until death, and this is what is required in defending the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
  • Scope of Protection (In this stage): The agreement stipulated support "if I come to you," meaning protection is obligatory within the boundaries of Medina (defensive). This is what Sa'd bin Mu'adh [سعد بن معاذ] understood later in Badr when he wanted to expand the scope to include offense outside Medina, confirming that they transcended the literal text to the spirit of sacrifice.

The Hereafter Reward: "And for you is Paradise"

When they asked: "So what is for us for that, O Messenger of Allah, if we fulfill it?" He did not promise them the kingdom of Chosroes nor the treasures of the earth (though they came later), but said one word: "Paradise." They spread their hands and said: "Profitable is the sale, we will not cancel nor request cancellation." It was a clear deal: Blood, money, and toil in the world, and pure Paradise in the Hereafter. This is more profound in raising the founding generation on detachment and sincerity, far from worldly greed and temptations of power.

The Political Condition and the Eternal Covenant: "The Blood is the Blood... and the Destruction is the Destruction"

At the peak of faith-filled enthusiasm, and while hands were extending to pledge allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ, a wise rational voice emerged, a voice looking at "what is after the enthusiasm" and foreseeing the political outcomes of this deal. It is the voice of the great companion Abu al-Haytham bin al-Tayhan [أبو الهيثم بن التيهان] (and in other narrations As'ad bin Zurarah [أسعد بن زرارة]), who decided to pause the pledge ceremony for moments, to pose a fateful question guaranteeing the rights of the Ansar and the future of their city.

First: The Political Obsession (Will You Leave Us?)

Abu al-Haytham realized deeply that this pledge was not just a religious change, but a declaration of comprehensive "war." He said addressing the Prophet ﷺ clearly and frankly: "O Messenger of Allah, indeed between us and the men are ropes (treaties), and we are cutting them - meaning the Jews -, so would you perhaps, if we did that, then Allah granted you victory, return to your people and leave us?"

Analyzing the Intervention:

  1. Cost of Decision: Abu al-Haytham clarifies that the Ansar will sacrifice their old alliances (ropes), especially with the Jews of Medina, and with the polytheist Arabs. This means total political and economic isolation for the city.
  2. Fears of the Future: The question was very legitimate: "We will sacrifice everything now and shelter you while you are weak, but if Allah grants you victory tomorrow, and Mecca is opened, will zeal for your people and clan take you, and you return to live among them as a king, leaving us in Medina having antagonized the Arabs and Jews for your sake?" The Ansar feared being just a "transitional phase" or a "bridge" used for empowerment then dispensed with.

Second: The Decisive Prophetic Response (Charter of Common Destiny)

Upon hearing this legitimate fear, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled, the smile of the loyal leader who appreciates the sacrifices of his men, and replied with words immortalized by history, which became a constitution for the relationship between the Muhajireen and the Ansar. He ﷺ said: "Nay, the Blood is the Blood, and the Destruction is the Destruction (Al-Hadm Al-Hadm)... I am of you and you are of me, I fight whom you fight, and I make peace with whom you make peace."

Significance of the Prophetic Slogan:

  1. The Blood is the Blood: Meaning my blood is mixed with your blood, so my blood is sought with your blood, and your blood will not be shed while I am safe. It is also said to mean: The shedding of blood is one, so whoever sheds your blood has shed mine.
  2. Al-Hadm Al-Hadm (The Destruction is the Destruction): (And in a narration: Al-Ladm Al-Ladm), meaning: My grave is your grave, and my honor is your honor. Meaning: I will live with you, and I will die where you die, and I will be buried in your land.
  3. Complete Fusion (I am of you and you are of me): With this declaration, the Prophet ﷺ dropped considerations of "Meccan Citizenship" and "Qurayshi Tribalism," and announced his complete integration into the Ansari fabric. He was no longer a guest, but became one of them, his destiny linked to theirs forever.

Third: Fulfilling the Covenant (Day of Opening Mecca)

These words were not just momentary reassurance, but a covenant fulfilled by the Prophet ﷺ literally. Eight years later, when Allah opened Mecca for him, and Quraysh submitted to him, and the Arabs surrendered, and the Ansar saw the Prophet ﷺ circumambulating the Kaaba surrounded by his family and clan, the old fear crept into their hearts. They whispered among themselves saying: "Do you see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, now that Allah has opened for him his land and city, that he will stay there?" The news reached the Prophet ﷺ while he was supplicating on Safa, so he finished his supplication and said to them: "God forbid! The life is your life, and the death is your death." So the Ansar wept, and apologized saying: "We only said that out of stinginess (possessiveness) for Allah and His Messenger" (meaning out of love and holding on). Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ returned to Medina, lived in it as a ruler, died in it, and was buried in its soil, in fulfillment of the Pledge of Aqaba, and confirming his saying "The Destruction is the Destruction."

Fourth: Declaration of World War (The Red and The Black)

In the context of emphasizing the danger of the pledge, and clarifying the meaning of "cutting the ropes," the Prophet ﷺ and the Ansar confirmed a terrifying strategic truth: that this pledge means antagonizing "The Red and The Black."

  • The Red and The Black: A metaphor for "Non-Arabs and Arabs," or "Jinn and Mankind," or "People of white and black skin."
  • Meaning: You are not antagonizing Quraysh only, but declaring a challenge to the entire world, to the superpowers (Persians and Romans) and to all Arab tribes. This total clarity in the "Sacrifice Invoice" before contracting is the peak of leadership integrity. The Prophet ﷺ did not deceive them with rosy promises, nor did he hide from them the size of the enemies, but placed them before the full picture: "If you are content, then you are the allies of Allah, and if you fear, then leave me from now."

This moment was the moment of the true birth of political and doctrinal "Loyalty and Disavowal"; loyalty to Allah, His Messenger, and the nascent State of Islam, and disavowal of every alliance and interest contradicting this religion, whatever the price, and however numerous the fronts of enmity.

Filtering the Ranks and Testing Truthfulness: The Last Moments Before the Handshake

While hearts were craning to extend hands, and souls yearing to conclude the deal with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Second Pledge of Aqaba witnessed an exceptional scene of "Harsh Frankness" and "Total Disclosure" of dangers. The leaders of the Ansar and their wise men did not want the matter to be done in a moment of emotional enthusiasm whose flame might fade at the first shock, but wanted the covenant to be built on "penetrating insight" and deep realization of the consequences of the stance. Two men from the best of Ansar took up this task: Al-Abbas bin Ubadah bin Nadlah [العباس بن عبادة بن نضلة] and As'ad bin Zurarah [أسعد بن زرارة].

First: Intervention of Al-Abbas bin Ubadah... Dotting the letters of "Death"

While the people were about to pledge allegiance, "Al-Abbas bin Ubadah" (an Ansari, not to be confused with Al-Abbas the Prophet's uncle) stood up and took hold of the conversation to stop the emotional rush and turn it into a strict mental decision. He said directing his speech to his people with a firm, booming voice: "O assembly of Khazraj, do you know upon what you are pledging allegiance to this man?" They said: Yes. He said: "Indeed you are pledging allegiance to him on warring against the Red and the Black of people..." Then he placed them before "two options" with no third, to cut off the line of retreat for any hesitant one:

  1. The First Option (Option to Withdraw Now): "So if you see that if your wealth is exhausted by calamity, and your nobles are killed, you will surrender him... then from now; for it is, by Allah, disgrace in this world and the Hereafter." Here Al-Abbas places them before the worst-case scenario: You will lose your money, and your masters and elders will be killed. If you will retreat upon the occurrence of these calamities, then leave him now. Withdrawal now is a "decision," but surrender later is "treason" and indelible shame.
  2. The Second Option (Option of Challenge and Fulfillment): "But if you see that you will fulfill to him what you have invited him to despite the exhaustion of wealth and killing of nobles, then take him... for he is, by Allah, the best of this world and the Hereafter."

The Collective Response of the Ansar: The people did not hesitate for a moment, but responded with one voice shaking Al-Aqaba: "We take him despite the calamity of wealth and the killing of nobles... So what is for us for that, O Messenger of Allah, if we fulfill it?" He ﷺ said one word: "Paradise." They said: "Extend your hand." This dialogue embodies the meaning of His saying Almighty: “Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties [in exchange] for that they will have Paradise” [At-Tawbah: 111]. The pledge here was not for worldly victory and empowerment, but was for "Death and Loss of Wealth" in exchange for "Paradise."

Second: The Final Warning... The Grip of "As'ad bin Zurarah"

After Al-Abbas bin Ubadah's speech, the Prophet ﷺ extended his hand, and people raced towards him. Here another situation occurred to ensure "documenting the contract." "As'ad bin Zurarah" (the youngest of the Nuqaba in age and the first of them to become Muslim, and Mus'ab's host) stood up and took the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to stop people from shaking hands temporarily. As'ad said: "Gently, O people of Yathrib... We did not beat the livers of camels (travel long distances) to him except knowing that he is the Messenger of Allah, and that bringing him out today is parting from all Arabs, and the killing of your best, and that swords bite you... So either you are patient on that, then take him and your reward is upon Allah, or you fear for yourselves a fear, then leave him, for it is more excusable for you with Allah."

Analyzing As'ad's Position:

  1. Severity of Documentation: As'ad was not hesitant, far from it, but he wanted "Exoneration before Allah." He wanted to hear from them the "Public Commitment" once again after hearing the details of terror (parting from Arabs, biting of swords, killing of best).
  2. Testing Insight: As'ad reminds them that they did not come for a picnic, but crossed deserts (beat the livers of camels) to die for this religion. He moves them from the jurisprudence of "Dervishism" to the jurisprudence of "Jihad."

Third: Decisive Insistence (We Will Not Cancel Nor Request Cancellation)

The people clamored and said to As'ad bin Zurarah with the enthusiasm of the certain: "Remove your hand, O As'ad... For by Allah, we will not leave this pledge, nor will we request its cancellation (Istiqala)."

  • We will not leave it: We will not leave it of our own accord.
  • Nor request cancellation: We will not ask the Prophet ﷺ to release us from it or cancel it. It is an eternal contract with no annulment or return.

Fourth: The First to Shake Hands with the Prophet ﷺ

Narrators and historians differed on "who was the first to strike the hand of the Prophet ﷺ" pledging allegiance that night. The most likely in the Seerah narrations is that it was: As'ad bin Zurarah [أسعد بن زرارة] may Allah be pleased with him. So after he was reassured of his people's resolve and heard their insistence, he was the first initiator to shake hands, to have the honor of "The Preceder of the Ansar" just as he had the honor of "The first of them to become Muslim" and "Mus'ab's first host." (It was also said that the first to pledge was Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur [البراء بن معرور] because he was the sheikh of the people and their elder).

Educational Lessons from Moments of Testing:

  1. Transparency in Leadership: The successful leader does not deceive his followers nor decorate the path with roses, but confronts them with thorns before fruits. Clarity in presenting "Costs" sorts the metals of men, keeping only the truthful.
  2. Importance of "Review" before "Signing": Stopping for a moment before making fateful decisions is not hesitation, but praiseworthy "verification." This is what Al-Abbas and As'ad did; stopped the torrent of emotion to ensure the presence of the mind.
  3. The Criterion is Endings and Steadfastness: A great lesson the Ansar learned: enthusiastic beginnings count for nothing if endings are betrayal. Therefore, the entire focus was on: "What will you do if wealth is exhausted and nobles are killed?".

With this difficult test, and decisive answers, the pillars of the pledge were completed, and the Ansar became "Supporters" (Ansar) in word and deed, before drawing a single sword, because they settled themselves on death in the way of Allah.

From Chaos to Organization: Establishing the "Council of Nuqaba" and Structuring the Nascent State

After the pledge was completed, and the storm of inflamed emotions calmed, the Prophet ﷺ moved immediately from the role of "The Caller" (Da'i) to the role of "Statesman and Administrative Leader." He realized with his supreme wisdom that enthusiasm alone does not build states, and that large crowds (73 men) if left without clear leadership and administrative reference, would turn into chaos, especially in a complex tribal society like Yathrib. Therefore, the next step was "Administrative Structuring."

First: The Prophetic Order for Organization (Bring Out to Me Captains)

In those critical moments of the night, and before the council dispersed, the Prophet ﷺ issued a decisive organizational order to the Ansar: "Bring out to me from among you twelve captains (Nuqaba), to be over their people regarding their affairs."

Significance of this Directive:

  1. Representative Representation: The Prophet ﷺ did not appoint the captains himself (although he knew them and their merit), but asked the Ansar to "bring them out" from among themselves. This is an early application of the principle of "Shura" and "Election." The leader chosen by his people is more obeyed by them and has stronger influence over them.
  2. Solidarity Responsibility (Sponsorship/Kafala): The Prophet ﷺ defined their tasks precisely saying: "You are guarantors (Kufala') over your people regarding their affairs like the sponsorship of the Disciples to Jesus son of Mary, and I am a guarantor over my people." The task of the Captain (Naqib) is not "Honorary," but it is "Sponsorship"; meaning total responsibility for following up with members of his tribe, ensuring their adherence to the pledge terms, solving their problems, and representing them before the Supreme Command (the Prophet ﷺ).

Second: Fair Demographic Distribution (9 Khazraj and 3 Aws)

The selection of the twelve captains came to accurately reflect the "Population and Tribal Map" of Medina, and respect the sensitive balances between Aws and Khazraj: Number of Captains: 12 Captains. Distribution: 9 from Khazraj, and 3 from Aws. This distribution was not bias, but fair because the Khazraj were the overwhelming majority in the city and in the pledge delegation, while the Aws were the minority.

Names of the Nuqaba (The First Shadow Government): These twelve are the ones who led the great transformation process in Medina, and managed the affairs of Muslims secretly and openly until the Hijrah:

Captains of Khazraj (The Nine):

  1. As'ad bin Zurarah (Banu Najjar) [أسعد بن زرارة]: The first of them to become Muslim, Mus'ab's host, and head of the Nuqaba.
  2. Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi' (Banu Al-Harith) [سعد بن الربيع]: Who was later martyred in Uhud.
  3. Abdullah bin Rawahah (Banu Al-Harith) [عبد الله بن رواحة]: The Mujahid poet.
  4. Rafi' bin Malik (Banu Zurayq) [رافع بن مالك]: The first to write the Quran in Medina.
  5. Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur (Banu Salmah) [البراء بن معرور]: Their master and sheikh.
  6. Abdullah bin Amr bin Haram (Banu Salmah) [عبد الله بن عمرو بن حرام]: Father of Jabir, and the first martyr in Uhud.
  7. Ubadah bin As-Samit (Banu Ghanm) [عبادة بن الصامت]: The jurist and commander.
  8. Sa'd bin Ubadah (Banu Sa'idah) [سعد بن عبادة]: Master of Khazraj and the banner holder.
  9. Al-Mundhir bin Amr (Banu Sa'idah) [المنذر بن عمرو]: Nicknamed "The one hastening to die" for his extreme daring.

Captains of Aws (The Three):

  1. Usayd bin Hudayr (Banu Abdul-Ashhal) [أُسيد بن حضير]: Master of his people and the one with the stance with Mus'ab.
  2. Sa'd bin Khaythamah (Banu Amr bin Awf) [سعد بن خيثمة]: Later hosted the Prophet ﷺ in Quba.
  3. Rifa'ah bin Abdul-Mundhir (Banu Amr bin Awf) [رفاعة بن عبد المنذر]: (And in a narration: Abu al-Haytham bin al-Tayhan [أبو الهيثم بن التيهان]).

Third: Philosophy of "Organized Work" and Necessity of Administration in Da'wah

This Prophetic procedure (appointing Nuqaba) presents a pivotal lesson for reformist and Da'wah movements in every age: "Randomness is the graveyard of calls." It is not enough to have loyal followers, and it is not enough to possess the truth, but you must possess "The System."

  1. Administrative Decentralization: The Prophet ﷺ did not confine all decisions to his hand, but distributed tasks. Each captain is responsible for a "cell" or "group," following up with them, teaching them, and organizing their financial (collecting charities and expenses) and military (equipment) affairs. This creates flexibility in movement and speed in execution.
  2. Specialization and Division of Roles: Working for religion is not just "preaching." Building a state needs specializations: People responsible for "Youth and Cubs." People responsible for "Money and Zakat" (Funding Da'wah). People responsible for "Social Aspect" and caring for families. People responsible for "Planning and Protection." This distribution of roles done by the Prophet ﷺ is what made the society of Medina transition smoothly from "warring tribes" to a "state of institutions" immediately upon his arrival.
  3. Middle Leadership (The Link): The Nuqaba were the "Middle Leadership" connecting the base (general Ansar) and the Supreme Command (the Prophet ﷺ). The existence of this link guarantees the arrival of directives accurately, guarantees raising problems realistically, and prevents disconnection between the leader and his soldiers.

Fourth: The Practical Result of this Organization

Thanks to this tight administrative structure: The Hajj season and return to Medina were managed with order and discipline, without the polytheists discovering their affair. Money was collected and houses prepared to receive the Muhajireen later. The city became prepared "administratively" and not just "doctrinally" to receive the Prophetic government.

In conclusion, appointing Nuqaba was not a formal procedure, but an announcement of the birth of "Islamic Organization" that respects specialization, appreciates responsibility, adopts Shura, and realizes that supporting religion needs "planning and institutional work" as much as it needs sincerity and supplication. “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power” [Al-Anfal: 60], and organization is one of the greatest causes of power.

Revealing the Secret and the Pursuit: The Scream of Satan and the Ordeal of Sa'd bin Ubadah

After the pledge was completed in the pitch-black darkness, and covenants and charters were documented between the Prophet ﷺ and the Ansar, and the twelve captains were chosen, and while the gathering was preparing to disperse and return to their saddles before dawn broke and exposed their affair, a sudden event occurred that almost stormed everything arranged, were it not for the care of Allah and His strengthening of His Prophet and the believers.

1. The Scream of "Azabb al-Aqaba" and Prophetic Steadfastness

In those critical moments, and while the Prophet ﷺ was directing the Ansar to return to their tents quietly, one of the devils discovered this secret meeting. This observer was not a human, but a devil from the devils of Al-Aqaba, who ascended a high place (heights overlooking Mina) and screamed at the top of his voice to let the sleeping pilgrims in Mina hear, saying words carrying incitement and threat: "O people of the dwellings (Al-Jabajib - meaning tents in Mina), do you have concern for Muzammam (Dispraised - meaning Muhammad ﷺ, dispraising him) and the Renegades (Sabi'ah) with him? They have gathered to wage war against you."

It was a terrifying voice in the stillness of the night, and a desperate attempt by Iblis and his soldiers to spoil this faith alliance that would demolish the strongholds of Shirk. Here the steadfastness of the Prophet ﷺ was manifested; he did not get confused nor panic, but turned to the source of the voice and said with confidence and certainty: ((This is Azabb al-Aqaba [أزب العقبة], listen, by Allah, O enemy of Allah, I will surely free myself for you)). "Azabb al-Aqaba" is a devil named "Azabb," or it is said to be a name for a snake or devil inhabiting that area. The Prophet's ﷺ threat to him contained a great Prophetic indication; his saying "I will surely free myself for you" means that this pledge will be completed, Islam will rise, the state will be built, and the Prophet ﷺ will devote himself to fighting Satan and his party and defeating them, which actually happened. Then the Prophet ﷺ ordered the Ansar to leave immediately saying: ((Disperse to your saddles)), meaning return to your places quickly and scatter.

2. Zeal of Al-Abbas bin Ubadah and Balance of Power

Upon hearing this threat and the exposure of the matter, the faith zeal of the Ansar erupted. Al-Abbas bin Ubadah bin Nadlah [العباس بن عبادة بن نضلة] the Ansari - who is different from Al-Abbas the Prophet's uncle - stood up and said with a tone of total readiness for sacrifice and immediate confrontation: "O Messenger of Allah, by the One who sent you with the truth, if you wish, we will surely fall upon the people of Mina tomorrow with our swords." They offered the Prophet ﷺ to start fighting immediately the next morning against the masses of polytheists in Mina. But the Prophet ﷺ, the wise commander who weighs matters with the scale of Revelation not the scale of abstract emotion, replied to them saying: ((We have not been commanded to do that)). Permission for fighting had not descended yet, and the balance of material power was not in favor of the Muslims then; fighting a battle with 73 men against thousands of Arab pilgrims gathered in Mina meant the eradication of the believing group before it started. Therefore, the order to return and lay low was the most appropriate strategy for that stage.

3. Diplomatic Investigation and Divine Intervention

News reached Quraysh in the morning, creating a state of alert. A large delegation of Quraysh leaders, armed and angry, headed to the camps of the people of Yathrib (Medina). With political intelligence, they did not go to the common people, but intended the "Big Head," Abdullah bin Ubayy ibn Salul [عبد الله بن أبي ابن سلول], the Khazraj leader groomed for kingship. They said to him and the polytheist leaders of Yathrib sharply: "O assembly of Khazraj, it has reached us that you came to this companion of ours to extract him from among us, and pledge allegiance to him on warring against us. And by Allah, there is no tribe of Arabs more hateful to us that war should break out between us and them than you."

Here Allah's planning worked in favor of the believers; Abdullah bin Ubayy ibn Salul stood up swearing by Allah in ignorance and total innocence: "This is false! And this did not happen, and my people would not overstep me with such a thing (meaning they don't decide without me), and if I were in Yathrib, my people would not have done this until they consulted me." Ibn Salul was truthful in his denial because he knew nothing, and the Muslims from the Ansar were looking at each other not uttering a word, while the polytheists of Medina confirmed to Quraysh the innocence of their arena. Quraysh was convinced by Ibn Salul's words; for it is unreasonable for a momentous matter like this to happen without their leader's knowledge, so they returned disappointed.

4. The Pursuit and Capture of Sa'd bin Ubadah

The Ansar caravan departed returning to Medina, but after they left, Quraysh confirmed the validity of the news through their spies or other clues, knowing they were deceived. They went mad and went out in a fast pursuit of the Ansar caravan hoping to catch one of them. The caravan had moved away, but Quraysh managed to catch two of the Captains who lagged behind a little or were at the rear of the caravan: Al-Mundhir bin Amr [المنذر بن عمرو] and Sa'd bin Ubadah [سعد بن عبادة]. As for Al-Mundhir, he baffled the people and escaped from them. As for Sa'd bin Ubadah may Allah be pleased with him - the master of Khazraj and owner of generosity - they caught him.

Scene of Torture and Ordeal: Quraysh dealt with Sa'd bin Ubadah with brutality unbecoming of his status as a tribal leader, indicating the extent of their rage. They tied his hands to his neck with the rope of his saddle, and began beating him and dragging him by his long hair until they entered him into Mecca. The situation was humiliating and severe, for the fools of Mecca gathered around him punching and beating him, while he was alone among them with no helper at that moment.

5. Survival thanks to "Common Interests" (Jurisprudence of Weakness)

While Sa'd was in this distress, a man from Quraysh (said to be Abu al-Bakhtari bin Hisham) came to him and whispered advising: "Woe to you! Is there no protection or covenant between you and anyone from Quraysh?" Sa'd remembered at that moment the trade relations and mutual interests. Sa'd shouted: "Yes, I used to protect the trade of Jubayr bin Mut'im bin Adi [جبير بن مطعم بن عدي], and prevent those who wanted to wrong them in my land, and likewise for Al-Harith bin Harb bin Umayyah [الحارث بن حرب بن أمية]." Sa'd bin Ubadah was the one securing the caravans of these two men when passing through Medina territories heading to the Levant, protecting them from bandits. So the man went quickly and called out in Quraysh: Indeed the man has protection with Jubayr bin Mut'im and Al-Harith bin Harb. So the two men came quickly and rescued Sa'd from the hands of the fools, saying: "He spoke the truth, by Allah he surely protects our trade and defends us."

Lessons Learned from this Situation:

  1. Importance of Secrecy: The success of the pledge relied entirely on secrecy, and even when the matter was exposed, the ignorance of the polytheist leadership (Ibn Salul) contributed to misleading the enemy.
  2. Investing Intersecting Interests: Sa'd bin Ubadah's survival was not by a supernatural miracle, but thanks to worldly (commercial) relations he established in Jahiliyyah. This teaches us that the Muslim and the caller must have presence, benefit, and influence in society, and that human and commercial relations can be a shield protecting the Da'wah in times of weakness.
  3. Sacrifice for Leaders: Sa'd, being the master of his people, was subjected to beating and humiliation, illustrating that the tax of Da'wah is paid by the seniors before the juniors, and leaders before soldiers.
  4. Verification and Self-Control: Despite Al-Abbas bin Ubadah's enthusiasm for fighting, the Prophetic leadership controlled the emotion according to legal and realistic interest (We have not been commanded to do that), which preserved the believing bloc from early annihilation.

Thus, Sa'd bin Ubadah returned to the Ansar caravan, and everyone arrived in Medina safe, folding the page of the Second Pledge of Aqaba with brilliant success, starting the stage of actual establishment for the Hijrah and state-building.

Conclusion: On Defining Manhood and Establishing the State (The Lesson from the Second Pledge of Aqaba)

In conclusion, and after reviewing the events of the Second Pledge of Aqaba in all its details, we stand contemplating those historic moments that drew the features of building the Islamic State, extracting from them a practical definition of manhood, and emphasizing the importance of commitment and steadfastness in supporting the truth.

1. Landmarks of Manhood in Pledge Situations

Manhood in this biography is not just a word or claim, but actions embodied in practical situations, summarized in:

  • Truthfulness in Speech and Covenant: Truthfulness was manifested in the Ansar's commitment to what they covenanted to the Prophet ﷺ, declaring they would defend him with all they possessed. The Almighty said: “Among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah. Among them is he who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is he who awaits, and they did not alter [the terms] by any alteration” [Al-Ahzab: 23].
  • Fulfilling the Promise and Steadfastness in Position: The Ansar did not waver before threats, nor retreat from their covenant, but remained firm on their position despite difficulties, and this is true loyalty. The Almighty said: “And fulfill the covenant. Indeed, the covenant will be questioned” [Al-Isra: 34].
  • Bearing Consequences and Sacrifice in the Way of Allah: Manhood was embodied in the Ansar's readiness to sacrifice their wealth and lives for the sake of Allah. The Almighty said: “The believers are only the ones who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then doubt not but strive with their properties and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is those who are the truthful” [Al-Hujurat: 15].
  • Altruism and Support: The Ansar preferred supporting the Prophet ﷺ over themselves and their families, and this is the peak of faith. The Almighty said: “And give preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful” [Al-Hashr: 9].
  • Insight and Awareness of the Future: When Abu al-Haytham bin al-Tayhan asked about their fate if Allah granted victory to the Prophet ﷺ in Mecca, the Ansar showed awareness of responsibility and realization of consequences, indicating that true manhood combines courage with good planning.

2. Manhood of the Ansar Facing Contemporary "Softness"

In this era where concepts are mixed, and standards of manhood have changed, the Ansar model stands out as a counter-model to all manifestations of "softness" (Muyo'ah) dominating society. Manhood is not in external appearance or fake adornment, but in: Adherence to Values. Giving and Sacrifice. Courage in Truth. Solidity Facing Falsehood. Endurance and Patience.

3. The Second Pledge of Aqaba and Building the Islamic State

The Second Pledge of Aqaba was the official declaration of the establishment of the State of Islam in Medina. Thanks to this pledge, the Prophet ﷺ and his companions moved from Mecca to Medina and began building an integrated Islamic society. The Islamic State was established on solid foundations, which are:

  • Belief in Allah and Pure Monotheism: “And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth, and to establish prayer and to give zakah. And that is the correct religion” [Al-Bayyinah: 5].
  • Justice and Equality: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded” [An-Nahl: 90].
  • Brotherhood and Love: “The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your brothers. And fear Allah that you may receive mercy” [Al-Hujurat: 10].
  • Shura and Cooperation: “And their affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves” [Ash-Shura: 38].
  • Enjoining Good and Forbidding Evil: “You were the best nation produced for mankind, you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong and believe in Allah” [Al Imran: 110].

The Second Pledge of Aqaba is a lesson in history, and a light illuminating the path for us in every time and place. It is a call to hold on to values, work with seriousness and diligence, and sacrifice for the sake of Allah, so that we may be worthy of achieving victory and empowerment. Following the footsteps of the Ansar, we march towards building a strong Islamic society capable of facing challenges and achieving good and justice for all. O Allah, make us among the people of faith, truthfulness, and loyalty, and guide us to what You love and are pleased with. Amen.

The Price of Faith and the Plot of Tyrants: From the Tragedies of Migration to the Conspiracy of Dar Al-Nadwa

First Element: The Decision to Migrate... Sacrificing Homeland and Safety

With the end of the Hajj season and the conclusion of the "Solemn Covenant" (Al-Mithaq Al-Ghaliz) with Al-Ansar (الأنصار), the page of passive patience in Mecca turned, and a new phase in the history of Islam began: the phase of building and establishment. As soon as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was reassured of the existence of a "Helper and Backer," and that in Yathrib (يثرب) there were hearts that had pledged allegiance to die for him, and homes opened to receive his religion, the Prophet’s general and concise permission was issued to the noble Companions: ((God Almighty has made for you brothers and a home where you will be safe)). In another narration, he specified the destination accurately, saying: ((I have been shown the land of your migration, a land of palm trees between two lava fields—the two Harrahs—)), and so it was Yathrib (يثرب).

1. The Philosophy of Migration: Not a Picnic, but a Detachment from Life

The decision to migrate (Hijrah) was not merely a geographical move from one city to another; rather, it was a painful process of "amputation," an uprooting from the land where one was born and grew old. The word "Hijrah" in the language carries the meaning of leaving and cutting off. The Companions had to translate this meaning into reality by leaving their homelands, their wealth, the homes they were accustomed to, and the memories of their childhood and youth.

Leaving one's homeland is akin to the parting of the soul. God Almighty paired killing oneself with leaving one’s home in His Book due to their difficulty on the human soul, saying: {And if We had decreed upon them, "Kill yourselves" or "Leave your homes," they would not have done it, except for a few of them} [An-Nisa: 66]. Therefore, the divine command to migrate was a test of the sincerity of faith, a sieve to distinguish the bad from the good, for no one could endure it except those who sold their worldly life for their Hereafter.

2. Mecca vs. Medina: The Paradox of the Known and the Unknown

The difficulty of the decision doubles when we realize the nature of the two places (the place being left and the destination):

  • Mecca (The Abode of Safety and Tranquility): It is God’s sanctuary, the birthplace, and the neighborhood of the Honorable Kaaba. Leaving it meant leaving spiritual and social security, and abandoning status and prestige among the Arabs. Even the Prophet ﷺ, the most steadfast of creation at heart, stood at Al-Hazwarah (الحزورة) bidding farewell to Mecca, his voice overcome with tears, saying: ((By Allah, you are the best of Allah’s earth, and the most beloved of Allah’s earth to me. Had your people not expelled me from you, I would not have left)) [Narrated by Al-Tirmidhi]. So how was it for the general Companions?
  • Yathrib (The Land of Epidemic): At that time, Medina was not the lush oasis we know today through the blessing of the Prophet’s ﷺ prayer. Instead, it was known as a "plagued" land, ravaged by the "Fever of Yathrib," which was proverbial among the Arabs for its severity. Migrating to it meant walking toward disease and the unknown, in addition to leaving stable livelihoods and profitable trade in Mecca to go to an agricultural society with a different lifestyle and economy.

3. The Certainty That Conquered the Impossible

Despite these immense psychological and material challenges, and despite the lack of a clear logistical plan for each individual guaranteeing housing or livelihood in Medina, the response was immediate and astounding. The Muslim community in Mecca turned into beehives working silently to arrange their departure.

No one asked about "future guarantees," nor did anyone say, "How will I live?" or "What will I do with my money and house?" They moved driven only by "Certainty" (Yaqeen), confirming God’s description of them: {For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and [His] approval and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful} [Al-Hashr: 8]. God named them "The Truthful" (Al-Sadiqoon) because their actions matched their words.

The Companions began to slip away in "waves" (small successive groups) under the cover of darkness, hiding from Quraish (قريش), leaving everything behind, carrying nothing but their religion and what was light to carry, relying on the Ever-Living who does not die. None held back from this blessed caravan except three categories:

  1. A Hypocrite: Faith had not mixed with the joy of his heart, so he preferred his worldly life.
  2. Incapable (Oppressed): Confined by illness or coercion. God excused these in His Book: {Except for the oppressed among men, women, and children who cannot devise a plan nor are they directed to a way} [An-Nisa: 98].
  3. Tempted (Maftoon): Those whose resolve weakened before the pressures of family and wealth, becoming a trial for them.

This migration was a practical declaration of the birth of a generation that knew no hesitation in God’s command, a generation ready to pay the "invoice of faith" in full, no matter how high the price.

Second Element: Models of Great Sacrifices... Stories Written in Pain and Light

The Migration was not merely lines written in history books, but human epics that make the skin crawl, where faith was placed in one scale and the entire world in another, and the scale of faith tipped the balance. The Immigrants (Muhajirun) presented amazing practical models of the concept of the "tax of faith." Here we review three stories that became icons of patience, detachment, and facing emotional blackmail.

1. The Tragedy of Abu Salama’s Family: Torn Limbs and Noble Adversaries

The story of Abu Salama (أبو سلمة) and his wife Umm Salama (أم سلمة) (Hind bint Abi Umayya) is a living embodiment of the human tragedy caused by the cruelty of Quraish (قريش) and tribal fanaticism. Abu Salama (أبو سلمة) was the first to decide to migrate with his family to Medina, a year before the Second Pledge of Aqaba. He loaded his wife and their child, Salama (سلمة), onto a camel and set off.

  • The Bloody Scene (Tearing the Family Apart): As soon as men from Banu al-Mughira (بني المغيرة) (the wife's tribe) saw them, they blocked their path and said to Abu Salama (أبو سلمة): "You have overcome us regarding yourself, but what about this companion of ours (your wife)? Why should we leave you to travel with her across the lands?" They snatched the camel's rein from his hand and took his wife by force. When Banu Abd al-Asad (بني عبد الأسد) (the husband's tribe) saw this, they got angry out of tribal pride for their son, not to support him but to dispute. They said: "We will not leave our son with her since you have snatched her from our companion." They pulled the small child, Salama (سلمة), between his mother and his father's tribe until they dislocated his arm, and the father's kin snatched him away. In a single moment, the family was scattered in three places: The husband fled with his religion to Medina alone, the wife was imprisoned by her family, heartbroken, and the child with the dislocated arm was a captive of his father's clan.
  • The Year of Grief at Al-Abtah (الأبطح): Umm Salama (أم سلمة) did not surrender to despair. She used to go out every morning to Al-Abtah (الأبطح) (a place in Mecca), sit, and weep over the separation from her husband and son until evening came. She remained in this state for nearly a full year until a man from her cousins passed by her and felt pity for her condition. He said to Banu al-Mughira (بني المغيرة): "Will you not release this poor woman? You have separated her from her husband and her son." So they allowed her to join her husband, and Banu Abd al-Asad (بني عبد الأسد) returned her son to her.
  • A Stance of Chivalry (Uthman ibn Talha): Umm Salama (أم سلمة) went out alone, crossing the desert with her child, without a companion or protector, heading for Medina. At the area of At-Tan'im (التنعيم), she met Uthman ibn Talha (عثمان بن طلحة) (who was then a polytheist and a custodian of the Kaaba). When he learned she was a lone migrant, the Arab chivalry and knightly honor stirred within him. He said: "By Allah, you have no one to leave you like this," and he took her camel's rein and set off to escort her to Medina. Umm Salama (أم سلمة) described his nobility saying: "I have never accompanied a man from the Arabs more generous than him; when he reached a stopping place, he would make my camel kneel, then withdraw from me (out of modesty). Once I dismounted, he would unload the camel, tie it to a tree, and move away to lie down under a tree... He continued to do this for me until he brought me to Medina." This situation establishes a profound moral lesson: Good character and chivalry can exist in souls even before Islam, and a Muslim acknowledges the favor of its people even if they differ in belief.

2. Suhayb Al-Rumi: The Deal of a Lifetime and the Profitable Sale

As for Suhayb ibn Sinan Al-Rumi (صهيب بن سنان الرومي), his tragedy and sacrifice were of a different kind; it was the trial of "Wealth." Suhayb (صهيب) had come to Mecca as a destitute pauper, then was blessed in trade until he became one of its wealthy men.

  • The Vile Bargain: When Suhayb (صهيب) intended to migrate, the disbelievers of Quraish (قريش) noticed him. They surrounded him and said with the language of material blackmail: "You came to us as a despicable pauper, then your wealth increased among us, and you reached the status you have reached, and now you want to leave with your money and yourself? By Allah, that shall not be." The choice was clear: Either wealth and remaining in disbelief, or poverty and salvation with religion.
  • Complete Detachment: Suhayb (صهيب) did not hesitate for a moment. Instead, he said to them with a confident heart: "What if I give you my money, will you let me go?" They said: "Yes." So he guided them to all his hidden treasures and gave up the toil of his lifetime in exchange for being left to flee with his religion. He left Mecca owning nothing but the clothes on his back, but he carried in his heart the richness of certainty.
  • The Prophetic Medal: Upon his arrival at the outskirts of Medina (Quba - قباء), the Prophet ﷺ saw him, his face beaming with joy, and welcomed him with the eternal glad tidings before Suhayb (صهيب) could utter a word: ((The sale has profited, O Abu Yahya... The sale has profited, O Abu Yahya)). Regarding this, Allah’s saying was revealed, immortalizing his mention: {And of the people is he who sells himself, seeking means to the approval of Allah. And Allah is kind to [His] servants} [Al-Baqarah: 207]. Suhayb (صهيب) taught us that money is a means, not an end, and that what is with Allah is better and more enduring.

3. Ayash ibn Abi Rabiah: The Trap of Affection and the Plots of Tyrants

The story of Ayash ibn Abi Rabiah (عياش بن أبي ربيعة) represents a strategic warning to every believer against "emotional blackmail" that families might use to divert their children from the path of truth. Ayash (عياش) had already succeeded in migrating with Umar ibn Al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) and they arrived in Medina, but Quraish (قريش) did not let their prey escape easily.

  • Abu Jahl’s Diabolical Plan: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham (أبو جهل بن هشام) and Al-Harith ibn Hisham (الحارث بن هشام) (who were his half-brothers from his mother) caught up with him in Medina. They did not come with weapons, but with the weapon of inverted "filial piety." They said to him: "Your mother has vowed not to let a comb touch her head until she sees you, nor to seek shade from the sun until she sees you." They played on the strings of overflowing emotion and the tenderness of Ayash’s (عياش) heart towards his mother.
  • Umar’s Insight and Warning: Umar ibn Al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب)—with his customary intuition—realized it was a trick. He advised and warned Ayash (عياش): "O Ayash, by Allah, your people only want to seduce you away from your religion, so beware of them; for by Allah, if lice were to annoy your mother she would comb her hair, and if the heat of Mecca became intense for her, she would seek shade." Umar (عمر) tried to awaken the voice of reason and realism in him and offered him his own she-camel (Umar's noble and docile camel) to flee on if he suspected anything from them. However, Ayash’s (عياش) emotion overcame his reason, and he decided to return to fulfill his mother's oath and retrieve his money.
  • Treachery and Imprisonment: On the way, the two brothers executed their vile plan; Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) claimed his camel was exhausted and asked Ayash (عياش) to carry him behind him. As soon as Ayash (عياش) dismounted, they pounced on him, bound him tightly, and entered Mecca with him in broad daylight, shouting: "O people of Mecca, do with your fools as we have done with this fool of ours." Ayash (عياش) was imprisoned and tortured for many years, and the Prophet ﷺ used to pray for him by name in his prayer (Qunut) saying: ((O Allah, save Ayash ibn Abi Rabiah, O Allah, save Salama ibn Hisham, O Allah, save Al-Walid ibn Al-Walid, O Allah, save the oppressed among the believers)) [Agreed Upon].

These three stories provide us with a clear map of the nature of the conflict: Sacrifice of family (Umm Salama), sacrifice of wealth (Suhayb), and caution against the exploitation of emotions (Ayash). It is the tax of the road paid by the first generation, which paved the way for the establishment of the state.

Third Element: Quraish’s Strategic Shift... From "Crisis Containment" to "War of Existence"

The sight of empty houses in Mecca, abandoned by their Muslim owners, was not just a passing event in the eyes of the leaders of Quraish (قريش); rather, it was an omen of doom and a beating of the drums of imminent danger. The Qurayshi political mind realized, in a moment of belated awakening, that what was happening was not merely "fleeing from torture" as was the case with the migration to Abyssinia, but rather a "strategic repositioning" aimed at building a parallel entity that threatened their sovereignty.

Here, a radical shift occurred in Quraish’s (قريش) combat and security doctrine, moving from a strategy of "persecution and containment" to a strategy of "eradication and physical liquidation," due to several fundamental considerations:

1. Yathrib is not Abyssinia: The Equation of Geography and Politics

Quraish (قريش) dealt with the migration to Abyssinia with relative coldness; the Negus (Al-Najashi) was a king with no ambition to invade Mecca, and Abyssinia lay across the sea, making the Muslims there isolated "exiles" who posed no direct military threat. However, Yathrib (يثرب) (Medina) was completely different:

  • Fighting Manpower: Yathrib (يثرب) was home to the tribes of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج), people of might and war, whose history in the "Day of Bu'ath" bore witness to their bloodiness and bravery. The transformation of these fighters into an "ideological army" under the command of Muhammad ﷺ meant the birth of a striking military force in the Arabian Peninsula that Quraish (قريش) could not match.
  • Political Independence: The Muslims in Medina would not be "refugees" as in Abyssinia, but "owners of the land" and decision-makers, in the process of establishing a "state" with its own system and law independent of Jahiliyyah customs.

2. The Economic Nightmare: Control over the "Lifeline"

Perhaps the most dangerous thing that kept the stalwarts of Quraish (قريش) awake was the geographical location of Medina. Mecca was a valley without cultivation, having no life except through trade, specifically the winter and summer journeys mentioned in the Holy Quran: {For the accustomed security of the Quraish - Their accustomed security [in] the caravan of winter and summer} [Quraish: 1-2].

  • The Road to Al-Sham (Levant): Medina is located on the eastern flank of the trade caravan route heading from Mecca to Al-Sham. This road was traversed by Quraish’s (قريش) caravans loaded with their wealth (their annual investments estimated at 250,000 gold dinars).
  • Threat of Blockade: Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) and Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف) realized that the Prophet’s ﷺ settlement in Medina meant possessing the ability to cut off this road and impose a suffocating "economic blockade" on Mecca. This was no longer just a religious conflict over idols, but turned into a struggle for "daily bread" and economic survival.

3. Failure of Traditional Solutions and Exhaustion of Options

Quraish (قريش) reviewed its record of dealing with the Call (Da'wah) over thirteen years and found that all its old tools had failed miserably:

  • Torture: Only increased the believers' firmness, and here they are migrating and leaving their wealth for the sake of their religion.
  • Economic Blockade (She'b Abi Talib): Failed, the siege was lifted, and the Muslims emerged stronger.
  • Bargains and Temptations: Rejected by the Prophet ﷺ entirely.
  • Media Distortion: Did not prevent Islam from entering the homes of Arabs and visitors during the seasons.

Quraish (قريش) had exhausted its balance of "soft solutions" and "limited repressive solutions." They became certain that the survival of the "Head" (the Prophet ﷺ) meant the body would continue to grow and move.

4. The Dangerous Decision: Targeting the "Leadership" Before Joining the "Base"

Quraish’s (قريش) spies and eyes noticed that the migration was happening in an organized manner, and that Mecca was almost emptying of Muslims, but the "Leader" Muhammad ﷺ, along with his two ministers Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) and Ali (علي), still remained. Quraish (قريش) understood the message: The Prophet ﷺ was the "rearguard" securing the exit of the soldiers, and he was preparing to join them. Here, the diabolical idea jumped into their minds: "The head must be separated from the body."

If Muhammad ﷺ succeeded in leaving and reaching his army in Medina, the matter would be settled, and the gates of hell would open upon Quraish (قريش). But if the Leader was "removed" now, while he was still alone without an army in Mecca, the danger would vanish, the immigrants in Medina would return to being a scattered group without a shepherd, and Yathrib (يثرب) would revert to its civil wars. This precise strategic analysis of the situation is what drove Quraish (قريش) to call for the "Emergency Meeting" at Dar Al-Nadwa (دار الندوة). It was not a meeting for ordinary consultation, but a "war room" to make the decision for a "knockout preemptive strike." They decided to cross all red lines and violate the sanctity of Hashemite blood because they saw in the survival of the Prophet ﷺ the end of their glory, authority, and trade. Thus, the atmosphere was set for the ominous day, the day of plotting to assassinate the Mercy to the Worlds, thinking they were capable of extinguishing the light of God with their mouths and swords.

Fourth Element: The Parliament of Evil... The Meeting at Dar Al-Nadwa and the Grand Conspiracy

On the morning of Thursday, the 26th of Safar in the 14th year of Prophethood (corresponding to September 12, 622 AD), Mecca witnessed unusual movement. It was not the movement of trade or pilgrimage, but the movement of the "Heads of Polytheism" heading towards Dar Al-Nadwa (دار الندوة), that political landmark established by Qusai ibn Kilab (قصي بن كلاب) to be the consultative council of Quraish (قريش), which was only opened for grave matters affecting the tribe's security and future. The call for the meeting carried the nature of "absolute secrecy" and "extreme urgency," and the goal was one: "What shall we do with Muhammad?"

1. The Attendees: An Alliance of Human and Jinn Devils

The political, military, and economic leaders of Mecca gathered in that hall, representatives from all clans of Quraish (قريش) (except Banu Hashim). Among the most prominent attendees were:

  • Abu Jahl ibn Hisham (أبو جهل بن هشام) (Representative of Banu Makhzum, and the head of disbelief).
  • Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (أبو سفيان بن حرب), and Utbah and Shaybah, sons of Rabiah (Representatives of Banu Abd Shams).
  • Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف) (Representative of Banu Jumah).
  • Al-Nadr ibn Al-Harith (النضر بن الحارث) (Representative of Banu Abd al-Dar).
  • Abu Al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham (أبو البختري بن هشام) (Representative of Banu Asad).
  • And other leaders of the people.

The Mysterious Guest (The Sheikh from Najd): As they were about to enter, they were intercepted at the door by a dignified old man wearing a heavy woolen garment (Hulla Habara), appearing to have the marks of prestige and experience. They asked him: "Who is the Sheikh?" He said: ((A Sheikh from the people of Najd, who heard of what you have gathered for, so he attended with you to hear what you say, and perhaps you will not lack an opinion and advice from him)). They allowed him to enter, thinking he was a wise Arab who came for consultation, not realizing they had admitted "Iblis" (Satan) in human form. Satan refused but to attend this decisive moment himself, to ensure that the decision issued would be bloody and decisive enough to eliminate the Divine Light.

2. Deliberations and Rejected Proposals (The Sinful Brainstorming Session)

The group opened the session by presenting the problem: "This man has done what you have seen, and by Allah, we do not feel safe from him leaping upon us with those who have followed him from other than us, so agree upon an opinion regarding him." Suggestions began to roll in, and "The Sheikh from Najd" was the arbiter refuting the opinions:

  • First Proposal: Exile and Expulsion: Abu Al-Aswad (أبو الأسود) (or another attendee) said: "Let us expel him from among us and banish him from our lands, and we care not where he goes or where he lands. If he is gone from us, our affairs will be set right, and our unity will return."
    Response of the Sheikh from Najd (Iblis): He objected immediately and strongly, saying: "No, by Allah, this is not a sound opinion for you! Have you not seen the beauty of his speech, the sweetness of his logic, and his dominance over the hearts of men with what he brings? By Allah, if you do that, you will not be safe from him settling among a tribe of Arabs, winning them over with his speech, then marching with them against you until he tramples you in your homes and takes your command from your hands."
    (The rejection here was based on political analysis: The charismatic leadership of the Prophet ﷺ would turn any exile he went to into a military base that would turn against Mecca).
  • Second Proposal: Life Imprisonment (Restraint/Al-Ithbat): Abu Al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham (أبو البختري بن هشام) said: "Imprison him in irons, lock a door upon him, and wait for him to meet the fate of the poets before him (like Zuhayr and Al-Nabigha) until death comes to him." Meaning a slow death in prison.
    Response of the Sheikh from Najd (Iblis): He ridiculed this opinion saying: "No, by Allah, this is not a sound opinion for you! By Allah, if you imprison him, news of him will escape from behind the door to his companions. They would soon leap upon you to snatch him from your hands, then outnumber you with him until they overcome you in your command."
    (Security Analysis: The immense love the Companions bore for their Prophet would make them storm Mecca to liberate him, meaning an internal civil war).

3. The Diabolical Plan (The Final Solution)

After all traditional solutions (Exile and Prison) fell, the group asked for the opinion of Abu Jahl (أبو جهل), who was saving his proposal for the end. The Pharaoh of this Ummah uttered a plan that had never occurred to the Arabs before, a plan that broke all tribal norms and sanctities of blood. Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) said: "By Allah, I have an opinion regarding him that I do not see you have touched upon yet." They said: "And what is it, O Abu Al-Hakam?" He said: ((I see that we take from every tribe a young, strong, noble, and mediating man among us. Then we give each young man among them a sharp sword. Then they should aim for him and strike him as one man and kill him, so we will be relieved of him. If they do that, his blood will be dispersed among all the tribes, and Banu Abd Manaf will not be able to war against all their people, so they will accept the blood money (Diyah) from us, and we will pay it to them)).

Analysis of the Plan:

  1. Collective Responsibility: involving a representative from every tribe makes the crime "societal" not "individual," which paralyzes Banu Hashim (بني هاشم) (the Prophet’s clan); they cannot fight all the Arabs to take revenge.
  2. Financial Solution: Forcing Banu Hashim (بني هاشم) to accept "Blood Money" in exchange for blood, thus closing the file of revenge and the Call forever.
  3. Immediate Execution: The simultaneous collective attack (strike of one man) ensures the target does not survive.

Here, the Sheikh from Najd (Iblis) shouted with overwhelming joy: ((The saying is what the man said; this is the opinion to which there is no other)).

4. Quranic Documentation of the Conspiracy

The council dispersed upon this sinful decision, and each leader returned to prepare the "youth of his tribe" to carry out the assassination that very night. While they thought they were weaving the conspiracy in closed rooms heard by no one, the Lord of Might was recording their plotting from above seven heavens, and revealed regarding that a Quran recited until the Hour, exposing the details of the meeting with amazing accuracy.

God Almighty says: {And [remember, O Muhammad], when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you or kill you or evict you. But they plan, and Allah plans. And Allah is the best of planners} [Al-Anfal: 30].

  • To restrain you: This is the proposal of imprisonment (Ithbat means confinement and binding).
  • Or kill you: This is Abu Jahl’s (أبو جهل) proposal which they adopted.
  • Or evict you: This is the proposal of exile.

The "Parliament of Evil" was planning to end Islam, not realizing that by this decision they had signed their own destruction warrant, and that God’s plan was faster and wiser. Gabriel (Jibreel), peace be upon him, descended with revelation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informing him of the details of the conspiracy and ordering him to migrate immediately, saying: ((Do not spend this night in your bed where you used to sleep)). Thus, the night of treachery they intended as an end for the Prophet ﷺ turned into the night of the launch of light and the building of the state that later crushed their thrones.

Fifth Element: The Divine Plot and Prophetic Arrangement... The Night of Migration and the Making of the Miracle

While Dar Al-Nadwa (دار الندوة) was buzzing with the noise of the conspiracy, and the "youth of Quraish" were sharpening their swords in preparation to spill noble blood, revelation was descending in the House of Prophethood, calm and decisive, to rearrange the cards of the game according to the Divine Will. It was not merely an "escape" from murder, but the inauguration of a journey to change the world, a journey prepared by the Heavens, with threads woven on Earth with extreme precision.

1. The Decisive Revelation: (Do not sleep in your bed this night)

Gabriel (Jibreel), peace be upon him, came down with the certain news: The people have agreed to kill you tonight. The divine command came clearly: ((Do not spend this night in your bed where you used to sleep)). This directive carried two implications: First, the necessity of hastening to leave before the security cordon tightened. Second, the necessity of using "camouflage"; the command not to sleep in the bed implicitly suggests that the bed must remain occupied by someone else so the killers think he is still sleeping. Here, divine planning (Revelation) met human planning (taking measures) in the most magnificent form.

2. The Mysterious Noon Visit... (Emergency Protocol)

Lady Aisha (عائشة), may Allah be pleased with her, narrates the details of these decisive moments with extreme precision in Sahih Al-Bukhari. She says: "While we were sitting in Abu Bakr’s (أبو بكر) house in the midday heat, someone said to Abu Bakr: 'This is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ masked, at an hour he did not used to come to us.'"

  • Timing of the Visit: The Prophet ﷺ chose the time of "Noon" (Zahr - nap time and intense heat), when the streets of Mecca are empty of pedestrians, and eyes are asleep, providing security cover for movement without being detected.
  • Appearance (Masking): He came "masked" (Mutaqanni'an), covering his head and part of his face with the edge of his garment, to increase concealment and camouflage, so no one would recognize him from afar.
  • Al-Siddiq’s Reaction: Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) was alarmed by this unusual visit and realized with his security sense that there was a grave matter. He said: "May my father and mother be sacrificed for him; by Allah, nothing brought him at this hour except a matter."

3. The Secret Planning Meeting (Send out who is with you)

The Prophet ﷺ entered Abu Bakr’s (أبو بكر) house and did not start speaking immediately, but asked to secure the place first. He said to Abu Bakr (أبو بكر): ((Send out who is with you)). Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) said reassuringly: "They are only your family, O Messenger of Allah" (referring to his daughters Aisha and Asma). This reflects the absolute trust Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) placed in his household, and the high security upbringing of his daughters who were keepers of the secret. Then the Prophet ﷺ revealed the mission: ((I have been given permission to leave)).

4. Tears of Joy... The Companionship, O Messenger of Allah

At that moment, time stopped for Abu Bakr (أبو بكر). He did not ask "Where to?" nor "How?", but one question jumped out, encapsulating all meanings of love and loyalty: Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) said eagerly: ((The companionship, O Messenger of Allah?)). The Prophet ﷺ said: ((The companionship)). Aisha (عائشة), may Allah be pleased with her, says describing the scene: "By Allah, I did not feel that anyone cries out of joy until I saw Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) weeping that day." They were not tears of fear of danger, nor sadness over leaving the homeland, but tears of joy that he had attained the honor of accompanying the Prophet of God on the most dangerous and greatest journey in history. Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) realized that by doing so, he was putting his neck on the line, but "Being with" the Messenger was more precious to him than life itself. Regarding this, Allah revealed His saying immortalizing this honor: {When he says to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us"} [At-Tawbah: 40].

5. Early Logistical Preparation (Feeding the Two Mounts)

The surprise that revealed Al-Siddiq’s (الصديق) foresight and long-term planning was that he had been ready for this moment for months. Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) said: "O Prophet of Allah, I have two she-camels that I had prepared for this." In a narration, he had been feeding them "Khabat" (crushed tree leaves) for four months so they would be strong enough for the arduous travel. Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) offered one of the camels to the Prophet ﷺ as a gift, saying: "Take one of them." But the Prophet ﷺ, who establishes the principle of "Independence and not relying entirely even on the closest kin," refused to take it except for its price, and said: ((For the price)). Here is a great lesson in self-esteem, and that the establishment of the religion and the state must be through pure money and personal sacrifice, so that no one has a favor in this establishment except Allah.

Completing the Plan: The two companions agreed on the details of the plan:

  • Exiting at night from a "back door" in Abu Bakr’s (أبو بكر) house (a small opening in the back of the house).
  • Heading south towards Ghar Thawr (غار ثور) (opposite the direction of Medina) for deception.
  • Staying in the cave for three nights until the pursuit calmed down.
  • Hiring an expert guide (Khirreet), who was Abdullah ibn Uraiqit (عبد الله بن أريقط) (he was a polytheist but trustworthy), and meeting him at the cave after three nights.

Thus, while Quraish (قريش) was mobilizing "youths and swords" around the Prophet’s ﷺ house, the Prophetic planning had outpaced them by stages, combining infallible Revelation, precise human arrangement, and psychological and material readiness, to write the first chapter of the epic of Migration.

Sixth Element (Conclusion): The Exit Plan and Camouflage... The Night of Heroism and Miracle

With the setting of the sun on that day, the siege began to tighten around the House of Prophethood. Eleven men from the fiercest of Quraish (قريش), led by Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) and Abu Lahab (أبو لهب), positioned themselves around the door, stealing glances through the cracks, waiting for the agreed zero hour (after midnight) to pounce with their swords all at once. The scene appeared outwardly decided in favor of material power, but inside the house, a battle of another kind was being managed; a battle led by certainty and genius planning.

1. The First Commando... Ali ibn Abi Talib in the Heart of Danger
