In those critical moments, the first "Commando" (Fida'i) operation in the history of Islam emerged. The Prophet ﷺ summoned his cousin, the young Ali ibn Abi Talib (علي بن أبي طالب) (who was then in his early twenties), and assigned him a dual mission requiring rare courage and absolute honesty:

  • First Mission (Camouflage): To sleep in the Prophet’s ﷺ bed and cover himself with the Prophet's "Green Hadhrami Mantle" (Burd) which the Prophet ﷺ used to cover himself with. The goal was to deceive the killers standing at the door; whenever they looked and saw the sleeper, they would think it was Muhammad ﷺ, so they would delay their storming waiting for him to come out. The Prophet ﷺ said to him reassuringly: ((Sleep on my bed, and cover yourself with this mantle of mine... for nothing from them that you dislike will reach you)). Here certainty manifests in its most splendid form; Ali (علي) sleeps peacefully under drawn swords, trusting the promise of the Truthful and Trustworthy One, unconcerned that he might be the substitute victim if they discovered the trick prematurely.
  • Second Mission (Trustworthiness): Staying in Mecca for days after the migration to return "deposits" to their owners. What an irony! Quraish (قريش) plans to kill him, yet they still entrust him with their precious wealth, and he who is fleeing for his life ensures he does not wrong them regarding their money. It is the sublimity of ethics that does not waver even in moments of war.

2. Breaking the Siege... And We Have Put a Barrier Before Them

The moment of exit arrived. The killers surrounded the door like a bracelet around a wrist, leaving no escape. Here, divine care intervened to suspend the laws of matter and senses. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out of his door, confident in his step, holding a handful of dust in his hand. He stood before them while they were armed to the teeth, eyes open, but God took away their sight, so they became like statues, seeing nothing. The Prophet ﷺ began to sprinkle dust on their heads one by one, while reciting verses from the beginning of Surah "Ya-Sin", until he reached the Almighty’s saying: {And We have put before them a barrier and behind them a barrier and covered them, so they do not see} [Ya-Sin: 9]. He passed among them like a breeze, leaving them waiting for an illusion, while he was making his way towards Ghar Thawr (غار ثور) in the south, to meet his travel companion Abu Bakr (أبو بكر), and begin a new page of history.

3. The Disappointment of Failure and the Morning of Truth

The killers remained stationed until morning, glancing at the sleeper (Ali) and saying: "Muhammad is still sleeping." When the sun rose, and Ali (علي) got up from the bed, the conspiracy collapsed into the mud. They asked him in astonishment: "Where is Muhammad?" He said: "I have no knowledge of him." They went mad, beat Ali (علي), and dragged him to the Sacred Mosque, but the "Head" had escaped, and the Body (the State) was on its way to formation. The prophecy of the Quran was fulfilled: {But they plan, and Allah plans. And Allah is the best of planners}.

Closing Link: The Duality of Cause and Reliance

The night of Migration summarizes the method of victory in Islam: It is a delicate balance between "exhausting human capacity" in planning (secrecy, camouflage, choosing the companion, the guide, the mount, an unfamiliar route), and "absolute heartfelt reliance" (Tawakkul) on Allah (walking out amidst swords, sleeping in the cave without guards). The Prophet ﷺ did not rely on the miracle alone and sit waiting for the Buraq to carry him, nor did he lean on material means alone and despair before the power of Quraish (قريش). Rather, he took the means as if they were everything, and relied on Allah as if the means were nothing. With this equation: The individual survived, the State was established, the Doctrine triumphed, and the Migration remained an eternal lesson for generations: That God does not waste those who preserve His religion, and that the plot of tyrants, no matter how great, is like a spider’s web before the power of God.

The Path of Hijrah (طريق الهجرة): The Genius of Planning, the Fall of Quraysh’s Chivalry, and the Care of Heaven

Element One: The Madness of Quraysh (قريش) and the Fall of "Jahili Chivalry" (المروءة الجاهلية)

The darkness of the night of conspiracy dissipated, and the morning revealed a dismal failure the likes of which Quraysh (قريش) had never witnessed in its history. The dreams of "Dar al-Nadwa" (دار الندوة) shattered against the rock of divine providence, and the plan for the "knockout blow" turned into a harsh slap that overthrew the pride of Mecca (مكة). When the cover was pulled back from the prophetic bed, and the assassins found no one but the young fedayeen (sacrificer) "Ali bin Abi Talib" (علي بن أبي طالب) — may Allah be pleased with him — the leaders of Quraysh realized that the "Head" had escaped, and that the project they had mobilized to bury had actually begun its journey of light towards Yathrib (يثرب). In the midst of this resounding shock, the Meccan leadership lost its mind, shifting from a state of "cold planning" to a state of "hysteria and madness," trampling upon all customs and covenants.

1. The Morning Shock... and the Wisdom of Security Concealment from the Closest People

The men went mad seeing Ali (علي) rising from the bed, calm and reassured. They screamed in his face, astonished: "Where is your companion?" He answered them with the steadfastness of the confident: "I have no knowledge of him. You ordered him to leave, so he left."

Quraysh could not bear this humiliating security breach. They fell upon Ali, beating him, violently dragging him to the Kaaba (الكعبة), torturing him, and pressuring him to extract a single piece of information that would lead them to the path of the Prophet ﷺ, but to no avail.

Here, a highly brilliant security and military lesson becomes evident; the Prophet ﷺ and his companion Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) concealed the details of the plan and the direction of travel (Cave of Thawr southwards - غار ثور) from the closest people to them, even from the first fedayeen, "Ali bin Abi Talib". Hiding the information was not out of doubt in Ali—God forbid—but rather a strict application of the principle of "restricting information to the narrowest scope" (Need to know). If Ali had known their hiding place, the information might have been extracted from him under severe torture. However, the Prophet ﷺ protected him and protected the plan by making him "truthful" when he said: "I do not know where he is."

2. The Moral Fall of Abu Jahl (أبو جهل).. The Day the Chivalry of the Arabs was Slaughtered

When the people despaired of Ali, they headed like savage beasts towards the house of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق), led by the Pharaoh of this nation, "Abu Jahl" (أبو جهل). They knocked violently on the door, and the young believing woman "Asma bint Abi Bakr" (أسماء بنت أبي بكر) — may Allah be pleased with her — came out to them.

Abu Jahl angrily initiated: "Where is your father, O daughter of Abu Bakr?" She replied with a courage no less than that of Ali: "I swear by Allah, I do not know where my father is."

At that moment, Abu Jahl lost the last atom of his mind, stripping himself of all meanings of magnanimity and manhood that the Arabs used to boast about. He raised his thick hand and struck Asma's face with a harsh, resounding slap—a slap so severe and cruel that her earring (قرطها) flew from her ear and scattered.

This situation does not merely reflect a passing cruelty; it represents a terrifying "moral collapse" of the pre-Islamic (Jahili) society in a moment of crisis. The Arabs, even in their days of ignorance and polytheism, found striking women repugnant and considered it a shame and a disgrace that would haunt a man and his tribe forever.

Perhaps history reminds us how chivalry stood as a barrier against striking women even in the heat of battle. In the Battle of Uhud (غزوة أحد), when the great companion "Abu Dujana" (أبو دجانة) took the sword of the Prophet ﷺ and began striking the heads of the polytheists, he saw a person inciting the enemy. He raised the sword against them, only to realize it was "Hind bint Utbah" (هند بنت عتبة). When he knew she was a woman, he moved the sword away from her and said: (I honored the sword of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from striking a woman with it - أكرمت سيف رسول الله ﷺ أن أضرب به امرأة).

Furthermore, historical accounts mention that Abu Jahl himself, after slapping Asma, realized the gravity of what he did by the standards of his people. He begged her not to tell any of the Arabs so that he would not be shamed for hitting women!

A Contemporary Projection (إسقاط معاصر):

Reflecting on this incident places us before a painful paradox in our contemporary times. If the disbelievers of Quraysh, despite their harshness, were ashamed to strike a woman, how can some who associate themselves with Islam today find it acceptable to insult wives and sisters and strike them on their faces under the pretext of guardianship (Qawamah) or anger? Islam came to decisively forbid this act. We have the best example in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Lady Aisha (عائشة) — may Allah be pleased with her — says: ((The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when striving in the path of Allah - ما ضرب رسول الله ﷺ شيئاً قط بيده، ولا امرأةً، ولا خادماً، إلا أن يجاهد في سبيل الله)) [Narrated by Muslim].

What we see today in dramas, soap operas, and even in some "games" of normalizing and taking lightly the issue of "slapping the face" (اللطم), considering it material for laughter or a proof of dominance, is in reality a regression of the sound human nature. It is an explicit violation of the decisive prophetic prohibition against striking and disfiguring the face, and a descent to something lower than the morals of the first days of ignorance!

3. The Open Financial Temptation.. and the Mobilization of Mercenaries

Faced with intelligence failure in finding the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, and the complete loss of their trail on the usual northern routes leading to Medina, Quraysh resorted to its last card: "Money."

The Meccan leadership declared a state of maximum emergency and issued a decree with a mythical prize that would make the mouths of all Arabs water: (One hundred camels - مائة ناقة, to whoever brings Muhammad and Abu Bakr, dead or alive).

One hundred camels at that time was not just a reward; it was a massive fortune equivalent to millions of dollars by today's standards, capable of taking its owner from extreme poverty to outrageous wealth overnight.

This decision did not target the people of Mecca alone; it was a public announcement mobilizing the surrounding Bedouin tribes, tempting the "mercenaries" (المرتزقة), and motivating the "Qaafah" (القافة - professional trackers who read footprints in the sand). The desert suddenly turned into an arena for a frenzied search. Eyes were watching, horses scoured the valleys and mountains, and everyone coveted the wealth and glory promised by Quraysh.

Quraysh thought that money would buy them the head of the call (Da'wah), not knowing that Allah, the Majestic, had surrounded His Prophet with care that cannot be penetrated by the swords of mercenaries, nor perceived by the eyes of trackers. The battle was no longer between Quraysh and two men, but between Quraysh and the Lord of the Worlds.

Element Two: Strategic Deception and the Operations Room of the "Family of Abu Bakr" (آل أبي بكر)

While Quraysh was floundering in Mecca, completely bewildered, distributing astronomical rewards in search of the two great emigrants, the prophetic planning was writing, that very night, the greatest plan of "strategic camouflage" known to human history. The Hijrah was not merely a random escape under the cover of darkness. It was an integrated institutional work where the genius of leadership combined with the optimal utilization of personnel. The house of Al-Siddiq Abu Bakr (أبو بكر الصديق) — may Allah be pleased with him — transformed into a miniature "operations room," managing the crisis with a security professionalism that baffled minds and paralyzed the most formidable surveillance apparatuses of Quraysh.

1. Geographical Deception: Walking South to Reach the North!

The first security rule adopted by the Prophet ﷺ was "defying expectations." It is axiomatic that anyone fleeing Mecca aiming for Yathrib (Medina) would automatically head "North," which is the usual route for caravans. Based on this classical assumption, Quraysh mobilized its knights and trackers to comb the northern routes.

However, the prophetic genius shattered these expectations. As soon as the Prophet ﷺ exited from the back door of Abu Bakr’s house, they directed their faces towards the "South," in the direction of the Yemen (اليمن) road. They walked a distance of about five miles (approx. 8 kilometers) on rugged, unpaved paths until they reached Mount "Thawr" (ثور).

They did not stop at geographical deception but applied the highest degrees of field concealment. Books of Seerah mention that the Prophet ﷺ walked that night on the "tips of his toes" (tiptoeing) until his honorable feet bled, so as not to leave a clear footprint that professional polytheist trackers could recognize. This behavior was a strict practical application of the doctrine of "taking the means" (الأخذ بالأسباب) which does not contradict reliance on Allah (Tawakkul), but is rather its very core.

2. Brilliant Distribution of Roles: An Entire Family in the Service of Faith

Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq was not just a companion on the journey; he was an integrated system of support for the Prophet ﷺ. He mobilized his entire household—its men, its women, and its freed slaves—to play specific, carefully studied roles. Every individual in this family acted as a "secret cell":

  • Abdullah bin Abi Bakr (عبد الله بن أبي بكر) - (The Intelligence Apparatus): He was a young man, described by Lady Aisha as (ثَقِفٌ لَقِنٌ - Thaqif Laqin), meaning highly intelligent, quick-witted, and perceptive. His role was to remain in Mecca during the day, mingling in the gatherings of Quraysh as if he had not lost his father, listening to their plots, analyzing their plans, and monitoring the movements of their knights. In the last third of the night, he would sneak under the pitch-black darkness to the Cave of Thawr to deliver the daily "security report" to the Prophet ﷺ and his father. He would then return before dawn, appearing in Mecca in the morning as if he had spent the whole night there.
  • Asma bint Abi Bakr (أسماء بنت أبي بكر) - (Logistical Supply - Dhat al-Nitaqayn / ذات النطاقين): This young woman bore the responsibility of sustenance. She would prepare food and bring it to them at night in the heart of the desolate desert. On the night of their departure from the cave, she prepared their travel provisions. When she wanted to tie the food container and the water skin, she could not find a rope. With the quick wit of a dedicated believer, she tore her "Nitaq" (نطاق - a belt or cloth a woman ties around her waist) into two halves. She tied the food with one half and the water with the other. When the Prophet ﷺ learned of her deed, he gave her glad tidings, saying: ((May Allah replace your Nitaq with two Nitaqs in Paradise - أبدلك الله بنطاقك هذا نطاقين في الجنة)), and she was immortalized in history with the title "Dhat al-Nitaqayn" (She of the Two Belts).
  • Amir bin Fuhayrah (عامر بن فُهيرة) - (Security Cover and Supply): He was a freed slave (Mawla) of Abu Bakr and used to herd his sheep. Amir was assigned a highly cunning dual mission. After Abdullah bin Abi Bakr or Asma finished visiting the cave, Amir would follow their footprints with a flock of sheep to erase them completely from the sand, leaving no trace. At the same time, he would pass by the cave with the sheep to milk them for the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr to drink.

3. Absolute Financial Detachment: The Wealth of Al-Siddiq and the Wisdom of Asma

Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq did not just risk his soul and his family; he provided a lesson in financial detachment unparalleled by anyone. He carried all his wealth with him on that journey, leaving not a single dirham in his house. He took with him approximately (five to six thousand dirhams) to place at the disposal of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for establishing the prospective Islamic state.

Here, a great family situation emerges, combining wisdom with reassuring the elders. "Abu Quhafa" (أبو قحافة) (the father of Abu Bakr, who was an elderly man who had lost his sight and had not yet embraced Islam at the time) entered upon his granddaughters and said with sorrow and anger: (By Allah, I think he has afflicted you with his wealth as he has with himself!).

Asma did not break down, nor did she show weakness that would gloat enemies or increase her grandfather's sorrow. Rather, with dazzling wisdom, she said: (No, O father, he has left us much good).

Asma proceeded to take stones and placed them in the niche (الكوة) where Abu Bakr used to hide his money, covered them with a cloth, then took her blind grandfather's hand and placed it on the cloth, saying: (O father, put your hand on this wealth). When he felt the stones under the fabric, he thought they were dirhams. His soul calmed down, and he said: (There is no harm; if he left you this, then he has done well).

This situation not only reflects Asma's quick wit and her use of "Ma'areed" (المعاريض - equivocation/double entendres) to alleviate the elderly man's worry without lying, but it also highlights the greatest trait in Abu Bakr's family: "Deep faith-based upbringing." Abu Bakr took all his wealth, leaving his daughters without a financial provider, yet Asma did not complain, nor did she blame her father. She was satisfied, anticipating reward, proud of what he did, and covering up his financial detachment to protect the Hijrah plan. It is a family molded from the clay of certainty, competing to sacrifice everything for the sake of Allah's religion.

Element Three: In the Cave of Thawr (غار ثور)... An Epic of Love, and the Pinnacle of Reliance (التوكل)

After a grueling march extending about five miles south of Mecca, on a rugged path unaccustomed to footsteps, the caravan of light reached Mount "Thawr" (جبل ثور). A towering mountain with sharp rocks and rugged trails, to the extent that the honorable feet of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ bled from the severity of treading on the stones and deliberately walking on his tiptoes to hide the trail. There, at the peak of that formidable mountain, lay the "Cave" (الغار) that would witness the greatest seclusion in human history. The cave was not an extended cavern, but rather a rocky hollow sinking downwards, requiring whoever enters to bend and sneak in, and whoever searches for it to bow their head to look beneath their feet.

1. The Silent Sacrificer: Shielding the Honorable Body with One's Soul

When they reached the mouth of the cave, the highest meanings of sacrifice and dedication manifested. The Prophet ﷺ was about to enter to rest from the hardships of the journey, but Abu Bakr — may Allah be pleased with him — stopped him with the firmness of an anxious lover, saying: (By Allah, you will not enter it until I enter before you, so if there is anything in it, it will strike me instead of you).

Al-Siddiq's logic in that moment stemmed from a firm belief: "If I am destroyed, I am but one man of the Ummah, but if you are destroyed, the Ummah and the religion are destroyed."

Abu Bakr entered that dark, desolate hole. He began feeling its walls with his hand, combing and wiping it inch by inch, fearing there might be a beast or a venomous creature of the earth. Whenever he found a hole or a crack, he tore a piece of his garment and clothes and plugged it with it, until his clothes ran out and nothing remained on him except what covered his Awrah (private parts). One hole remained for which he found nothing to plug, so he placed his "heel" (كعبه) over it to block it with his own body!

Only then did he permit the Prophet ﷺ to enter. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ slept from extreme exhaustion, placing his honorable head on Abu Bakr’s thigh. In that still moment, Abu Bakr was bitten from the hole he blocked with his foot. The venom coursed through his body, and the pain intensified until his heart almost tore out. But—out of his immense politeness and love—he refused to move a single inch so as not to wake the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. However, the silent tears of pain overcame him, and drops fell onto the honorable face. The Prophet ﷺ woke up and asked him: ((What is wrong with you, O Abu Bakr? - ما بك يا أبا بكر؟)). He said: I have been bitten, may my father and mother be sacrificed for you. The Prophet ﷺ wiped his honorable saliva over the wound, and it healed immediately as if nothing had happened to it, in a prophetic miracle that increased the tranquility in Al-Siddiq's heart.

2. Three Nights of Unique Companionship: The Ascension of Love

The two companions stayed in this sunken cave for three nights (Thursday night, Friday night, and Saturday night). Those nights were not merely a "period of security hiding"; they were a "spiritual retreat" (اعتكافاً روحياً) and an unparalleled isolation of faith.

Imagine this great honor: At a time when the companions were sacrificing everything precious to catch a glimpse of the Prophet ﷺ or a touch of his hand, and at a time when Quraysh was turning the desert upside down looking for him, Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq was enjoying the Prophet ﷺ all to himself. He served him, kept him company, and received the overflow of his prophethood in an area not exceeding a few meters. These nights were the crowning of a lifetime of truthfulness and support, a divine medal immortalized by the Holy Quran with a description no human has ever attained: {When he said to his companion - إِذْ يَقُولُ لِصَاحِبِهِ}, Thus, Allah affirmed "companionship" (الصحبة) for him from above seven heavens.

3. The Ultimate Equation of Reliance (Tawakkul): (Do not be sad; indeed, Allah is with us - لا تحزن إن الله معنا)

On the third day, hearts reached the throats. Despite all the camouflage and erasing of footprints, the physiognomy and tracking skills led the knights of Quraysh to the top of Mount Thawr, until they stood exactly at the mouth of the cave.

Here, the heart of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq shook, and his being trembled—not out of fear for himself, but out of terror for the life of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the fate of the message. Abu Bakr whispered in a voice filled with concern: (O Messenger of Allah, if one of them were to look down at his feet, he would see us).

In this critical moment, where material means completely vanish, and the distance between life and death becomes a mere downward glance, the truth of "Absolute Reliance" (التوكل المطلق) manifests. The Prophet ﷺ turned to him, and with an amazing tranquility and an unshakable confidence, he said his immortal words: ((O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two, the third of whom is Allah? Do not be sad; indeed, Allah is with us - يا أبا بكر، ما ظنك باثنين الله ثالثهما؟ لا تحزن إن الله معنا)).

Why did Abu Bakr fear, and why was the Prophet ﷺ reassured?

Abu Bakr's fear was not a deficiency in faith, but because he was the "Man of Means" (رجل الأسباب). He had planned, prepared, paid his wealth, organized his family, and utilized all possible material means. So, when he saw the means exhausted and the polytheists at the door of the cave, he feared. As for the Prophet ﷺ, he was teaching us that the heart should not be attached to the "means", but to the "Lord of the means", and that mobilizing human effort does not mean relying on it.

Here emerges a magnificent creedal subtlety in his saying ﷺ: {Indeed, Allah is with us - إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا}. The Prophet ﷺ included Abu Bakr in the divine accompaniment (المعية الإلهية). If we draw a Quranic comparison between this situation and the situation of the Prophet of Allah, Musa (موسى) — peace be upon him — when Pharaoh and his soldiers caught up with him at the sea, and his people said: {Indeed, we are to be overtaken - إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ}, we find that Musa (AS) said: {No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me - كَلَّا ۖ إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ} [Ash-Shu'ara: 62]. Musa singled out the accompaniment for himself due to the weak certainty of those with him. But our Prophet ﷺ, knowing the true certainty of Al-Siddiq and his high status, shared the divine accompaniment with him: {Indeed, Allah is with us - إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا}. In this verse alone lies the destruction and refutation of all the fabrications and suspicions that have attacked the faith of Al-Siddiq — may Allah be pleased with him — throughout history.

4. A Note on the Story of the "Spider's Web and the Dove's Nest" (نسيج العنكبوت وعش الحمامة)

In the midst of the narrative about the polytheists standing at the cave, the story of the spider weaving its web at the mouth of the cave and the dove nesting to lay its eggs frequently emerges in Islamic culture as the reason for the polytheists turning away.

From a Hadith and methodological perspective; scholars have differed on the authenticity of this story. Many verifiers (like Al-Albani / الألباني and others) weakened it due to a weakness in its chain of transmission, while others (like Ibn Hajar / ابن حجر and Ibn Kathir / ابن كثير) graded it as acceptable (Hasan) based on supporting narrations. However, the methodology of scholars in dealing with the "Prophetic Biography" (السيرة النبوية) is characterized by methodological broad-mindedness. As long as a narration does not establish a jurisprudential ruling, does not build a creed (Aqeedah), and does not contradict an established text, they cite it to extract lessons (as Ibn Hisham / ابن هشام and others did).

Whether the story of the spider is authentic or not, the true and definite miracle, according to the text of the Quran, is the "Divine Blinding" (التعمية الإلهية) of the polytheists' eyesight and insight. Allah diverted their vision while they stood at the door of the cave, and sent down soldiers from Him unseen to the naked eye, as the Almighty said: {And Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with angels you did not see - فَأَنزَلَ اللَّهُ سَكِينَتَهُ عَلَيْهِ وَأَيَّدَهُ بِجُنُودٍ لَّمْ تَرَوْهَا} [At-Tawbah: 40]. Divine care does not need visible means to intervene, and when Providence takes charge of protecting a human being, the eyes of tyrants go blind even if they remain open!

Element Four: Setting Off Towards Yathrib (يثرب)... Utilizing Competencies and Not Forsaking the Reward (الأجر)

The three heavy nights passed in the depths of the cave of "Thawr" (ثور). The fury of Quraysh calmed down, and the search patrols retreated after exhausting their efforts combing the usual northern routes, despairing of finding the two wanted men. At this moment, the time came to transition from "static concealment" to "strategic movement" towards Yathrib. The departure journey was not a leap into the unknown, but rather governed by precise planning and professional measures, wherein the genius of Prophethood manifested in managing human resources, laying the foundations for state-building, and setting the most wonderful examples of high ambition and self-respect.

1. The Polytheist Expert (Abdullah bin Urayqit - عبد الله بن أريقط): Utilizing Competence over Affiliation

The plan required taking a rugged, untrodden path—the coastal route parallel to the Red Sea (البحر الأحمر)—to avoid Qurayshi checkpoints and commercial caravans. This complex route required a guide highly skilled in the desert, one who knew its secrets and paths like the back of his hand, or what the Arabs call an (Al-Khirrit - الخِرِّيت).

Here, the genius of leadership emerged in choosing "Abdullah bin Urayqit al-Dili" (عبد الله بن أريقط الديلي). He was a polytheist man, following the religion of the disbelievers of Quraysh, yet he was the sole available expert for this complex mission.

Imagine the magnitude of the security risk: Quraysh was offering a mythical reward (one hundred camels) to whoever brought Muhammad ﷺ, and Abdullah bin Urayqit was a polytheist man. With a single word, he could betray them and seize wealth and glory in Mecca! Nevertheless, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr trusted him, handed over their two riding camels (their only means of survival), and made an appointment with him at the Cave of Thawr after three nights. He kept his promise, and the greed of the world did not overcome him.

Strategic Lessons from this Situation:

  • Prioritizing Professional Competence: In worldly matters, building states, and establishing civilizations, "competence and specialization" are presented as the criteria for success. The Prophet ﷺ did not look for a Muslim guide with modest experience; rather, he hired the best available expert, establishing the rule: {Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy - إِنَّ خَيْرَ مَنِ اسْتَأْجَرْتَ الْقَوِيُّ الْأَمِينُ} [Al-Qasas: 26]. State-building requires people of precise specialization.
  • Fairness to Opponents and Human Chivalry: This situation proved that moral values, such as trustworthiness, chivalry, and fulfilling covenants, may be deeply rooted in the souls of some who differ in creed. Islam does not deprive people of their due, and recognizes virtue wherever it is found. (Hadith scholars and historians differed on the later fate of Ibn Urayqit; Imam al-Dhahabi (الإمام الذهبي) leaned towards him having embraced Islam, while others like Al-Nawawi (النووي) believed he died on his polytheism, but his historical role in that journey remains preserved and appreciated).

2. The Camel for a Price (الناقة بالثمن): Perfection of Reward and the Pride of Leadership

At the appointed time (the dawn of the fourth day), the guide arrived with the two riding camels that Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq — may Allah be pleased with him — had prepared and fed with "Al-Khabat" (الخَبَط - tree leaves) for months prior in preparation for this moment. Driven by sincere love and boundless dedication, Abu Bakr offered the best of the two camels (which was the famous camel Al-Qaswaa - القصواء) to the Prophet ﷺ as a pure gift, saying: (May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, take one of them).

Although Abu Bakr is the one about whom the Prophet ﷺ later said: ((No wealth has ever benefited me as the wealth of Abu Bakr has benefited me - ما نفعني مالٌ قط ما نفعني مالُ أبي بكر)), and although Abu Bakr had offered himself, his family, and all his wealth for this journey, the Prophet’s ﷺ response was decisive and gentle at the same time: ((As for without a price, then no - أما بغير ثمن فلا)), and in another narration: ((With the price, O Abu Bakr - بالثمن يا أبا بكر)).

Why did the Prophet ﷺ refuse the gift and insist on buying?

  • Completing the Reward of Hijrah: Hijrah is not merely a journey; it is the most arduous and greatest physical, financial, and psychological act of worship of that era. It is the seed upon which the Islamic state would be built, and in its scale of good deeds, everyone who embraces Islam until the Day of Judgment will be recorded. The Prophet ﷺ wanted no one to share the reward of his personal Hijrah. He refused to forsake any part of this immense reward, choosing to migrate with his own wealth so that the effort and expenditure would be purely for Allah the Almighty.
  • The Pride of Leadership and State-Building: The Greatest Legislator wanted to establish a moral principle for leaders and reformers; the foundation of the nation's entity must be free from personal favors. Despite the high status of Abu Bakr, the Prophet ﷺ paid the price for his mount to teach generations that the tax of faith is paid from one's own pure wealth, and that self-respect is not compromised even before the most generous of friends and those closest to the heart.

Thus, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ paid the price of "Al-Qaswaa," mounted her, and the blessed caravan (the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, Amir bin Fuhayrah riding behind Abu Bakr, and the polytheist guide leading them) set off, cutting through the barren desert sands on a journey that would change the face of the map and reshape human history forever.

Element Five: On the Desert Road... The Care of Heaven Never Ceases

Leaving the Cave of "Thawr" did not mean the end of danger; rather, it was the beginning of a new chapter of challenges. The vast open desert between Mecca and Yathrib was teeming with highway robbers, trackers, and those greedy for the grand Qurayshi prize (one hundred camels). Amidst this perilous expanse, the care of Heaven manifested in its most glorious forms, painting a series of miraculous situations and educational lessons confirming that whoever is mindful of Allah, Allah protects him, and that prophets are never stopped by trials from fulfilling their mission.

1. Suraqah bin Malik (سراقة بن مالك بن جعشم): From a Greedy Hunter to a Faithful Guard

In one of the gatherings of Banu Mudlij (بني مُدلج), news of the mythical prize arrived. "Suraqah bin Malik" was a fierce knight. When he heard a hint about a caravan spotted heading towards the coast, his intuition told him it was the prophetic caravan. He kept the matter a secret from his companions to win the prize alone. Suraqah slipped away, put on his armor, mounted his swift horse, and launched like a spear cutting through the desert.

Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq — may Allah be pleased with him — describes those terrifying moments, saying: "We traveled while the people were searching for us, and no one caught up with us except Suraqah bin Malik bin Ju'shum on a horse of his. I said: 'This pursuit has caught up with us, O Messenger of Allah!' He replied: ((Do not be sad; indeed, Allah is with us - لا تحزن إن الله معنا))."

Abu Bakr was looking right and left out of extreme anxiety, while the Prophet ﷺ was looking straight ahead without turning, reciting the Quran with an amazing tranquility.

As soon as Suraqah drew near, the miracle occurred; his horse's front legs sank into the solid desert sand up to its knees, and Suraqah fell off. He got up and drew out the "Azlam" (الأزلام - divining arrows of the pre-Islamic era) to cast lots: Should he continue or return? The arrow he hated came out (Do not do it). But the glitter of the hundred camels blinded him, so he mounted again and got closer, until he heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Quran. Here, his horse's legs sank violently into the ground again, and dust rose from it like smoke.

At this defining moment, worldly greed vanished from Suraqah's heart. He became certain that this man was protected by an overwhelming power and that his cause would prevail. He called out for safety and asked the Prophet ﷺ to write him a "Document of Security" (كتاب أمن) to be his guarantee if the matter of Islam became victorious. The Prophet ﷺ ordered Amir bin Fuhayrah, who wrote it for him on a piece of leather (أدم).

Here another miracle of Prophetic certainty unfolds; the hunted Prophet ﷺ, threatened with murder, who possessed neither an army nor a state, looked at Suraqah and gave him glad tidings of a prophecy that transcended the borders of the Arabian Peninsula, saying: ((How will it be with you, O Suraqah, when you wear the bracelets of Khosrau? - كيف بك يا سراقة إذا لبست سواري كسرى؟)).

Suraqah returned to Mecca, transforming from a "fierce hunter" to a "hidden guard." He would meet no one searching for the Prophet ﷺ except that he turned them away, saying: "You have been sufficed regarding what is here" (I have checked this area for you). Glory be to the One who turns hearts and diverts enemies!

2. The Tent of Umm Ma'bad (أم معبد): The Miracle of Blessing.. and Love in a Sip of Milk

The blessed caravan continued on its exhausting path, suffering from intense thirst and hunger, until they passed by two tents belonging to a woman from Khuza'ah (خزاعة) named "Umm Ma'bad" (أم معبد - Atikah bint Khalid / عاتكة بنت خالد). She was a tough woman sitting in the courtyard of her tent. They asked to buy meat or milk from her, but they found nothing with her, for it was a year of severe drought and famine.

The Prophet ﷺ looked and saw an emaciated sheep in the corner of the tent, left behind by the flock due to exhaustion. He asked her permission to milk it. Astonished, she said: "It is too weak for that!" The Prophet ﷺ wiped his honorable hand over its udder, invoked the name of Allah, and supplicated. In a pure divine miracle, the sheep yielded abundant milk.

The Prophet ﷺ milked it into a large vessel and offered it to Umm Ma'bad, and she drank. Then he gave his companions to drink, and he was the last to drink, acting upon his own guidance ﷺ: ((The one who serves the people drink is the last of them to drink - ساقي القوم آخرهم شرباً)).

In this scene filled with blessing, Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq uttered a sentence immortalized by history, summarizing all meanings of altruism and the melting of the lover into his beloved. He said: "So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drank until I was satisfied! - فشرب رسول الله ﷺ حتى رضيتُ!"

Ponder this stunning expression: The milk enters the stomach of the Messenger of Allah, and the quenching, hydration, and satisfaction take place in the heart of Abu Bakr! It is the peak of true companionship that cannot be measured by ordinary human standards.

Then the Prophet ﷺ milked another vessel, left it for Umm Ma'bad, and departed. (She is the one who described the Prophet ﷺ to her husband when he returned with the greatest and most eloquent physical and moral description known in the books of Seerah).

3. Buraydah bin Al-Husaib (بريدة بن الحصيب الأسلمي): The Caller Who is Not Stopped by Pursuit

The Hijrah was not a journey to save one's own life; it was a movement of Da'wah (Calling to Islam). Along the way, they were intercepted by a caravan comprising eighty men from the tribe of "Aslam" (أسلم) led by "Buraydah bin Al-Husaib Al-Aslami", who were searching for the Qurayshi reward.

Instead of hiding, the Prophet ﷺ faced them with courage and steadfastness, and asked their leader: ((Who are you? - من أنت؟)). He said: Buraydah. The Prophet turned to Abu Bakr, optimistic and rejoicing, saying: ((Our matter has cooled and improved [a play on the word Buraydah, meaning coolness] - برد أمرنا وصلح)). Then he asked him: ((From whom? - ممن؟)) He said: From Aslam. He said: ((We are safe [a play on Aslam] - سلمنا)). He asked: ((From Banu Sahm? - من بني سهم؟)) He said: ((Your arrow [Sahm] has come out, O Abu Bakr - خرج سهمك يا أبا بكر)).

Then the Prophet ﷺ, the one whose head was wanted, stood to call Buraydah and his people to Islam!

With what level of ambition did this great Prophet move? Danger surrounded him from every side, yet he did not miss a single opportunity to convey the message of his Lord. These words and the light emanating from his face ﷺ resulted in the immediate conversion of Buraydah to Islam on the spot, and all eighty families converted with him. They prayed the Isha prayer behind the Prophet ﷺ. Furthermore, Buraydah took off his turban and tied it to his spear, making it a white flag advancing ahead of the caravan of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as a declaration of peace and victory.

4. The Auspicious Arrival: The End of Wandering and the Beginning of the State

The distances of the barren desert were folded, and the features of the black volcanic tracts (Harras) of Yathrib appeared on the horizon, along with its tall palm trees that the emigrants had long awaited.

There in Yathrib, hearts were boiling with longing. The crowds would go out every morning to the outskirts of the city at "Al-Harrah," waiting for the appearance of the full moon, only returning when the heat of the midday sun forced them back. Until that bright, auspicious day came, when a Jew climbed upon one of their fortresses (Aatum / أطُمٍ) for some business of his, and caught a glimpse of the caravan of light appearing from afar, shimmering in the mirage. He screamed at the top of his voice: "O gathering of Arabs! This is your grandfather (your luck and your glory) whom you are waiting for - يا معشر العرب! هذا جدكم الذي تنتظرون."

Yathrib moved in its entirety, the city shook with the Takbeer (Allahu Akbar), and the Muslims set out with their weapons to welcome the Prophet ﷺ in the suburb of "Quba" (قُباء).

Here the journey of pursuit ended, and here the page of Meccan weakness was folded, to begin the greatest page in human history... the page of building the state, establishing society, and creating civilization, the radiant details of which we will live in our next station, Allah willing.

1. The Blessed Arrival at the Outskirts of the City (قباء): Anticipation, Joy, and Light

Yathrib (يثرب) was experiencing an unprecedented state of momentum and anticipation; the news had spread, and the sole "trend" in the streets of the city at that time was: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) is on his way to us." Despite the absolute secrecy that surrounded the journey of the Hijrah (الهجرة), to the extent that no one in the city knew exactly when the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) would arrive, the hearts of the Ansar (الأنصار) raced ahead to meet him.

Every day, with the first threads of morning light, the people of the city would go out to the "Harrah" (الحَرّة) (the highlands with black stones surrounding the city). They would stand there in rows, their eyes gazing toward the desert horizon, waiting for the blessed caravan. They remained in this state for long hours until the scorching September midday sun stung them, leaving them no choice but to return to their homes exhausted, only to repeat the exact same scene the following day.

One day, after the Muslims had returned to their homes to escape the blazing heat of the sun, it was the will of Allah that the first eye to spot the Prophetic caravan was that of a Jewish man. He was standing in an elevated place when he caught sight of a caravan cloaked in the mirage from afar. He instinctively realized that this was the momentous event the Muslims were waiting for, and unable to contain himself, he shouted at the top of his voice: "O gathering of Arabs (يا معشر العرب)! Here is your grandfather (meaning your fortune and glory) whom you are waiting for!"

As soon as this cry echoed, a revolution of joy erupted in the city; the houses shook with Takbir (التكبير) [saying Allahu Akbar], and the Muslims rushed out in the most magnificent display of reception. They did not just go out; they strapped on their swords and carried their weapons in the intense heat, rushing toward the outskirts of the city to deliver a practical message to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ): "We are here to protect you, and we are ready to defend you with our souls."

When the two groups met, and the Ansar (الأنصار) crowded to welcome their great guest, a situation occurred that reflected the peak of social intelligence and refined manners from Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق), may Allah be pleased with him. Most of the Ansar (الأنصار) had never seen the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) before. When they approached, they found two men cloaked in awe and majesty, and some were confused, not knowing which of them was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ), while embarrassment prevented them from asking. Here, Al-Siddiq (الصديق) intuitively grasped the situation. With a graceful and wise movement, he stood up, took off his cloak, and used it to shade the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) from the heat of the sun. In that exact moment, without a single word being spoken, everyone realized who was the servant and who was the master. Al-Siddiq (الصديق) introduced the people to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ), relieving them of the embarrassment of asking.

It was a majestic day in which the features of history and the geography of the place changed, until the name "Yathrib" (يثرب) transformed into "Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah" (المدينة المنورة). Perhaps the most eloquent description of this immortal day is what the honorable companion Anas bin Malik (أنس بن مالك), may Allah be pleased with him, said, describing that moment when the feet of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) stepped onto the soil of Madinah: "I witnessed the day when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) entered the city, and by Allah, everything in it became illuminated!"

2. The Days of Quba (قباء): Trusts Returned... and the First Mosque Built

When the Prophetic procession reached the outskirts of the city, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) chose his first stop to be in the area of "Quba" (قباء), specifically in the dwellings of Banu Amr bin Awf (بني عمرو بن عوف). There, two noble companions attained the great honor of hosting him; the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) stayed to sleep and settle in the house of "Kulthum bin Al-Hadm" (كلثوم بن الهدم), while he used the house of "Sa'd bin Khaithamah" (سعد بن خيثمة) as a gathering place to receive the crowds of Muslims and delegations that came to welcome him. The house of the first became a residence for rest, and the house of the second became an arena for Dawah and meetings.

During those four days that the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) spent in Quba (قباء), one of the most magnificent scenes of loyalty in human history was completed when the young hero Ali bin Abi Talib (علي بن أبي طالب), may Allah be pleased with him, arrived to join the caravan. Ali (عليّ) had remained in Makkah (مكة) for three days after the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) departure for two great purposes: The first was camouflage to delay the pursuit of Quraysh (قريش), and the second—which is the most astonishing—was to return trusts to the people of Makkah (مكة)!

Here, a strange contradiction in human nature is revealed; the disbelievers of Quraysh (قريش) who accused the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) of magic, madness, and lying, and conspired to kill him, could not find a single man in all of Makkah (مكة) whom they trusted with their wealth and valuables except him ﷺ. Despite the harm and the chase, the Greatest Teacher refused anything but to return rights to their owners, acting upon the principle: "Fulfill the trust to him who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." After Ali (عليّ), may Allah be pleased with him, successfully performed this dangerous sacrificial mission, he set out migrating on the trail of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), crossing that vast distance and barren desert "walking on his feet" in steadfastness and bravery until he caught up with the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) while he was still in Quba (قباء).

The days in Quba (قباء) were not just a warrior's rest after an arduous journey; rather, they were the practical beginning of establishing the new state. In this place, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) left an immortal mark that remains until the Day of Judgment, as he participated with his companions in building "Masjid Quba" (مسجد قباء), making it the first mosque founded on piety in Islam after Prophethood.

This mosque was deeply connected to the heart of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ). After he later settled in the heart of the city, he never forgot the site of his first step in it. It was his ﷺ custom to visit Masjid Quba (مسجد قباء) every Saturday, walking or riding, to pray in it. He did not stop there; he urged his Ummah to honor this blessed mosque, granting a great virtue to whoever intended to visit it when he said: "Whoever purifies himself in his house, then comes to Masjid Quba (مسجد قباء) and prays in it, will have a reward like that of an Umrah (عُمرة)." Thus, this mosque remains a beacon to which the hearts of visitors yearn across the ages.

3. The Majestic Entry into the Heart of Yathrib (يثرب): Leadership Wisdom and Divine Care

After the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) established the foundations of his first mosque in Quba (قباء), Allah permitted the blessed caravan to continue its march toward the heart of the city. On Friday morning, the Prophetic procession moved, and halfway there—between Quba (قباء) and the site of his current mosque—the Friday prayer caught up with him while he was in the dwellings of "Banu Salim bin Awf" (بني سالم بن عوف). There, in the belly of the valley, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) gathered with his companions, who numbered nearly a hundred men, to hold the first Friday prayer in the history of Islam, serving as an opening of goodness and blessings for the new society.

Before the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) entered the streets of the city, his leadership genius and social astuteness were manifested in a highly significant scene. He ﷺ sent for his maternal uncles from "Banu Al-Najjar" (بني النجار) (they were the maternal uncles of his father Abd Al-Muttalib (عبد المطلب), as his grandfather Hashim (هاشم) had married "Salma" (سلمى) from the people of Yathrib (يثرب)). As soon as the call reached them, they rushed out with their swords drawn to surround him like an honor guard, escorting him into the city in a majestic procession. The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) was not in dire need of military protection at that moment, for the entire city was opening its arms to him, but he wanted to establish a great lesson in "social appreciation"; giving prestige to leading families, putting them forward, and showing respect for their status is a key to unlocking hearts and a smart step in building alliances and harmonizing souls in any society.

As soon as the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) she-camel stepped into the streets of Yathrib (يثرب), the pathways and houses shook with Takbir (التكبير) and Tahmid (التحميد) [praising Allah], and the city celebrated him in a way it had never seen before. Whenever he passed by the dwellings of an Ansar (الأنصار) tribe, they blocked the path of his camel and clung to its reins, pleading with him out of passionate love: "Come to us, O Messenger of Allah... to numbers, equipment, and fortification!" Every house in the city hoped to attain the honor of hosting him, and here a delicate social challenge emerged; the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) choice of one tribe over another might breed resentment or stir up sensitivities among the Ansar (الأنصار) families at this early stage of establishment.

However, divine revelation was present to untie this knot with a genius solution that extinguished any possibility of conflict. The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) told them with an affectionate smile: "Leave her path, for she is commanded." With these eloquent words, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) delegated the matter to Allah Almighty, so everyone surrendered, accepted the choice of Heaven, and stood waiting to see where this blessed she-camel would lay down its saddle.

The camel walked slowly as eyes followed it, until it knelt in a spot (which is the location of the Prophet's Mosque today). To confirm the divine choice, the camel rose, walked a little, then turned around and returned to kneel in the exact same spot. Here, an incredibly beautiful divine surprise was revealed; this spot was located in the dwellings of "Banu Al-Najjar" (بني النجار)! The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) had secretly hoped in his heart to lodge among his maternal uncles to honor them and draw strength from them, but out of courtesy with Allah, he did not ask for it. So Allah took it upon Himself to fulfill his heartfelt, unspoken wish. This validates what Lady Aisha (عائشة), may Allah be pleased with her, later said: "I see that your Lord hastens to fulfill your desires." Glory be to the One who inspired the she-camel to please the heart of His Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) and bring joy to his uncles.

4. Hosted by Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari (أبو أيوب الأنصاري)... and the Gathering of the Prophetic Family

When the commanded she-camel knelt in the land of "Banu Al-Najjar" (بني النجار), and everyone was certain that this was the spot chosen by Allah Almighty for His Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) turned to the expectant faces around him and asked with a friendly smile: "Which of the houses of our family is closest?" In that decisive moment, the quick-wittedness of the noble companion Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari (أبو أيوب الأنصاري) (Khalid bin Zayd - خالد بن زيد), may Allah be pleased with him, became evident. He realized that his door was the closest, so he did not just issue a verbal invitation; rather, he rushed into a smart practical initiative. He stepped forward briskly, carried the "saddle" (baggage and belongings) of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), and took it into his house.

Some of the Ansar (الأنصار) tried to dissuade Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) from doing this, hoping for the honor of hosting, but the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) settled the matter with a beautiful customary rule that pleased everyone and left no room for dispute, saying: "A man is with his saddle." Thus, Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari (أبو أيوب الأنصاري) became the official host of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ). As for the blessed she-camel, the noble companion As'ad bin Zurarah (أسعد بن زرارة), may Allah be pleased with him, gained the honor of caring for her; he took her reins and led her away to provide her with food and care. Thus, the honor of the reception was distributed among the senior Ansar (الأنصار).

The Two-Story Dilemma... and the Etiquette of Love and Veneration

The house of Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari (أبو أيوب الأنصاري) consisted of two floors (a lower room and an upper room). As was the custom of the Arabs in honoring guests and making their entry and exit easy, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) settled on the ground floor, while Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) and his wife (Umm Ayyub - أم أيوب) went up to the top floor. As soon as night fell and the door was closed, Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) felt the gravity of the situation! He looked at the floor he was standing on and realized that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) was residing directly beneath it.

A shiver mixed with terror and shyness struck Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب), and he turned to his wife in panic, saying: "Woe to us! What have we done? Are we to walk on a roof under which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) is? Will dust fall from us onto him? Are we to stand between him and the revelation of heaven?" Out of extreme manners and veneration, the couple could not walk in the middle of the room. Instead, they moved to the edges of the walls, creeping along the walls out of fear that their feet would step on a spot directly above the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) head.

The matter did not stop there; biography books narrate an exceedingly sweet incident when a water jar belonging to Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) broke on the upper floor. He and his wife panicked out of fear that the water would leak through the cracks of the roof and fall onto the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), causing him discomfort. On that cold night, they had nothing but a velvet blanket (quilt) to cover themselves with. They took it and hurriedly began wiping the water with it intensely and desperately, preferring the bitter cold over letting a single drop of water touch the body of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ).

Easier for the Guests... and Conversing with Heaven

With the dawn of the morning, Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) could not bear this psychological burden, so he went down to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) begging and pleading: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be a ransom for you, I hate to be above you while you are below me, so come up and be in the upper part, and we will go down to be in the lower part." But the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), the nurturing leader who places the comfort of his Ummah and his Dawah above all considerations, answered him with wisdom and mercy: "O Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب), the lower part is easier for us, and for those who visit us." He ﷺ knew that delegations of Muslims would flock to him day and night to learn and ask questions, so staying on the ground floor was easier for the people and less restrictive for the household.

Despite the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) settlement downstairs, Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) continued seeking blessings from him. He would cook food and send it to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), and when the leftovers were returned, Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) and his wife would trace the spots where the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) fingers had been and eat from there, seeking blessings and good omens. One day, Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) sent food that contained raw garlic and onions, and the food came back exactly as it was, untouched. Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) panicked and hurried down, asking fearfully: "Is it forbidden, O Messenger of Allah?" The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) answered, clarifying a refined ruling of taste and faith: "No, but I dislike it because of its smell; I converse privately with those whom you do not converse with." The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) did not forbid garlic and onions, but he abstained from them because the angels, led by Jibril (جبريل) peace be upon him, who brought him the revelation, are offended by what offends the children of Adam. Through this, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) established an Islamic methodology of paying close attention to pleasant scents and avoiding repulsive smells, especially in places of worship and social gatherings. He is the one who said: "Made beloved to me from your world are: women and perfume, and the coolness of my eyes was placed in prayer," ensuring that purity and pleasant fragrance remain a hallmark of a Muslim in both appearance and essence.

The Gathering of the Family and the Arrival of the Emigrants

With the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) settlement in the house of Abu Ayyub (أبو أيوب) and the start of arranging the affairs of the new state, he ﷺ turned his attention to his family whom he had left behind in Makkah (مكة) amidst an environment brimming with hostility. Despite the danger of the situation, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) sent Zayd bin Harithah (زيد بن حارثة) (his freedman and formerly his adopted son) and Abu Rafi' (أبو رافع), provided them with two camels and five hundred dirhams, and tasked them with returning to Makkah (مكة) to bring his family.

By the care and protection of Allah, the mission was successfully completed; his wife, the Mother of the Believers Sawdah bint Zam'ah (سودة بنت زمعة), may Allah be pleased with her, arrived, along with his daughters Fatimah Al-Zahra (فاطمة الزهراء) and Umm Kulthum (أم كلثوم) (as for Ruqayyah (رقية), she had already migrated with her husband Uthman bin Affan (عثمان بن عفان), and Zaynab (زينب) was held back in Makkah (مكة) by her husband Abu Al-Aas bin Al-Rabi' (أبو العاص بن الربيع) for a period). They were also accompanied by Usamah bin Zayd (أسامة بن زيد) and Umm Ayman (أم أيمن).

In the same caravan, the noble companion Abdullah bin Abi Bakr Al-Siddiq (عبد الله بن أبي بكر الصديق) came, escorting the family of Al-Siddiq (الصديق), led by Umm Ruman (أم رومان), Lady Aisha (عائشة) (who was engaged to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) at the time), and Lady Asma bint Abi Bakr (أسماء بنت أبي بكر), "The One with the Two Waistbands," who completed her migration while in the final months of her pregnancy. Upon her arrival in Quba (قباء), she gave birth to her son "Abdullah bin Al-Zubayr" (عبد الله بن الزبير), making him the first child born to the Muhajirun (المهاجرين) in Madinah. The Muslims shouted 'Allahu Akbar' in joy over his birth, which refuted the Jewish superstitions that they had cast magic on the Muslims so that no males would be born to them.

With the arrival of this caravan, the Prophetic family was united, and the Muhajirun (المهاجرين) arrived one after another, turning the page on Makkah (مكة) with all its pains and persecutions, and beginning new chapters in the corridors of Madinah—a story of stability, building, and launching toward universality.

5. The Ordeal of "God's Most Disease-Ridden Land"... and the Nostalgia of the Emigrants Soothed by Prayers of Heaven

The migration to Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة) was not merely a geographical move from one spot to another; it was an extremely harsh test of faith, psychology, and physical endurance. No sooner had the joy of arrival subsided, and the Muhajirun (المهاجرين) settled into the homes of the Ansar (الأنصار), than they collided with a severely bitter environmental and health reality. The agricultural nature of "Yathrib" (يثرب) and its abundance of water and palm trees differed radically from the dry, pure air of Makkah (مكة) where they had grown up.

Historically, before the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), Yathrib (يثرب) was known as a disease-ridden environment, plagued by a fierce endemic fever known as "Yathrib Fever" (حمى يثرب). The Mother of the Believers Aisha (عائشة), may Allah be pleased with her, described this harsh reality by saying: "We came to Madinah, and it was the most disease-ridden land of Allah (أَوْبَأُ أَرْضِ اللَّهِ)." Soon, this epidemic swept through the bodies of the Muhajirun (المهاجرين), who were already exhausted by travel, weakened by hunger, and affected by climate change. They collapsed into their beds, stricken by a severe fever that inflamed their bodies and drained their strength, marking the beginning of a new chapter of trials, affirming the Almighty's saying: {And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient - وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم بِشَيْءٍ مِّنَ الْخَوْفِ وَالْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْأَنفُسِ وَالثَّمَرَاتِ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ الصَّابِرِينَ}.

Between Fever and Nostalgia for the Homeland... The Moans of Al-Siddiq and Bilal

Among those hit hardest by the fever were the successor of the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق), his Mu'adhin (caller to prayer) Bilal bin Rabah (بلال بن رباح), and the companion Amir bin Fuhayrah (عامر بن فُهيرة), may Allah be pleased with them all. Lady Aisha (عائشة) narrates that she entered to visit them while they were sick before the veil (Hijab) was mandated, and found them in a state of severe exhaustion and delirium from the intense heat.

She asked her father Al-Siddiq (الصديق): "O father, how do you find yourself?" And from the intensity of the fever that made him lose and regain consciousness, he saw death right before his eyes, and recited poetry saying:
Every man wakes up safe among his family...
Yet death is closer to him than the strap of his sandal.
(Meaning that a person may wake up safely among his family, while death is closer to him than his shoelace).

She then turned to Bilal (بلال), that towering mountain who bore the rock of Umayyah bin Khalaf (أمية بن خلف) on the scorching sands of Makkah (مكة) without uttering a groan. Now, she found him defeated by the fever, and whenever he woke from his delirium, he would raise his voice with verses dripping with pain and an overwhelming longing for Makkah (مكة). He wished he could return to spend just one night in its valleys, breathing in the scent of its desert plants (Idhkhir and Jalil), drinking from the waters of its markets (Majannah), and soothing his eyes by looking at its mountains (Shamah and Tafil). He would chant mournfully:
Would that I knew if I shall ever spend a night...
In a valley with Idhkhir and Jalil around me.
And shall I ever, one day, go down to the waters of Majannah...
And shall Shamah and Tafil ever appear to me?

Bilal (بلال) did not stop at nostalgia; he remembered the leaders of polytheism who were the reason for driving them out of their birthplace to this disease-ridden land, and he cursed them fervently, saying: "O Allah, curse Shaybah bin Rabi'ah (شيبة بن ربيعة), Utbah bin Rabi'ah (عتبة بن ربيعة), and Umayyah bin Khalaf (أمية بن خلف), just as they drove us out of our land to the land of disease."

This nostalgia was a pure human instinct; souls are naturally predisposed to love their homelands. So how could it be when this homeland was "Makkah" (مكة), the most beloved of Allah's lands to Allah, and the most beloved of Allah's lands to the heart of His Messenger ﷺ? The Muhajirun (المهاجرين) were overwhelmed by the alienation of being away from home, the loss of wealth, physical illness, and psychological depression.

The Prophetic Intervention: A Prayer that Rewrote Geography and History

The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) saw the affliction that had befallen his companions and knew that building the state of Islam could not rise on sickly bodies and souls attached to a distant past. Here, material solutions were of no use against an endemic disease. Thus, the Merciful Leader raised his hands to the One who holds the keys of the heavens and the earth, and supplicated with a comprehensive prayer that changed the nature of Madinah forever, saying:
"O Allah, make us love Madinah as much as we love Makkah or even more, make it healthy, bless us in its Sa' (صاع) and Mudd (مُد) [measures of food], and transfer its fever and place it in Al-Juhfah (الجُحْفة)."

This Prophetic prayer acted as a comprehensive cure (psychological, environmental, and economic). He first asked Allah to uproot the pain of alienation from their hearts and plant in its place a love for Madinah that exceeded their love for Makkah (مكة). Then he asked to "make it healthy," meaning to purify its environment from diseases, and asked for economic blessing in its measuring units (Sa' and Mudd) to compensate them for the wealth they had left behind. Finally, he asked Allah to tear this epidemic out by its roots and move it to a distant area called "Al-Juhfah" (الجُحْفة) (which is the Miqat [station for entering Ihram] for the people of the Levant and Egypt today, and was back then the territory of polytheists).

Divine Response and the Glad Tidings in a Dream

The support of Heaven was not delayed; Allah fully answered the prayer of His Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ). The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) narrated a dream to his companions—and the dreams of Prophets are revelation and truth—as glad tidings that the hardship would vanish, saying: "I saw in a dream a black woman with disheveled hair (meaning frizzy hair and a frightening appearance) leaving Madinah until she settled in Mahya'ah (which is Al-Juhfah - الجُحْفة), so I interpreted it that the epidemic of Madinah had been transferred to it."

Since that promised day, the fever dissipated, the air of Madinah was purified, and the pains of the companions vanished. Even greater than that, Allah poured into their hearts an astonishing love for Yathrib (يثرب), until its old name was abrogated and the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) named it "Taybah" (طَيْبَة) and "Tabah" (طَابَة) due to its goodness and purity.

In fact, the blessing of this Prophetic prayer is still active in the hearts of believers until the Day of Judgment; there is no Muslim who visits Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة) today except that he feels a tranquility that overwhelms his soul, a love that captivates his heart, and a psychological comfort that he does not find in any other place on earth. Through the prayers of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), "God's most disease-ridden land" was transformed into a sanctuary for faith, a capital of light, and a safe haven where hunting and cutting its trees are forbidden just as Makkah (مكة) was made forbidden [sacred]. Thus, it became a homeland to which the hearts of the believers flock, and a refuge they yearn for whenever they are away from it.

6. The Map of the New Medinan Society: A Mosaic of Challenges and the Birth of a State

The "Yathrib" (يثرب) to which the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) migrated did not resemble "Makkah" (مكة) in any way. Makkah (مكة) was a relatively homogeneous society governed by the customs of Quraysh (قريش) and overshadowed by the doctrine of polytheism. Madinah, on the other hand, was a highly complex demographic, social, and religious "mosaic," torn by wars, congested with conflicts, and its power centers were distributed among mutually hostile forts and tribes.

The entry of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) into this battlefield was not mere political asylum or a relocation of displaced preachers; rather, it marked the establishment of a state that required an exceptional political mind, and a Prophet supported by revelation, to deal with a societal map divided into three main blocs, each with its own motives, ambitions, and fears.

First: The Believers (Muhajirun and Ansar)... The Striking Force and the Solid Foundation

The first bloc was the solid core of the nascent state, consisting of two halves that merged to create a human miracle:

  • The Muhajirun (المهاجرون): These are the ones who left their homes, wealth, and history in Makkah (مكة), arriving in Madinah owning nothing but their pure faith. They stripped themselves of all worldly fortunes for the sake of Allah, and regarding them, the Almighty's verse was revealed: {For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and [His] approval and supporting Allah and His Messenger, [there is also a share]. Those are the truthful - لِلْفُقَرَاءِ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ الَّذِينَ أُخْرِجُوا مِن دِيَارِهِمْ وَأَمْوَالِهِمْ يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًا مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوَانًا وَيَنصُرُونَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الصَّادِقُونَ}.
  • The Ansar (الأنصار) (Aws and Khazraj - الأوس والخزرج): These were the owners of the land and agriculture, who opened their homes and hearts to their displaced brothers. They did not just provide shelter; they willingly shared their wealth and farms with the Muhajirun (المهاجرين). The Quran immortalized them with the greatest medal: {And [also for] those who were settled in the Home [Madinah] and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what they [the emigrants] were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation - وَالَّذِينَ تَبَوَّءُوا الدَّارَ وَالْإِيمَانَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ يُحِبُّونَ مَنْ هَاجَرَ إِلَيْهِمْ وَلَا يَجِدُونَ فِي صُدُورِهِمْ حَاجَةً مِّمَّا أُوتُوا وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ}. This genius integration created the "striking force" that would defend the state entity and carry the message of Islam to the worlds.

Second: Polytheists and Hypocrites... The Broken Crown and the Grudge of "Ibn Salul"

Not all the people of Madinah entered Islam at once; a segment of Arabs remained upon polytheism. They were divided into two parts:

  • The Neutrals: A group of elders and commoners who clung to the religion of their forefathers out of habit, but they did not show direct hostility toward the Muslims. They remained observing the scene until their chests were later opened to Islam through daily interaction with the morals of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) and his companions.
  • The Spiteful and Power-Hungry: Here emerges the most dangerous figure in Medinan history: Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul (عبد الله بن أُبيّ بن سلول). To understand the complex of this man, we must go back in time five years before the Hijrah (الهجرة), to the "Day of Bu'ath" (يوم بُعاث); a grinding civil war that consumed everything between the tribes of Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج), wherein senior leaders of both tribes were killed. After the war exhausted them, the Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج) agreed for the first time to appoint a king over them to stop the bloodshed, and the choice fell on "Ibn Salul" (ابن سلول) (the leader of Khazraj). They were actually forging the crown for him and stringing its beads to crown him king of Yathrib (يثرب). Just as he was preparing to ascend the throne, the light of Islam shone, and the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) entered Madinah. The Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج) rallied around the Prophetic leadership, and the dream of "Ibn Salul" (ابن سلول) evaporated in a single moment. Ibn Salul (ابن سلول) looked at the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) not as a Prophet, but as a "usurper of his kingdom." Although he showed explicit enmity initially, after the crushing victory of the Muslims in the Battle of "Badr" (بدر), he realized that an open confrontation was a lost cause. So, he falsely wore the cloak of Islam to strike the religion from within, establishing the most dangerous fifth column in history, fittingly becoming the "Head of the Hypocrites" about whom Allah said regarding him and his followers: {Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire - إِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ مِنَ النَّارِ}.

Third: The Jews... The Racial Complex and Awaiting the Promised Prophet

The third and most complex bloc was the Jewish tribes (Banu Qaynuqa' - بنو قينقاع, Banu Al-Nadir - بنو النضير, and Banu Qurayzah - بنو قريظة). The important historical question is: What brought the Jews from the cold lands of the Levant to settle in the hot, desolate oases of the Hijaz? The answer lies in the "Torah" (التوراة). The Jews had suffered massacres and displacement at the hands of the Assyrians, then the Romans, so they knew from the prophecies in their holy books that the Prophet of the End of Times would soon be sent, and that his place of migration would be in a land of palm trees between two Harrahs (black volcanic lands). The rabbis tracked the signs until they settled in Yathrib (يثرب) and its surroundings (like Khaybar - خيبر and Fadak - فدك), waiting for the emergence of this Prophet so they could be his first followers, and reclaim their lost glory through him.

The Jews entirely controlled the economy of Madinah; they monopolized the weapons industry, gold trade, and agriculture, and enslaved the Arabs through the exorbitant system of "Usury" (الربا). Whenever a dispute arose between them and the Arabs (Aws - الأوس and Khazraj - الخزرج), they would act arrogantly toward them and threaten them, saying: "The time of a Prophet has overshadowed us; we will follow him and together we will slaughter you with the slaughter of 'Aad and Iram!" The Quran recorded this strange threat in the Almighty's words: {And previously they used to seek victory against those who disbelieved - وَكَانُوا مِن قَبْلُ يَسْتَفْتِحُونَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا}.

However, when the Promised Prophet appeared and migrated to Madinah, the great shock struck the Jewish rabbis. They found the Prophet matching all the descriptions literally, as the Almighty said: {Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their [own] sons - الَّذِينَ آتَيْنَاهُمُ الْكِتَابَ يَعْرِفُونَهُ كَمَا يَعْرِفُونَ أَبْنَاءَهُمُ}. But the complex lay in the "lineage"; the Prophet came from the descendants of "Ishmael" (إسماعيل) (the Arabs), and not from the descendants of "Isaac and Jacob" (إسحاق ويعقوب) (the Children of Israel) as they had desired.

Nationalistic arrogance, racial discrimination, and the fear of losing their spiritual and economic monopoly blinded them, so they disbelieved in the Prophet they had long awaited. They transformed from bearers of glad tidings about him into his most bitter enemies, fulfilling the eloquent Quranic statement: {But when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it; so the curse of Allah will be upon the disbelievers - فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُم مَّا عَرَفُوا كَفَرُوا بِهِ ۚ فَلَعْنَةُ اللَّهِ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ}.

In the midst of this complex, mine-filled scene: between the enthusiasm of the new believers, the conspiracies of a dethroned king hiding behind hypocrisy, and a Jewish religious and economic bloc overflowing with racism and envy... the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ) had to lay the foundations of the first civil state in Islam, with political and educational steps of sheer genius.

7. The Test of Absolute Truth: Jewish Rabbis Between the Blindness of Arrogance and the Insight of Fairness

When the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) settled in Madinah, the Jewish community was experiencing a state of silent turmoil. The man they had threatened the Arabs with had appeared, migrating to the land designated by their Torah, possessing the exact physical attributes and precise signs. It was not the common Jews who took center stage in those historical moments, but rather the "Ahbar" (الأحبار) (Rabbis); the senior scholars who memorized the sacred texts by heart.

In those early days, the reactions of the senior Jewish scholars divided into two contradictory human models; the first representing the peak of arrogance and racial envy, and the second representing the peak of detachment, fairness, and the pursuit of truth.

The First Scene: Huyayy bin Akhtab (حُيَيّ بن أخطب)... The Testimony of Truth and the Blindness of Arrogance

"Huyayy bin Akhtab" (حيي بن أخطب) was the leader of the Banu Al-Nadir (بني النضير) tribe and one of the greatest Jewish rabbis in the Arabian Peninsula. As soon as he heard of the Prophet's ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) arrival in Quba (قباء), he and his brother "Abu Yasir" (أبو ياسر) went out early in the morning and did not return until sunset. They spent the entire day closely observing the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), scrutinizing his features, probing the depths of his speech, looking for the "Seal of Prophethood" (خاتم النبوة) between his shoulders, and matching everything they saw with the attributes of the Promised Prophet in the scriptures they had.

The brothers returned to their home exhausted, dragging their feet heavily, clad in deep gloom. Here emerges the narration of Lady "Safiyyah bint Huyayy" (صفية بنت حيي) (who was a little girl at the time, and later became the Mother of the Believers). Safiyyah (صفية), may Allah be pleased with her, narrates that she was the most beloved of her father's and uncle's children to them. As soon as she saw them, she ran toward them as usual to welcome them and play with them, but the shock was that they did not pay attention to her out of the sheer worry and grief that dominated their features.

The little girl stepped back, watching the scene in amazement, and listened to a historic dialogue between the two brothers—a dialogue that unveiled the deepest diseases of the human soul. Abu Yasir (أبو ياسر) asked his brother Huyayy bin Akhtab (حيي بن أخطب) in a trembling voice: "Is it him?" (Meaning, is he the Prophet written about in our Torah?). Huyayy (حيي) answered with absolute certainty: "Yes, by Allah, it is him!" Abu Yasir (أبو ياسر) said: "Do you recognize him and confirm it?" (Are you completely sure of his signs?). Huyayy (حيي) said: "Yes." Then Abu Yasir (أبو ياسر) asked him the most dangerous question: "So what is in your soul regarding him?" (What shall we do now that we know the truth?). Huyayy bin Akhtab (حيي بن أخطب) uttered his phrase that history recorded as the title of stubbornness: "His enmity, by Allah, for as long as I live!"

Huyayy bin Akhtab (حيي بن أخطب) was absolutely certain of the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) without a shadow of a doubt, but he could not bear the idea that Prophethood would transfer from the tribes of the Children of Israel (descendants of Isaac and Jacob) to the Arabs (descendants of Ishmael). National envy blinded him from following the truth, so he decided to fight a losing battle against Allah and His Messenger. The Holy Quran immortalized this complex psychological state in the Almighty's saying: {Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed, out of envy from themselves [even] after the truth has become clear to them - وَدَّ كَثِيرٌ مِّنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ لَوْ يَرُدُّونَكُم مِّن بَعْدِ إِيمَانِكُمْ كُفَّارًا حَسَدًا مِّنْ عِندِ أَنفُسِهِم مِّن بَعْدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الْحَقُّ}, and His Almighty saying: {But when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it - فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُم مَّا عَرَفُوا كَفَرُوا بِهِ}. (It is an amazing irony that the little girl "Safiyyah" (صفية) memorized this incident in her heart, and it was one of the greatest reasons for her later conversion to Islam when she fell into captivity in the Battle of Khaybar (خيبر), as she knew her father was fighting a Prophet whose truthfulness he had acknowledged).
