The Second Scene: Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سَلَام)... The Light of Insight and the Speed of Slander

In stark contrast to Huyayy (حيي), there was a man named "Al-Husain bin Salam" (الحُصين بن سَلَام) (whom the Prophet ﷺ later named Abdullah). This man was an elder of the Banu Qaynuqa' (بني قينقاع) tribe, and one of their rabbis, attested to for his piety, abundant knowledge, and absolute impartiality.

When the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) arrived and people gathered around him, Al-Husain (الحصين) went to push through the crowds to see this man. He was not looking for flaws; rather, he was opening the windows of his soul in search of the light of truth. As soon as his eyes fell on the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ), the sun of faith rose in his heart before he even heard a single letter from him. Describing that defining moment in his life, Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سلام) says: "When I clearly saw his face, I knew that his face was not the face of a liar." He read in the radiant features of Prophethood, his luminous forehead, and his calm and dignity, the message of Heaven that no human could fabricate.

Then he strained his ears to catch the first words to be spoken by this Prophet coming to establish a state. Were they the words of a bloodthirsty leader? Or a king seeking power? No, he heard the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) say in his gentle, sweet voice: "O people, spread peace, feed the hungry, maintain the ties of kinship, and pray at night while people are sleeping, and you will enter Paradise in peace." Words dripping with mercy, overflowing with humanity, linking the righteousness of society to the worship of the Creator, the Glorious and Exalted. Ibn Salam (ابن سلام) became certain that this was the clear truth, so he rushed to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) and declared his Islam immediately, and his household embraced Islam with him.

However, Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سلام) was an expert on the psychological makeup of his people, aware of their tribalism and their propensity to twist facts. So, he asked the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) to conduct a test for them that would reveal their true nature before the Muslims. He said to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, the Jews are a people of slander (they quickly slander and lie against people), and if they learn of my Islam before you ask them about me, they will slander me before you."

The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) hid Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سلام) in a room inside his house and sent for the senior Jews. When they sat down, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) asked them to get their admission: "What kind of man is Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سلام) among you?" They all chimed in, praising him with the finest descriptions, saying: "He is our best and the son of our best, our master and the son of our master, our most knowledgeable and the son of our most knowledgeable." The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) then pre-empted them by asking: "What would you think if Abdullah (عبد الله) embraced Islam?" They panicked and said in one voice, denouncing the idea: "May Allah protect him from that! God forbid he becomes a Muslim!"

In that decisive moment, Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سلام) emerged from the room, stood tall before them, and pronounced the two testimonies of faith (Shahadah): "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." What happened? Did they respect the man they were describing just seconds ago as their "master and most knowledgeable"? Never; they flipped instantly, wore the garment of slander, and shouted, insulting him with the ugliest words, saying: "He is our worst and the son of our worst, and our most ignorant and the son of our most ignorant." And they began belittling and cursing him.

Abdullah bin Salam (عبد الله بن سلام) turned to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) saying: "Did I not tell you, O Messenger of Allah, that they are a people of slander?" The Holy Quran immortalized the stance of this great, fair scholar in Surah Al-Ahqaf (الأحقاف), serving as an argument against anyone who knew the truth and concealed it, as the Almighty said: {Say, "Have you considered: if the Qur'an was from Allah, and you disbelieved in it while a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to something similar and believed while you were arrogant... ?" Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people - قُلْ أَرَأَيْتُمْ إِن كَانَ مِنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ وَكَفَرْتُم بِهِ وَشَهِدَ شَاهِدٌ مِّن بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ عَلَىٰ مِثْلِهِ فَآمَنَ وَاسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ}.

Thus, the features of the conflict began to take shape in Madinah; a conflict between hearts that opened to the light and became enlightened, and minds closed by arrogance and envy, getting lost in the darkness of stubbornness.

8. The Pillars of the Great Foundation: How Did the Prophet ﷺ Build the Greatest State in History?

The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) had barely settled in the hospitality of Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari (أبو أيوب الأنصاري) when he immediately began transforming "Yathrib" (يثرب) from merely a fragmented tribal oasis into a "state" with sovereignty and institutions. State-building was not random; it was built upon three solid strategic pillars representing spirit, society, and law.

The First Pillar: The Mosque and the Adhan... Building the Spirit and the Center of Leadership

The first and most sacred task was designating a space from which the lights of Prophethood would launch; to be a mosque, a school, a headquarters for leadership, and a parliament for consultation (Shura). The place where the she-camel knelt was a "Mirbad" (مِرْبَد) (a place for drying dates) belonging to two orphan boys named Sahl (سهل) and Suhayl (سهيل) under the guardianship of the companion As'ad bin Zurarah (أسعد بن زرارة). The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) called the two boys and offered to buy the land from them. With pure nature and love, they said: "Rather, we gift it to you, O Messenger of Allah." However, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), the Supreme Legislator, refused to build the first edifice of Islam on a grant taken from the rights of orphans. He insisted on buying it for its price to ensure justice and clear his conscience, and he paid for it from the wealth of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق), may Allah be pleased with him.

The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) ordered the preparation of the land; old graves of polytheists located there were dug up (since they held no sanctity), palm trees were cut down, and the ground was leveled. Then the construction began, and here the greatest forms of leadership were displayed. The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) did not sit on a throne directing the workers; rather, he rolled up his honorable sleeves and engaged with the companions, carrying unbaked bricks (Laban - اللبِن) and stones until his chest was covered in dust. The building was materially modest but spiritually towering; its walls were of mud, its pillars were palm trunks, its roof was made of palm fronds and leaves, and its Qiblah (direction of prayer) at the time was toward Jerusalem (بيت المقدس). During the work, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) chanted poetry to raise the morale of his companions, saying:
O Allah, there is no life but the life of the Hereafter...
So forgive the Ansar (الأنصار) and the Muhajirah (المهاجرة).
And the companions responded to him with immense enthusiasm:
This burden is not the burden of Khaybar (خيبر)...
This is more righteous in the sight of our Lord, and purer.
(Meaning that the fatigue in building the mosque carries greater blessing and a purer reward than the spoils and luxuries of Khaybar). This majestic scene moved one of the companions to recite:
(If we sit while the Prophet works... then our action is a misguided deed).

As the mosque was completed, a problem arose: How do we gather for prayer? The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) consulted his companions. One suggested raising a flag, which he disliked. Others suggested lighting a fire (like the Magians/Zoroastrians), ringing a bell (like the Christians), or blowing a horn (like the Jews). The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) disliked all of these out of a desire for the independence of the Ummah and its distinction from other nations. The companions returned to their homes carrying the concern of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (رسول الله ﷺ). That night, the honorable companion "Abdullah bin Zayd" (عبد الله بن زيد) had a wondrous dream; he saw a man carrying a bell, so he asked to buy it from him to call to prayer. The spiritual man in the dream said to him: "Shall I not guide you to what is better than that? You say: Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar... (and he taught him the words of the Adhan and Iqamah)." When morning broke, Abdullah bin Zayd (عبد الله بن زيد) rushed to the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) to narrate his dream. The face of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) beamed with joy and he said: "It is a true vision, if Allah wills. Stand with Bilal (بلال), impart to him what you have seen, and let him call the Adhan with it, for he has a more resonant voice than you." As soon as Bilal (بلال) raised his melodious voice with the Adhan (الأذان), Umar bin Al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) rushed out dragging his cloak, swearing that he had seen exactly what Abdullah (عبد الله) saw. Thus, the legislation descended as a purely heavenly solution, and the Adhan (الأذان) became the emblem of the Ummah—not struck by iron hammers, but resounding from human throats, declaring Monotheism five times every day.

The Second Pillar: Brotherhood (Mu'akhah - المؤاخاة)... Integrating Society and the Miracle of Altruism

The second challenge was a social and economic one that almost tore the state apart. The Muhajirun (المهاجرين) arrived in Madinah barefoot, naked, and stripped of their wealth, while the Ansar (الأنصار) were people of agriculture and orchards. To bridge this massive gap, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) held a historic pact in the house of Anas bin Malik (أنس بن مالك) (and some say in the Mosque) called the "Mu'akhah" (المؤاخاة) (Brotherhood).

The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) established brotherhood between ninety men (half of them Muhajirun and half Ansar)—a true brotherhood, not mere slogans. It was a brotherhood based on sharing wealth and inheriting after death (before the verse of inheritance was later abrogated by the verses of fixed inheritances). In this event, the Ansar (الأنصار) recorded the greatest epic of altruism in human history, to the point that Allah immortalized their deed in the Quran: {And they give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation - وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ}. Among the most magnificent examples of this epic is what happened between the Ansari (الأنصاري) "Sa'd bin Al-Rabi'" (سعد بن الربيع) and the Muhajir (المهاجري) "Abd al-Rahman bin Awf" (عبد الرحمن بن عوف). Sa'd (سعد) took his brother Abd al-Rahman (عبد الرحمن) and said to him with a sincerity that shakes the soul: "O my brother, I am the wealthiest of the people of Madinah, so look at half of my wealth and take it! And I have two wives, so see which of them is more pleasing to you so I may divorce her, and when her waiting period ends, you can marry her!" What giving goes beyond the limits of the human mind! But Abd al-Rahman bin Awf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف), representing the dignity, chastity, and ambition of the Muhajirun (المهاجرين), responded with words written in gold: "May Allah bless you in your family and your wealth; show me the way to the market." Abd al-Rahman (عبد الرحمن) went to trade in dried yogurt and ghee, starting from scratch, until he became one of the wealthiest companions. Through this Mu'akhah (المؤاخاة), the ice melted, class divisions were erased, the economic crisis was solved, and the ranks of the Muslims were welded together like a solid structure.

The Third Pillar: The Document of Madinah (وثيقة المدينة)... The First Civil Constitution in History

After securing the internal front for the Muslims, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), the Great Political Leader, turned his attention to securing the external front of Madinah and defining the relationship with the other blocs, especially the Jews and the polytheists. The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) drafted a written book (document) which, by modern political standards, is considered the "first comprehensive civil constitution" known to history. Islam was not imposed on anyone by the sword; rather, it established the concept of "shared citizenship."

The document included genius clauses, among them:

  • 1. Unity of the Islamic Ummah: The Muslims, both Muhajirun (المهاجرين) and Ansar (الأنصار), are one Ummah to the exclusion of other people.
  • 2. Freedom of Belief and Religious Tolerance: The constitution explicitly acknowledged religious freedom for the Jews: "The Jews have their religion, and the Muslims have their religion."
  • 3. Mutual Defense: Yathrib (يثرب) (Madinah) is a sacred sanctuary for the people of this document, and the Muslims and Jews must jointly defend it if it is attacked by an external enemy, with each party spending from its own wealth during war.
  • 4. Criminal and Social Solidarity: Cooperation in paying blood money (Diyyat - الديات) and ransoming captives.
  • 5. The Supreme Reference of Revelation: This is the most important clause that imposed the sovereignty of the Islamic State; that any dispute between the factions of Madinah must have its judgment referred back to Allah and His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ. This is an application of the Almighty's saying: {And if you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger - فَإِن تَنَازَعْتُمْ فِي شَيْءٍ فَرُدُّوهُ إِلَى اللَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ}.

Through these three pillars: (The Mosque to purify souls and connect them to Heaven), (The Brotherhood to unite the internal ranks and solve crises), and (The Document to regulate political and legal relations)... the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) succeeded in record time in transforming a group of displaced emigrants and previously warring Ansar into a single body. Thus, he established the greatest launchpad that would carry the light of Islam from the muddy alleys of Madinah to the palaces of Chosroes and Caesar, and to the eastern and western ends of the earth.

1. The Practical Role Model and the Secret Mix Between "Reality" and "Online" (1. القدوة العملية وسر الخلطة بين "الواقع" و"الأونلاين")

When the caravan of the migration settled in the heart of the city, the foundation of the new state did not begin with formal decrees and protocols, but rather with "fieldwork." The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) began building the Prophet's Mosque (المسجد النبوي), and here the genius of Islamic leadership manifests; the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) did not sit on a chair to direct the workers or merely theorize, but rolled up his honorable sleeves and engaged in the construction. He carried stones and adobe (اللَّبِن) with his companions until his chest was covered in dust, and he chanted poetry to raise morale, saying:
"This burden is not the burden of Khaibar (خيبر)... This is more pious and purer to our Lord."

In this chant lies a precise nuance; "Khaibar (خيبر)" in the Arab consciousness at that time represented immense wealth, money, and sprawling farms, to the point that the Mother of the Believers, Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her (عائشة رضي الله عنها), later said: "We did not eat our fill of barley bread until after the conquest of Khaibar" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari). The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) was instilling in their souls that this exhaustion and the dirt covering their bodies in building a house of Allah is greater, purer, and more blessed than all the treasures of the world and the luxury of Khaibar (خيبر).

This practical scene ignited the enthusiasm of the Companions, so they rushed to work with maximum energy, chanting:
"If we were to sit while the Prophet works... That would be from us a misguided deed."

The Crisis of Theorizing and the Absence of Role Models:

From this foundational scene, we derive a golden rule in Dawah (calling to Islam) and reform: "Reality needs practical role models, not excessive theorizing." Texts, lectures, books, and resonant sermons fill the horizons, but what truly changes societies is the "living role model." This Prophetic methodology was evident in various situations, such as his digging of the trench with his companions on the Day of the Confederates (الأحزاب), and his initiative to slaughter his sacrificial animal and shave his head on the Day of Al-Hudaibiyah (الحديبية) when the people hesitated; as soon as they saw him do that, they raced to follow his example. This fulfills the Almighty’s saying: {There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern}.

Here emerges an individual duty upon every Muslim; instead of lamenting one's luck, constantly complaining about the corruption of the times, and weeping over the absence of role models, sheikhs, and preachers in mosques and neighborhoods, the question should be: "Why don't you be this role model?". If your neighborhood lacks someone to teach people the Quran, be the teacher. If your mosque lacks a circle of knowledge or fatwa, strive to fill this gap yourself. A Muslim must not live the role of a passive victim; rather, he must carry the concern of the religion and make of himself a role model for the youth to follow, even if it requires a period of patience and qualification.

The Mosque as an Incubator for Upbringing... and the Issue of "Online" vs. "Reality":

The first Prophet's Mosque (المسجد النبوي) was simple in its structure; its pillars were palm trunks, and its floor was gravel, but it was "everything" in the life of the nascent nation. It was a university for sciences, a parliament for consultation, a headquarters for leadership, and a shelter for the poor and full-time seekers of knowledge (Ahl As-Suffah - أهل الصُّفَّة) like Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him (أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه). Within its walls, minds were shaped, and souls were refined through direct interaction.

From here, we move to a highly important contemporary projection that touches the life of every seeker of knowledge and religion today: Where do we learn? And how are we raised?
Technology has brought about a real revolution; distance learning (Online) has become a great blessing that breaks the barriers of time and space. A Muslim can now, while in his car or room, listen to senior scholars in the East and West, and complete texts and courses in record time. But, is "Online" enough to build a sound Muslim or a true seeker of knowledge?

The definitive answer: No.
Distance learning may give you the "information" quickly, but it never gives you "manners, behavior, and upbringing." The "Online" student of knowledge might listen to the greatest lessons of creed or jurisprudence while leaning back on his bed, or wearing inappropriate clothes, or eating, drinking, and playing, and if he gets bored, he pauses (Pause) the lesson to attend to worldly matters. This pattern, despite its cognitive benefit, strips knowledge gatherings of their prestige, deprives the student of the tranquility of the angels that cover circles of remembrance, and produces a generation that may memorize much but lacks the simplest rules of humility and respect for knowledge.

The pious predecessors used to prioritize "upbringing and manners" over the acquisition of information. The mother of Imam Malik (الإمام مالك) told him when he was a boy: "Go to Rabiah (ربيعة) and learn from his manners before his knowledge," and Abdullah bin Al-Mubarak (عبد الله بن المبارك) said: "We are in more need of a little manners than a lot of knowledge."

Actually sitting in the mosque, bending one's knees before the teacher, adhering to the etiquette of the gathering from beginning to end, and bearing the hardship of sitting and discipline... is what inherits the tranquility of knowledge. In a direct meeting, you don't just learn from the words, but you learn from the "margins of the lesson"; you learn how the teacher enters, how he smiles, how he greets, how he answers the questioner, and how he gets angry for the sake of Allah. Sisters learn from their female teacher her modesty and demeanor before her tongue even speaks.

Furthermore, "Righteous Companionship" is not built through phone screens and virtual social media groups. True brotherhood requires physical and spatial interaction; where glances intersect, flaws are discovered and corrected with advice, and we share the smiles, humor, consolation, and situations that polish souls and melt their hardness.

Conclusion: The successful equation in our era is "mixing and balancing." Take from the "Online" its speed, abundance, and diversity to increase your cognitive outcome and fill your free time. But beware of abandoning "Reality"; establish for yourself a permanent foothold in a mosque, a knee you bend before a sheikh or educator, and righteous companions you sit with face-to-face, to acquire the manners, demeanor, and chivalry that can never be transmitted through wires and screens.

2. The Story of the Adhan: Between "Tacit Sunnah" and the Jurisprudence of Specializations (2. قصة الأذان: بين "السنة التقريرية" وفقه التخصصات)

The method of approving the "Adhan" (Call to Prayer) as a slogan for prayer was not merely a passing event in the Prophetic Biography; rather, it was an integrated school that established profound fundamental, administrative, and educational rules. Regardless of the details of the dream seen by the venerable companion Abdullah bin Zaid, may Allah be pleased with him (عبد الله بن زيد رضي الله عنه), the way the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) dealt with this event opens before us doors of jurisprudence and solid institutional understanding.

The Jurisprudential Lesson: Closing the Door to Innovation and Establishing the "Tacit Sunnah":

It is known in the principles of Islamic Jurisprudence (Usul al-Fiqh) that the "Prophetic Sunnah" from which legal rulings are derived is divided into three categories:

  1. Verbal Sunnah (سنة قولية): What the Prophet ﷺ spoke of hadiths and commands.
  2. Actional Sunnah (سنة فعلية): What the Prophet ﷺ performed of actions (like his method of prayer and pilgrimage).
  3. Tacit Sunnah (سنة تقريرية): Which is the focus here; it means that the Prophet ﷺ sees an action, or hears a saying from one of the companions, and he approves of it, agrees with it, and does not denounce it.

When Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) came to tell his dream, it could have been understood that "dreams" are valid as a source of legislation. This is a dangerous slippery slope where factions later stumbled, building their acts of worship and litanies on dreams they claimed to see. But the strict fundamentalist rule here is that the dream of Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) in itself is neither a revelation nor a legal proof, but rather it transformed into a "binding legislation" and "divine revelation" only at the moment the infallible Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) spoke, saying: "It is a true vision, God willing" (Narrated by Abu Dawood).

So, the approval of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) is what elevated the dream from being just a human dream to the rank of "Tacit Sunnah." And because revelation ceased with the death of the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), fulfilling the Almighty's saying: {This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion}, the door of legislation has been completely closed. No one has the right after the Prophet's ﷺ passing to the Highest Companion to invent an act of worship or a ruling under the pretext that he saw it in a dream; because the legislator and approver of rulings is no longer among us to ratify it. The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) settled this matter when he saw a man standing in the sun and asked about him. They said: Abu Israel (أبو إسرائيل), he vowed to stand and not sit, not to seek shade, not to speak, and to fast. The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) did not approve of this, and invalidated this extremism, saying: "Command him to speak, seek shade, sit down, and complete his fast" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari), confirming that the religion is by following what was approved, not by innovation and absolute personal reasoning.

The Administrative and Educational Lesson: The Jurisprudence of Specializations and Prioritizing Competence Over Emotion:

After the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) approved the dream of Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد), it would have come to mind, and even been customary by human standards, that the owner of the dream would attain the honor of raising this eternal call, as a kind of emotional reward for his precedence and the heavens honoring him with this vision.

But the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ), the leader and founder, was building a "state" where there is no room for favoritism at the expense of quality. The Prophet ﷺ looked at the nature of the task; the Adhan is an announcement and a call that needs to reach far distances, and it requires a tone that humbles hearts and is familiar to the ears. Here, the genius of the "jurisprudence of specializations" manifested, so the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) said to Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) clearly and decisively: "Stand with Bilal (بلال) and cast upon him what you have seen, and let him call the Adhan with it, for he has a more carrying (melodious) voice than you."

With these words: "a more carrying voice than you," Islam established an eternal administrative rule: "Tasks are assigned to those with competencies and specializations, not to those with precedence and emotions." The precedence of the dream did not intercede for Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) to take on a task for which he did not possess the best physical and vocal qualifications. This Prophetic methodology was repeated often; when the venerable companion Abu Dharr Al-Ghifari (أبو ذر الغفاري) wanted leadership, while he was of the most truthful in speech and earliest in Islam, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) clearly prevented him, saying: "O Abu Dharr, you are weak, and it is a trust, and on the Day of Resurrection it will be a disgrace and regret" (Narrated by Muslim). And when the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) called out on the Day of Uhud: "Who will take this sword with its right?", he bypassed senior heroes of the companions like Ali (علي), Az-Zubair (الزبير), and Umar (عمر), and gave it to Abu Dujanah (أبو دُجانة) because he possessed the specialization and combat skill required for that moment.

Purity of Heart and the "Seeking the Spotlight" Disease:

In contrast, the venerable companion Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) presented us with a refined human model of "selflessness and purity of heart." He did not argue, he did not get angry, he did not say, "This is my dream and it is my right to be at the forefront." Rather, he simply took the hand of Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him (بلال رضي الله عنه), and taught him the words to call out, and Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) never called the Adhan throughout his life!

This selflessness exposes the diseases of our present era, where many fight over positions of prominence, leading gatherings, microphones, and fame "trends," even if they do not possess the minimum level of competence and qualification. Abdullah bin Zaid (عبد الله بن زيد) understood a great Islamic rule: "The one who guides to good is like the one who does it" (Narrated by At-Tirmidhi). He knows with certainty that the reward of the Adhan raised by Bilal (بلال) also pours into his own scale without him standing in the front rows. Sincerity is performing your role that you master to serve the religion and society, whether you are in leadership and under the spotlight, or in the shadows behind the scenes.

Historical Benefit: The Institutional Distribution of Muezzins:

Confirming this institutional approach in assigning tasks, the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) was not content with one muezzin, but distributed this noble task among four of the companions known for the moisture and strength of their voices, to cover the geographical area of the nascent state. They were:

  1. Bilal bin Rabah (بلال بن رباح): The first and primary muezzin in the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah.
  2. Abdullah bin Umm Maktum (عبد الله بن أم مكتوم): The second muezzin in Madinah. He was a blind man, who alternated the Adhan with Bilal, especially in the Fajr (Dawn) prayer. About him the Prophet ﷺ said: "Bilal calls the Adhan at night, so eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls the Adhan" (Agreed upon).
  3. Abu Mahdhurah - Aws bin Mi'yar (أبو مَحْذُورَة - أوس بن مِعْيَر): The Prophet ﷺ appointed him as a muezzin for the people of Mecca after its conquest due to the beauty of his voice.
  4. Sa'd Al-Qaraz (سعد القَرَظ): The Prophet ﷺ made him a muezzin for the Quba Mosque (مسجد قُباء).

This precise distribution confirms that building states and societies is not based on randomness or monopolizing tasks, but rather on delegating authorities to those with carrying voices, sharp minds, and specialized skills in every field.

3. The Genius of "Brotherhood": Psychological Compatibility as a Tool for Dawah and Building Societies (3. عبقرية "المؤاخاة": التوافق النفسي كأداة للدعوة وبناء المجتمعات)

The story of "Brotherhood" (Al-Mu'akhah) between the Emigrants (المهاجرين) and the Helpers (الأنصار) is often presented in biography books, sermons, and lectures only from the angle of "emotional altruism and economic support." Despite the greatness of this aspect, a deep contemplation of this event, in which the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) gathered ninety men (half from the Muhajireen and half from the Ansar) in the house of Anas bin Malik (أنس بن مالك), reveals an unprecedented "administrative genius and psychological strategy" in social engineering and cultural integration.

The Depth of the Bond: A Brotherhood That Transcends Emotions to "Inheritance":

This brotherhood was not merely a slogan to be raised, nor a passing word said like "You are my brother in Allah," but it was a true legal and social contract with strong obligations; such as financial support, backing, sheltering the stranger, and even reached the point of "Inheritance". An Emigrant (المهاجر) would inherit from his Ansar (الأنصاري) brother after his death instead of his polytheist relatives, and the Ansari would inherit from his Muhajir brother. The Holy Quran descended confirming and approving this contract in the early days of the Medinan era. Allah says: {And for all, We have made heirs to what is left by parents and relatives. And to those whom your oaths have bound[to you] - give them their share} [An-Nisa: 33].

This great ruling continued for nearly two years, which were enough to fully integrate the Muhajireen into the fabric of the Medinan society and stabilize the pillars of the nascent state. When the situation settled, and the Muhajireen found jobs and trades, and the Muslims were victorious in the Great Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) and their power was established, revelation descended to return matters to their natural order, abrogating the ruling of inheritance through brotherhood, and returning inheritance to blood ties and kinship, fulfilling the Almighty’s saying at the end of Surah Al-Anfal: {But those of [blood] relationship are more entitled [to inheritance] in the decree of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things}.

The Strategy of "Psychological and Professional Compatibility":

The greatest challenge facing the Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) was not only providing food and shelter for the Muhajireen, but addressing the "shock of alienation"; an emigrant left behind his history, environment, and friends. Here the Prophetic genius in the integration process manifested, as the Prophet ﷺ did not link any two people randomly, but he read souls accurately, and paired those with "similarity and closeness in temperaments, skills, and thinking".

The Prophet ﷺ (النبي ﷺ) based these choices on a great psychological rule he later uttered when he said: "Souls are recruited troops; those who recognize one another will be friendly, and those who do not recognize one another will differ" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari and Muslim). Based on this spiritual harmony and mental similarity, the Prophetic choices were astounding:

  1. Compatibility of Commercial Mindset: The Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف) and Saad bin Ar-Rabi' (سعد بن الربيع). Both possessed a formidable economic mindset and were among the major merchants of Mecca and Madinah, creating a common language and mutual understanding of the secrets of the market and trade.
  2. Compatibility of Wisdom and Asceticism: The Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between Salman Al-Farsi (سلمان الفارسي) and Abu Ad-Darda (أبي الدرداء). Both carried a deep philosophical spirit, profound wisdom, asceticism in the world, and an aspiration to worship Allah and reflect on His creation. (The impact of this compatibility appeared later when Salman visited Abu Ad-Darda and corrected his lifestyle with his famous saying full of wisdom: "Your Lord has a right over you...").
  3. Compatibility of Knowledge and Jurisprudence: The Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between Muadh bin Jabal (معاذ بن جبل) and Ja'far bin Abi Talib (جعفر بن أبي طالب). Both were seekers of knowledge of the highest caliber. Muadh was the most knowledgeable of the Ummah regarding the lawful and prohibited, and Ja'far had an exceptional jurisprudential mind that manifested in his historical dialogue with An-Najashi (النجاشي) in Abyssinia (الحبشة).
  4. Compatibility of Chivalry and Courage: The Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between Talhah bin Ubaidullah (طلحة بن عبيد الله) and Ka'b bin Malik (كعب بن مالك). Both were known for valor, chivalry, and physical strength, so each provided military and psychological support to the other later on the battlefields of Uhud (أُحد) and others.

Contemporary Projection: The Art of "Individual Dawah" and Societal Integration:

This precise Prophetic methodology carries for us today a highly important message in the field of "Calling to Allah" (Dawah), specifically in what is known as (Individual Dawah). When a new youth begins practicing the religion, or enters a mosque for the first time, he feels an "alienating loneliness" because his old environment and interests differ from the environment of the mosque and the worshippers.

If we leave this youth to integrate randomly, he might clash with someone whose temperament does not match his, and he might turn away from the path of uprightness entirely. Therefore, the wise preacher is the one who uses the "strategy of Prophetic brotherhood and compatibility" in connecting this invitee with the (righteous environment). If the new youth is a programmer or interested in technology, we connect him with a righteous brother in the mosque who has the same tech interests so they can speak their common language. If he is an athlete, we connect him with a practicing athletic youth who shares his hobby. If he loves reading and research, we entrust him to an educated and well-read youth to discuss with him.

This permissible (worldly similarity), whether in hobbies, specializations, or even personal traits (calmness, outgoingness, enthusiasm), is the safe bridge over which the meanings of religion and commitment cross smoothly. When the new youth finds someone who is like him, shares his worldly interests, and supports him in them, while at the same time helping him with his prayers and remembering his Lord, the "loneliness of beginnings" melts away completely. Religion transforms in his heart from mere dry commands and prohibitions into an integrated lifestyle and a righteous companionship that takes him by the hand to Paradise.

4. Societal Balance: When the Modesty of "Abdul Rahman" Meets the Generosity of "Saad" (4. التوازن المجتمعي: حينما تلتقي عفة "عبد الرحمن" بكرم "سعد")

In the midst of the epic of "Brotherhood", a historical situation stands out that is considered one of the greatest lessons in sociology and Islamic economics, which is the meeting that brought together the Muhajiri Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف), and the Ansari Saad bin Ar-Rabi' (سعد بن الربيع), may Allah be pleased with them. This situation is not just a story told to elicit emotions, but it is a school in psychological and societal balance.

The Imaginary Offer and Easy Solutions:

Saad bin Ar-Rabi' (سعد بن الربيع) was the wealthiest of the Ansar and had the most money. When the Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between him and Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف), who came to Madinah "from scratch" after being stripped of all his wealth in Mecca, Saad stood up to present an offer that breaks all materialistic human standards. He told him with complete sincerity: "I am the wealthiest of the Ansar, so I will divide my wealth in half, and I have two wives, look at the one that pleases you more, name her to me, I will divorce her, and when her waiting period ends, you marry her."

This is "absolute generosity," an offer that provides Abdul Rahman with a magical solution that saves him years of misery and fatigue; half the wealth of the richest man in Madinah, a house, and a wife, without any significant effort! The Quran recorded this high status by saying: {And they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful}.

The Pride of the Believer and Starting from Scratch:

But here the greatness of the Prophetic upbringing manifests in the soul of Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف). He was not overcome by the glitter of the offered wealth, nor did he exploit the feelings of his brother and his overflowing emotion, nor did he say: "I will take the money to get on my feet and then return it later." Rather, he replied with words dripping with modesty, chivalry, and certainty: "May Allah bless your family and your wealth for you; show me the way to the market."

Abdul Rahman did not sit crying over his lost commercial glories in Mecca, nor did he stipulate that he begin in Madinah as a manager or a major merchant as he was. Instead, he asked about the market of "Bani Qaynuqa (بني قينقاع)," and went down to start from zero. He bought and sold simple commodities that do not require massive capital, such as (Al-Aqit - الأَقِط) which is dried yogurt, and (Ghee - السَّمْن). He operated by the great Islamic rule established by the Prophet ﷺ when he said: "It is better for one of you to take his rope, bring a bundle of firewood on his back, sell it, and Allah protects his face by it, than to ask people, whether they give him or refuse him" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari), and in his saying: "Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one's own hands."

The Blessing of Striving and the Quick Marriage:

Only a few days of tireless work and perseverance passed until Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف) came to the Prophet ﷺ bearing traces of "Khaluq" (خَلُوق - a yellow perfume and adornment worn by a groom). The Prophet ﷺ rejoiced and asked him, surprised by the speed of the accomplishment: "Mahyam?" (مَهْيَم - meaning: what is your situation or your news?). He replied with the confidence of a self-made man: "I married a woman from the Ansar." So the Prophet ﷺ asked him: "How much Mahr (dowry) did you give her?" He said: "A gold piece the weight of a date pit." The Prophet ﷺ said to him, blessing his effort and modesty: "May Allah bless you; give a wedding banquet (Walimah), even with one sheep" (Agreed upon).

With this tremendous effort, Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف) proved that "movement is a blessing," and that a positive Muslim does not accept unemployment and does not wait for subsidies as long as a vein beats in his body.

The Golden Rule: When Does Generosity Die in Societies?

In our contemporary time, many complain about the hardness of hearts and the absence of solidarity, asking with regret: "Why is there no longer anyone in our lives like Saad bin Ar-Rabi'? Why has this generosity disappeared?".

The answer lies in a precise sociological rule: "Absolute generosity in any society inevitably dies if modesty and self-restraint disappear from it."

The existence of "Saad bin Ar-Rabi' (سعد بن الربيع)" is conditional on the existence of "Abdul Rahman bin Auf (عبد الرحمن بن عوف)." Saad was offering half his wealth with a reassured heart because he knew he was offering it to a man overwhelmed with pride and dignity, who would only take what sustains him in the direst of necessities. However, when modesty disappears, and people turn to exploiting the generous, and subsidies are taken as a means for laziness, unemployment, and disguised begging, the doors of generosity close, hands tighten, and the wealthy person fears helping the needy, assuming he will be drained and exploited.

Therefore, Allah praised the modest and made them a reason for the continuation of good in the Ummah, saying: {[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. An ignorant[person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently}. And the Prophet ﷺ summarized this great psychological rule by saying: "Whoever seeks to be chaste, Allah will make him chaste, and whoever seeks to be independent of means, Allah will make him independent" (Agreed upon). If the needy show restraint and preserve their dignity, the trust of society increases, the generosity of the liberal overflows, and economic and psychological balance is achieved in its finest forms.

5. The Charter of Madinah: The First "Confederal" System and Guarantees of Societal Security (5. وثيقة المدينة: أول نظام "كونفدرالي" وضمانات الأمن المجتمعي)

The "Charter of Madinah" (وثيقة المدينة) was not merely a passing peace treaty between scattered tribes; rather, by the standards of modern political science, it was a "genius constitution" whose clauses established the features of an advanced institutional state and invented a political and rights system centuries ahead of its time. He who contemplates the details of this constitution away from mere historical narration will find legislative answers and administrative solutions to the most complex societal and security issues.

1. Gradual Solidarity: The "Aaqilah" and Rescuing the "Mufrah":

On the social and financial side, the constitution balanced between "family responsibility" and the "state's safety net." The Prophet ﷺ established the system of the "Aaqilah" (العاقلة), where each tribe or family bears its internal responsibilities in ransoming its captives and paying blood money (financial compensation for accidental killing), which enhances family solidarity and shared responsibility.

But, what if the family is unable? And what if debts accumulate on an individual until they destroy him? Here intervenes a genius clause in the charter stating: "And the believers shall not leave anyone destitute (Mufrah) among them without giving him[help] in goodness for ransom or blood money."

The "Mufrah" (المُفْرَح) is the person weighed down by debts and unable to pay. In this case, the "State" (the group of believers) intervenes to rescue him and pay his debt from Zakat funds and the public treasury (Bait Al-Mal). This is a practical application of the Almighty’s saying regarding the categories of Zakat recipients: {And for those in debt}[At-Tawbah: 60], and establishing the principle of "comprehensive social insurance" which the Prophet ﷺ later expressed by saying: "I am closer to the believers than their own selves; whoever dies leaving a debt, its payment is upon me" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari).

2. Strict Justice: Standing Against the Oppressor Even if He Were "The Son of One of Them":

To guarantee internal security, the constitution cut off the root of pre-Islamic tribal bigotry based on the blind pre-Islamic concept of "Support your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." The charter stipulated: "And the pious believers shall stand against whoever among them rebels, or seeks to spread injustice, sin, enmity, or corruption among the believers; and their hands shall be united against him, even if he were the son of one of them."

This clause obliterates any tribal or familial cover for criminals; if a person steals, kills, or corrupts, his father, his family, and his tribe must be the first to stand against him and hand him over to justice. This is a practical embodiment of the Almighty’s saying: {O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives}[An-Nisa: 135], and the strict Prophetic principle: "If Fatima bint Muhammad (فاطمة بِنْتَ مُحَمَّدٍ) were to steal, I would cut off her hand" (Agreed upon).

3. Flexible Diplomacy: Between "Individual Protection" and "State Treaties":

In a clause that reflects Islam’s respect for the value of the individual, the charter stipulated that: "The protection (Dhimmah) of Allah is one; the least of them may grant protection[to someone] which is binding on them all." This means that the right of "political asylum" or "protection" is not exclusive to leaders; rather, the simplest Muslim citizen has the right to grant safety and protection to a polytheist person, and the entire state is obligated to respect this safety. This was evident when Umm Hani, may Allah be pleased with her (أم هانئ رضي الله عنها), granted protection to two polytheist men on the day of the conquest of Mecca, and the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "We have given protection to whomever you have given protection, O Umm Hani" (Agreed upon), confirming the Almighty’s saying: {And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah. Then deliver him to his place of safety} [At-Tawbah: 6].

However, the charter cleverly differentiated between "protection by individuals" and "protection by states"; an individual's protection is for specific persons for the purpose of a visit, trade, or hearing the truth. As for alliances, making treaties with hostile entities, and protecting armies and tribes, these fall under the jurisdiction of the "Supreme Leadership" (the State). The charter also strictly prohibited the polytheists living in Madinah (before their conversion to Islam) from granting any protection to the state's primary enemy, Quraish (قريش), stipulating: "No polytheist shall grant protection to any wealth or person of Quraish."

4. Jewish Semi-Autonomy (The Confederal System) and the National Security Line:

The greatest political genius, however, manifested in dealing with the Jewish entity in Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ used with them what is known in contemporary politics as a "Confederal System" or "Semi-Autonomous Rule."

The charter gave the Jews broad independence in their internal affairs, stipulating: "For the Jews is their religion, and for the Muslims is their religion," and "The Jews must bear their expenses and the Muslims their expenses." The Jews had their own economy, fortresses, weapons, and even their independent internal judiciary in personal affairs as long as they did not bring the matter to the Muslims, fulfilling the Almighty’s saying in giving the Muslim leadership the choice when they come to them for judgment: {So if they come to you, [O Muhammad], judge between them or turn away from them}[Al-Ma'idah: 42]. (And the Prophet ﷺ did judge between them by the Torah in the story of the two Jews who committed adultery when they asked him to arbitrate).

When Does Autonomy Fall?

This financial and judicial independence was governed by a ceiling of "National Sovereignty and National Security." If the actions of the Jews shifted from the personal sphere to "public corruption" in the Muslim society, or spreading vice, or threatening internal security, or collaborating with a foreign enemy... the "Supreme Constitution" immediately intervenes, and their independence falls.

Therefore, the charter strictly stipulated: "There shall be mutual help between them against anyone who fights the people of this document," and "Whatever you differ in, its reference is to Allah and to Muhammad."

This explains why the Prophet ﷺ moved militarily against Bani Qaynuqa (بني قينقاع) when they harassed a Muslim woman in their market and killed a Muslim; because the matter turned into public corruption and an transgression against Muslim blood and honor. It also explains the decisive action of ending the presence of Bani Quraiza (بني قريظة) and inheriting their lands and homes after they colluded with the Confederates; because their treason was a strategic threat to the "Supreme Constitution" that mandates the joint defense of Madinah.

Through this precise charter, the Prophet ﷺ transformed Yathrib (يثرب) from a mere geographical spot where tribes fought and rights were lost, into a pioneering "state of institutions," where justice prevails, blood is preserved, and authorities are defined, presenting to the world the first and finest model of civic coexistence governed by the rule of law.

6. Conclusion: The Architecture of Your Personal Commitment (Mosque, Brotherhood, Covenants) (6. الخاتمة: هندسة التزامك الشخصي (مسجد، تآخي، عهود))

Studying the Prophetic Biography is not merely a recounting of historical events that have passed and ended; rather, it is a living "roadmap" that can be replicated in every time and place. Just as the Prophet ﷺ faced the challenge of transforming a group of scattered individuals into a cohesive "state" and a divine society, every person who decides to walk the path of guidance and commitment (the spiritual migration from sin to obedience) faces a similar challenge in building his "internal state" and engineering himself anew.

The practical projection of the pillars of building the state of Madinah (the Mosque, Brotherhood, and the Charter) represents the three pillars without which no personal commitment succeeds:

The First Pillar: The Mosque (Incubator of Knowledge, Upbringing, and Role Models)

The settlement of the Muhajireen was not complete until the bricks of the first mosque were laid, and the same applies to the youth returning to his Lord; his faith will not stabilize unless he makes the "Mosque" the starting point and anchor in his life.

For a practicing Muslim, the mosque is not just walls where quick prayer cycles (Rak'ahs) are performed and then left; rather, it is an "educational incubator." In it, circles of knowledge are held that protect him from intellectual confusion, and in it descends the rain of mercy, fulfilling the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it together, but tranquility descends upon them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them to those who are with Him" (Narrated by Muslim).

Most importantly, the mosque is the place where you interact with "direct role models." You need a sheikh or an educator before whom you bend your knees, learning from his demeanor and being influenced by his manners before drawing from his knowledge. You need to see the application of Islam walking on the ground before your eyes, for that to be a shield for you against deviation or apathy.

The Second Pillar: Brotherhood (Righteous Companionship and the Safety Belt)

True commitment is a type of "Migration" (Hijrah), and an emigrant always feels the loneliness of alienation when he leaves his old environment and past interests. Therefore, a young man or woman cannot continue on the path of uprightness through isolated individual effort. Here comes the role of "Brotherhood" represented in searching for (Righteous Companionship).

You need brothers in Allah who act as "Ansar" (Helpers) for you; they support you psychologically, share your permissible interests, and help you up if you stumble. The Quran pointed to the inevitability of this integration with the righteous environment in the Almighty’s saying: {And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance. And let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring adornments of the worldly life}[Al-Kahf: 28].

The Prophet ﷺ warned against isolation, and made one's companion a standard for the steadfastness of religion when he said: "A man follows the religion of his close friend; so each one should consider whom he makes his close friend" (Narrated by Abu Dawood and At-Tirmidhi). The wolf only eats the sheep that strays from the flock, and true brotherhood with someone who shares your aspirations and temperaments is the "safety belt" that protects you from relapse.

The Third Pillar: Covenants and the Charter (The Constitution of Personal Commitment)

After the Prophet ﷺ secured the internal front with the mosque and brotherhood, he established the "Charter of Madinah" to define the shape of relationships and set boundaries and red lines in dealing with the other components of society.

Similarly, when a person moves to the stage of commitment, he must write a "personal constitution" or make "strict covenants" with himself that define the features of his new life. The practicing Muslim cannot keep the doors of his old relationships wide open as they were.

You must draw a dividing line and strict rules:

  • Your old relationships: Which of my past friends should I stay completely away from because they drag me into sin? And which of them can I keep in touch with to invite them and win their hearts without being influenced by them?
  • Your boundaries with prohibitions: What are the places I will decisively stop frequenting? What are the clips and pages I will unfollow in compliance with the Almighty’s saying: {And when you see those who engage in [offensive] discourse concerning Our verses, then turn away from them until they enter into another conversation}[Al-An'am: 68]?
  • Your internal discipline: What is the fixed daily portion of the Quran that I will not compromise on no matter how busy I get? What is my stance on gatherings of backbiting and wasting time?

This "personal constitution" governed by the rulings of Sharia spares you from hesitation at every situation, and makes your commitment solid, not shape-shifting according to pressures. It is a practical application of the comprehensive Prophetic advice: "Be mindful of Allah, and Allah will protect you. Be mindful of Allah, and you will find Him in front of you" (Narrated by At-Tirmidhi).

In summary:

If you want to build a firm faith in your heart that the winds of trials cannot scatter, make the Prophetic Biography a reference for your foundation. Start with a (Mosque) that enlightens your mind and raises your soul, wrap yourself in (Companionship and Brotherhood) that strengthens your back and comforts your loneliness, and conclude with a clear (Constitution and Covenants) that separates truth from falsehood. By doing so, the architecture of your commitment will be complete, and you will establish within yourself a solid base from which you launch towards the pleasure of Allah and winning His Paradise.

1. The Four Phases of Societal Change: Methodological Gradualism Before Empowerment (1. المراحل الأربع للتغيير المجتمعي: التدرج المنهجي قبل التمكين)

Empowerment in the Prophetic methodology (المنهج النبوي) does not represent a sudden leap or the product of an arbitrary movement isolated from the context of human foundation. Rather, it is the mature fruit of a long cumulative path that spanned thirteen years in Makkah Al-Mukarramah (مكة المكرمة), followed by the early years in Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة). This deliberate and systematic arrangement confirms a foundational reality: building the human structure and shaping the social fabric necessarily precedes any manifestation of material power or political empowerment. This foundational path can be traced through four successive phases that drew the philosophy of change and nation-building:

Phase One: General Da'wah and Addressing Everyone (Building the Cognitive and Emotional Foundation) (المرحلة الأولى: الدعوة العامة ومخاطبة الجميع (بناء القاعدة المعرفية والوجدانية))

This phase begins by addressing the call (الدعوة) to the general society without discrimination or exclusion, focusing on instilling the basics of creed (العقيدة), purification of the soul (التزكية), and servitude to Allah (العبودية لله) Almighty. It is an ongoing phase that does not stop with the establishment of the state, but remains the permanent channel for connecting people to the primary source.

This focus was evident in the Makkan era (العهد المكي) through absolute preoccupation with creedal and emotional development, as well as warning against the consequences of denial. The Mother of the Believers, Aisha (عائشة رضي الله عنها), described this methodology precisely, saying:

"Indeed, what was first revealed of it was a Surah from the Mufassal (المفصل), in which Paradise and the Fire were mentioned, until when the people returned to Islam, the Halal (الحلال) and Haram (الحرام) were revealed. If the first thing revealed had been: 'Do not drink wine,' they would have said: 'We will never leave wine.'" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari (البخاري)).

The objective here is to build public awareness and prepare hearts to accept obligations, which is a general duty accessible to every individual according to their capacity and knowledge, as Allah says:

{وَقُرْآنًا فَرَقْنَاهُ لِتَقْرَأَهُ عَلَى النَّاسِ عَلَىٰ مُكْثٍ وَنَزَّلْنَاهُ تَنزِيلًا}
"And [it is] a Qur'an which We have revealed in portions that you might recite it to the people over a prolonged period. And We have sent it down progressively." [Al-Isra: 106] (الإسراء: 106).

Phase Two: Selecting and Building Distinguished Cadres (Creating the Solid Core) (المرحلة الثانية: اصطفاء وبناء الكوادر المميزة (صناعة النواة الصلبة))

As the range of those responding to the general call expanded, an urgent need arose to transition from "quantity" to "quality." In this phase, the focus shifts to nurturing distinguished talents and elites capable of carrying the burdens of the project and building the pillars of the emerging state. The Prophetic care for these individuals was not standardized or uniform; rather, it was a diagnostic mentorship that invested in and refined the unique personal strengths of each individual.

This specialized differentiation is affirmed in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"The most merciful of my Ummah (أمتي) to my Ummah is Abu Bakr (أبو بكر), the strongest of them in the command of Allah is Umar (عمر), the most truthful of them in modesty is Uthman (عثمان), the most knowledgeable of them in the lawful and unlawful is Mu'adh ibn Jabal (معاذ بن جبل), the best reciter of the Book of Allah among them is Ubayy (أبي), and the most knowledgeable of them in inheritance laws is Zayd ibn Thabit (زيد بن ثابت)..." (Narrated by Al-Tirmidhi (الترمذي) and authenticated by Al-Albani (الألباني)).

Shaping these specialized cadres—such as Mus'ab ibn Umayr (مصعب بن عمير), who was dispatched to open Al-Madinah (المدينة) through knowledge, and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (جعفر بن أبي طالب), who led the Abyssinian (الحبشة) front diplomatically—represented the preparation of a solid core that received deep education and was qualified to lead the rest of the societal structures.

Phase Three: Institutionalization, Integration, and Distribution of Roles (Organized Collective Work) (المرحلة الثالثة: المأسسة والتكامل وتوزيع الأدوار (العمل الجماعي المنظم))

After completing the development of qualified individual personalities, the next step is to transfer these scattered capabilities from the realm of individual achievement to the realm of institutional work and collective integration. Nations are not built by the isolated efforts of individuals, no matter how brilliant they are, but by a system that connects them and directs their energies toward common goals.

This organizational transition was clearly manifested in the Second Pledge of al-Aqabah (بيعة العقبة الثانية). The Prophet (ﷺ) did not settle for verbal covenants; rather, he requested the institutionalization of this alliance and the appointment of an intermediary leadership to represent the ranks and manage their affairs. He said to them:

"Bring out to me twelve leaders (نقيباً) from among you, to be responsible for their people regarding what is among them." (Narrated by Ahmad (أحمد)).

Consequently, administrative and mutual-solidarity bodies were immediately formed, and alliances for joint work were drafted, paving the way for the construction of logistical and social support networks within Al-Madinah (المدينة). This phase allows for the flexible utilization of all available societal, political, and economic means to distribute roles and stabilize the foundations of the emerging entity.

Phase Four: Empowerment and Confrontation (The Fruit of Self-Building) (المرحلة الرابعة: التمكين والمواجهة (ثمرة البناء الذاتي))

When the first three phases are successfully completed (building public awareness, creating solid cadres, and organizing collective action), the natural ground is prepared for the descent of empowerment (التمكين), the establishment of power, and the building of a state capable of protecting truth and confronting adversaries.

Empowerment in the Islamic vision is not a primary goal sought for its own sake through coercive means; rather, it is a divine promise conditional upon human building and true servitude, as stated in the decisive verse:

{وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِن كُنتُم وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ كَمَا اسْتَخْلَفَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ وَلَيُمَكِّنَنَّ لَهُمْ دِينَهُمُ الَّذِي ارْتَضَىٰ لَهُمْ وَلَيُبَدِّلَنَّهُم مِّن بَعْدِ خَوْفِهِمْ أَمْنًا ۚ يَعْبُدُونَنِي لَا يُشْرِكُونَ بِي شَيْئًا}
"Allah has promised those who have believed among you and done righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession [to authority] upon the earth just as He granted it to those before them and that He will surely establish for them [therein] their religion which He has preferred for them and that He will surely substitute for them, after their fear, security, [for] they worship Me, not associating anything with Me." [An-Nur: 55] (النور: 55).

This verse connects succession, empowerment, and security to a prior condition: belief, righteous deeds, and complete servitude—which are the details of the first three phases.

Methodological Warning Against "Skipping Phases" (التحذير المنهجي من "حرق المراحل")

Here emerges the most critical lesson in the understanding of movements and societies: the strict warning against "rushing the fruit before it ripens," or what is known as "skipping phases" (حرق المراحل). Jumping directly into military confrontation or political empowerment without passing through human building, deep-rooted education, and organizing the ranks inevitably leads to the destruction of gains and a regression back to point zero.

The Prophetic methodology established this control clearly on the night of the Second Pledge of al-Aqabah (بيعة العقبة الثانية). When the pledge was successfully concluded, enthusiasm flared in the hearts of the Ansar (الأنصار). Al-Abbas ibn Ubadah ibn Nadlah (العباس بن عبادة بن نضلة) said to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"O Messenger of Allah, by He Who sent you with the truth, if you wish, we will surely fall upon the people of Mina (منى) tomorrow with our swords!"

The Prophet (ﷺ) replied with the dignity of leadership and the insight of methodology, curbing this emotional haste:

"We have not been commanded to do that yet; but return to your camps." (Narrated by Ahmad (أحمد) and Ibn Hisham (ابن هشام)).

Insisting on confronting the enemy before possessing the means of survival, as well as sufficient educational, societal, and organizational readiness, is a strategic mistake. Those who rush into clash during periods of weakness out of zeal for the religion often end up bringing about massive harms that ruin progress and obstruct the path of Da'wah (الدعوة) for many years, replacing the deliberate Prophetic methodology with impulsive emotion that does more harm than good.

2. The Fiqh of Managing the Internal Front: Extinguishing Sedition and Thwarting Schemers (2. فقه إدارة الجبهة الداخلية: إخماد الفتن وتفويت فرصة المتربصين)

Managing and protecting the internal front from fracturing represents one of the most delicate challenges facing emerging entities. Any internal breach or civil strife is capable of undermining the pillars of the state before it grows strong. The new Madinan society in its first foundational phase faced double threats where external conspiracies combined with internal malice. This required exceptional leadership policies that balanced strategic firmness with diplomatic flexibility, prioritizing societal peace over personal triumph or victory of the self.

First: Confronting External Conspiracy (The Threatening Letter of Quraysh) (أولاً: مواجهة المؤامرة الخارجية (رسالة قريش التهديدية))

Quraysh (قريش) was not oblivious to the danger of the Muslims stabilizing in Yathrib (يثرب) and allying with the Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج). Because direct war at that stage was of high cost, Quraysh resorted to the weapon of internal discord and incitement. Their leader, Abu Jahl (أبو جهل), sent an explicit letter of warning and threat to Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (عبد الله بن أبي بن سلول)—who represented the leadership of the polytheists and doubters in Al-Madinah (المدينة) before the Battle of Badr (معركة بدر)—and to the idolators with him.

The books of Sunan (السنن) narrate the details of this threat. The text of Quraysh's letter stated:

"You have given refuge to our companion. We swear by Allah that you must either fight him or expel him, or we will march against you with all of us, until we kill your fighters and enslave your women." (Narrated by Abu Dawud (أبو داود)).

This letter stirred the hidden malice and desire for leadership in Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (عبد الله بن أبي بن سلول), who saw the Prophetic migration as a usurpation of his expected kingship. He gathered his allies from among the polytheists of Al-Madinah (المدينة), and they resolved to fight the Muslims and ignite a civil war.

Here, quick and direct leadership wisdom was manifested. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not wait for the catastrophe to occur. Instead, he walked to them himself and confronted the crowd to dismantle the justifications for their fighting, addressing their minds and honor, saying:

"The threat of Quraysh has reached its limit with you. They cannot plot against you with more than what you want to plot against yourselves. Do you want to fight your brothers and your sons?!" (Narrated by Abu Dawud (أبو داود)).

These words shocked the polytheists of Al-Madinah (المدينة) into awareness. They realized that following Quraysh's threat meant that brother would kill brother, and the uncle would eradicate his nephew—due to the overlapping clans of the Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج) between Islam and polytheism. The crowds dispersed, and the sedition was extinguished without a single drop of blood being spilled, after the Prophet (ﷺ) deprived them of the pretext and minimized the instigating role of Ibn Salul (ابن سلول).

Second: Dealing with Verbal Provocations (The Incident of the Prophetic Passage) (ثانياً: التعامل مع الاستفزازات اللفظية (حادثة الممر النبوي))

The hypocrites and polytheists did not despair of trying to drag the Muslim ranks into an internal clash that would show the Muslims as aggressors against their compatriots. These provocative attempts were manifested in a famous incident narrated by Bukhari (البخاري) and Muslim (مسلم) in their Sahihs on the authority of Anas ibn Malik (أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه).

The Prophet (ﷺ) was riding a donkey on his way to visit Sa'd ibn Ubadah (سعد بن عبادة رضي الله عنه) who was ill. He passed by a gathering containing a mixture of Muslims, polytheistic idolators, and Jews. Among the gathering was Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (عبد الله بن أبي بن سلول)—before he outwardly declared Islam hypocritically. When the dust of the animal reached the gathering, Ibn Salul (ابن سلول) covered his nose with his cloak and said with arrogance and provocation: "Do not kick up dust on us."

The provocation did not stop there. After the Prophet (ﷺ) dismounted, greeted them, invited them to Allah, and recited the Qur'an to them, Ibn Salul (ابن سلول) said to him with coldness and harshness:

"O man, there is nothing better than what you say if it is true. So do not bother us with it in our gatherings. Return to your mount, and whoever comes to you, relate it to him."

This verbal transgression angered the Muslims in the gathering. Abdullah ibn Rawahah (عبد الله بن رواحة رضي الله عنه) stood up to defend: "Indeed, O Messenger of Allah, bring it to us in our gatherings, for we love that." The Muslims, polytheists, and Jews in the gathering began insulting one another until they almost came to blows. The Prophet (ﷺ) stood among them, not seeking victory for himself, but striving to extinguish the fire and calm the souls. He kept quietening and calming them until they all fell silent.

Then he rode his mount and went to Sa'd ibn Ubadah (سعد بن عبادة), telling him what Ibn Salul (ابن سلول) had done. Sa'd (سعد), with the wisdom of one who knew the souls of his people, said:

"O Messenger of Allah, pardon him and overlook. For by Allah, Allah has given you what He has given you, and the people of this lake (meaning Al-Madinah) had agreed to crown him and bind his head with the turban. When Allah prevented that through the truth He gave you, he choked on it; that is what made him do what you saw." (Agreed upon/متفق عليه).

The Prophet (ﷺ) pardoned him and overlooked his personal insult to protect the society from division.

Third: "The Fiqh of Overlooking" as a Pillar of National Security (ثالثاً: "فقه التغاضي" كركيزة للأمن القومي)

These incidents establish a golden rule in Islamic politics (السياسة الشرعية) and social reform: "the fiqh of overlooking" (فقه التغاضي) and prioritizing civil peace and internal cohesion over individual disputes and personal triumphs. The early Madinan environment was fragile, burdened with the wounds of the long Bu'ath war (حرب بعاث) between the Aws (الأوس) and Khazraj (الخزرج). Any internal clash was capable of reproducing that destructive civil war.

The Prophetic methodology realized that the external enemy—Quraysh (قريش) and its allies—fed on the internal crises of the Muslims and saw civil strife as a free tool to end the Islamic state without military cost. Therefore, the Quranic directives were decisive in ordering patience and forgiveness in that sensitive phase to avoid falling into the trap of provocation, as Allah says:

{وَدَّ كَثِيرٌ مِّنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ لَوْ يَرُدُّونَكُم مِّن بَعْدِ إِيمَانِكُمْ كُفَّارًا حَسَدًا مِّنْ عِندِ أَنفُسِهِم مِّن بَعْدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الْحَقُّ ۖ فَاعْفُوا وَاصْفَحُوا حَتَّىٰ يَأْتِيَ اللَّهُ بِأَمْرِهِ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ}
"Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed, out of envy from themselves after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook until Allah delivers His command. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent." [Al-Baqarah: 109] (البقرة: 109).

And He says:

{وَلَتَسْمَعُنَّ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا أَذًى كَثِيرًا ۚ وَإِن تَصْبِرُوا وَتَتَّقُوا فَإِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ}
"And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with Allah much abuse. But if you are patient and fear Allah - indeed, that is of the matters [worthy] of determination." [Aal Imran: 186] (آل عمران: 186).

The wise caller and insightful politician are those who possess the ability to distinguish between major, fateful battles and minor, side battles. Thus, they overlook personal provocations, ignore passing offenses, and deny adversaries their opportunities by closing the channels of regional or tribal conflict. Preserving the cohesion of the internal front and the unity of the ranks is the true safety valve for the success of any reformist project; without it, strength turns to fragmentation, and truth to division.

3. The Fiqh of Power and Deterrence: Why Falsehood Respects Only the Strong (3. فقه القوة والردع: لماذا لا يحترم الباطل إلا الأشداء؟)

The conflict between truth and falsehood is an ongoing cosmic law. Anyone who looks into the laws of succession and state-building realizes that truth stripped of power is unable to protect itself; indeed, the weakness of the person of truth only arouses the appetite of falsehood to devour and dominate. Falsehood, by its arrogant nature, is not moved by values of justice nor prevented by soft appeals. Rather, it is deterred when the person of truth possesses the elements of strength and the tools of deterrence. This profound social rule was demonstrated in a decisive stance recorded by one of the great companions, the leader of the Aws, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ رضي الله عنه), in his historical confrontation with the head of disbelief, Abu Jahl (أبو جهل), in the heart of Makkah (مكة).

First: The Historical Confrontation in the Courtyard of the Sanctuary (أولاً: المواجهة التاريخية في فناء الحرم)

Al-Bukhari (البخاري) narrates in his Sahih the details of this meeting. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ رضي الله عنه) went after the Hijrah (الهجرة) to perform Umrah (العمرة) in Makkah (مكة), and stayed as a guest with his friend and old business partner, Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف). There was an alliance and mutual business interests between them; whenever Umayyah (أمية) passed by Al-Madinah (المدينة) on his way to Ash-Sham (الشام), he stayed with Sa'd (سعد), and whenever Sa'd (سعد) passed by Makkah (مكة), he stayed with Umayyah (أمية).

Sa'd (سعد) asked Umayyah (أمية) to find a quiet hour for him to perform Tawaf (الطواف) around the Kaaba away from the eyes of Quraysh (قريش) to maintain peace and avoid trouble. Umayyah chose the midday hour when it was very hot and people had left the Tawaf. While Sa'd (سعد) was performing Tawaf, Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) met them. He turned with an interrogative question to Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف), belittling Sa'd's position: "O Abu Safwan (أبا صفوان), who is this with you?" Umayyah said: "This is Sa'd (سعد)."

At this, Abu Jahl addressed Sa'd with an explicit threat and arrogant warning, violating the sanctity of the Haram (الحرم) and the sanctity of neighborhood protection, saying:

"Do I see you walking in Makkah safely, while you have given refuge to the apostates (meaning the Muslims) and claimed that you will help and support them? By Allah, were it not that you are with Abu Safwan (أبي صفوان), you would not have returned to your family safely."

Sa'd (سعد رضي الله عنه) did not hesitate, did not flatter, and was not shaken by the threat while in the heart of his enemy's home, isolated from his people and supporters. Rather, he raised his voice with the dignity of the strong and the confidence of one who relies on his Lord, directing a strategic blow that shook Abu Jahl's pride, saying with decisiveness:

"By Allah, if you prevent me from this, I will surely prevent you from what is much harder on you: your route through Al-Madinah (المدينة)!" (Narrated by Al-Bukhari (البخاري)).

Second: The Strategic Trade Artery and Economic Deterrence (ثانياً: شريان التجارة الإستراتيجي وقوة الردع الاقتصادي)

Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's (سعد بن معاذ) threat to Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) was not merely an emotional outburst or a passing enthusiasm. It was an eloquent and calculated threat that hit Makkah in its most critical spot. Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة) was geographically situated as a "strategic strait" through which passed the commercial lifeline of Quraysh towards Ash-Sham (الشام) (the summer journey/رحلة الصيف). Preventing Quraysh from passing through this route meant signing a sentence of total economic death for Makkah, whose entire life depended on trade, as Allah says:

{إِيلَافِ قُرَيْشٍ * إِيلَافِهِمْ رِحْلَةَ الشِّتَاءِ وَالصَّيْفِ}
"For the accustomed security of the Quraysh - Their accustomed security [in] the caravan of winter and summer." [Quraysh: 1-2] (قريش: 1-2).

Sa'd (سعد رضي الله عنه) understood the points of strength and weakness in the political and economic landscape. He knew that directly threatening Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) militarily might not deter him while he was in his stronghold, but threatening to cut off Quraysh's economic lungs would silence him and change his calculations immediately. Indeed, Abu Jahl fell silent and did not reply. Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف) tried to calm the situation, fearing the consequences of this threat, saying to Sa'd: "Do not raise your voice against Abu al-Hakam (أبي الحكم), for he is the chief of the valley." Sa'd replied with another psychological blow that shook Umayyah's own being: "Leave this, O Umayyah, for by Allah, I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, they will kill you!'" Umayyah was terrified and remained keen never to leave Makkah, until he was dragged against his will to his death at Badr (بدر).

Third: Comprehensive Power as the True Guarantee of Security (ثالثاً: القوة الشاملة والضمانة الحقيقية للأمن)

This great confrontation establishes a legal and cosmic rule: "Weak truth only excites the appetite of falsehood, and mutual deterrence is the only guarantee of security." A weak language of peace that lacks protective claws is interpreted by forces of aggression as inability and surrender, prompting them to commit more tyranny.

Allah Almighty legislated the preparation of comprehensive power and made its primary goal "deterrence"—meaning preventing war from occurring in the first place by displaying the strength that frightens adversaries and stops them from even thinking of aggression, as Allah says:

{وَأَعِدُّوا لَهُم مَّا اسْتَطَعْتُم مِّن قُوَّةٍ وَمِن رِّبَاطِ الْخَيْلِ تُرْهِبُونَ بِهِ عَدُوَّ اللَّهِ وَعَدُوَّكُمْ وَآخَرِينَ مِن دُونِهِمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَهُمُ اللَّهُ يَعْلَمُهُمْ}
"And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know but whom Allah knows." [Al-Anfal: 60] (الأنفال: 60).

The word {تُرْهِبُونَ} ("you may terrify/deter") in the verse is the precise Quranic embodiment of the concept of "military, economic, and psychological deterrence." Preparation and possessing power are not meant for injustice and aggression, but to restrain the hands of aggressors, protect the land of Islam, and safeguard the oppressed. Comprehensive power includes three main dimensions:

  1. Military and Organizational Power (القوة العسكرية والتنظيمية): The capability to inflict harm on the adversary and disrupt their plans militarily.
  2. Economic and Geopolitical Power (القوة الاقتصادية والجيوسياسية): Activating material and economic pressure points (such as controlling trade routes, boycotts, and strategic straits).
  3. Psychological and Faith-based Power (القوة النفسية والإيمانية): Enjoying internal resilience and dignity that prevents the believer from breaking before the power of tyrants, looking at them with a sense of spiritual superiority.

Gentleness, kindness, and mercy belong among the believers and their brothers. But with aggressors and oppressors, the only language they understand and respect is that of power and peer-to-peer deterrence.
