Without it, the people of truth remain oppressed, and their sanctuaries and rights remain a target for every greedy and tyrannical force.

4. Self-Guarding and Taking Precautions: The Initiative of "Ibn Abi Waqqas" and the Miracle of Infallible Protection (4. الحراسة الذاتية والأخذ بالأسباب: مبادرة "ابن أبي وقاص" ومعجزة العصمة)

Amidst the security dangers surrounding Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة) and the multiple sources of threat from Quraysh (قريش), hypocrites, Jews, and Bedouins, the threat of assassination was constantly hovering over the Prophetic leadership. In this delicate situation, the Prophetic methodology and the actions of the noble companions provided profound lessons in balancing complete material security measures (taking precautions/الأخذ بالأسباب) with deep certainty and reliance on Allah Almighty (التوكل على الله). This context also saw the development of the concept of "self-initiative" in protecting the Da'wah and guarding its frontiers without waiting for instructions.

First: The Initiative of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Filling the Gaps Automatically (أولاً: مبادرة سعد بن أبي وقاص وسد الثغور تلقائياً)

The Mother of the Believers, Aisha (عائشة رضي الله عنها), narrates in the Sahihayn (الصحيحين) a security scene that reflects the weight of fear and threat at the beginning of the Madinan era. The Prophet (ﷺ) was awake and anxious one night after arriving in Al-Madinah (المدينة). Speaking with the natural concern of a human wary of the plots of his enemies, he said:

"If only a righteous man from my companions would guard me tonight." (Agreed upon/متفق عليه).

While they were in this state of anticipation, the clinking of weapons and the sound of iron reached them. The Prophet (ﷺ) woke up with the alertness of a cautious leader and asked: "Who is this?" A familiar, dignified voice replied: "I am Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (سعد بن أبي وقاص), I have come to guard you." The Prophet (ﷺ) asked him what brought him without being summoned, and Sa'd said in words filled with love, loyalty, and security intelligence: "A fear for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arose in my heart, so I came to guard him." The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed for him, and then slept so deeply that his snoring could be heard.

This incident establishes the concept of "self-initiative and filling the gaps automatically" (المبادرة الذاتية وسد الثغور تلقائياً). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (سعد بن أبي وقاص رضي الله عنه) did not wait for an official military order, nor did he stand idle waiting for an administrative task. Instead, his sense of responsibility and his intelligence in estimating dangers led him to immediate action, filling that security gap himself with his weapon. This positive behavior represents a pillar in the movement of societies: where every individual searches for a vacant gap in specialty, culture, or aid, and fills it voluntarily, without complaining or waiting for others.

Second: The Revelation of the Verse of Infallible Protection and the Transition to Absolute Certainty (ثانياً: نزول آية العصمة والتحول نحو اليقين المطلق)

The companions continued to take turns guarding the Prophet (ﷺ) and surrounding his house and tents at night to protect him from the plots of enemies. This continued until the divine revelation resolved this issue, instilling absolute peace in the Prophet's heart through a divine protection system that could not be breached by doubts or swords, as stated in the verse:

{يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّسُولُ بَلِّغْ مَا أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِن رَّبِّكَ ۖ وَإِن لَّمْ تَفْعَلْ فَمَا بَلَّغْتَ رِسَالَتَهُ ۚ وَاللَّهُ يَعْصِمُكَ مِنَ النَّاسِ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الْكَافِرِينَ}
"O Messenger, announce that which has been revealed to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people." [Al-Ma'idah: 67] (المائدة: 67).

Aisha (عائشة رضي الله عنها) narrates the effect of this verse's revelation on security measures, saying:

"The Prophet (ﷺ) used to be guarded until this verse was revealed: {وَاللَّهُ يَعْصِمُكَ مِنَ النَّاسِ} (And Allah will protect you from the people). Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put his head out of the tent and said to them: 'O people, leave me, for Allah has protected me.'" (Narrated by Al-Tirmidhi (الترمذي) and authenticated by Al-Albani (الألباني)).

This stance represents clear evidence of prophethood and a manifest divine miracle. It does not fit human, material logic for a person in an environment filled with enemies to voluntarily dismiss his loyal guards upon the revelation of mere words, unless he was of absolute certainty, free from any doubt, that his Lord Who sent him had guaranteed him absolute protection until he conveyed the message.

Third: The Story of the Bedouin and the Sword Under the Tree (The Practical Application of Protection) (ثالثاً: قصة الأعرابي والسيف تحت الشجرة (التطبيق العملي للعصمة))

The miracle of protection and certainty was demonstrated in various practical situations, most notably what occurred in the Battle of Dhat ar-Riqa (غزوة ذات الرقاع). The Muslims dismounted to rest at midday and dispersed to seek shade under the trees. The Prophet (ﷺ) sat under a Samurah tree (سَمُرة—a thorny tree), hung his sword on it, and slept.

A Bedouin from among the polytheists named Ghawrath ibn al-Harith (غَوْرَث بن الحارث) took advantage of the companions being scattered. He slipped in until he stood over the head of the Prophet (ﷺ) and unsheathed the sword. The Prophet (ﷺ) woke up while the sword was drawn in the Bedouin's hand. The Bedouin said, filled with the pride of material control: "Who will protect you from me?" The Prophet (ﷺ) replied with the steadfastness of prophets and the peace of one connected to Allah, without fear or hesitation: "Allah."

As soon as the Prophet (ﷺ) uttered this word, repeating it three times, the Bedouin shook, and the sword fell from his hand. The Prophet (ﷺ) took it, raised it, and said to the Bedouin: "Who will protect you from me?" The Bedouin said, broken: "Be the best of those who take." The Prophet (ﷺ) pardoned him and let him go after the Bedouin promised him not to fight him nor to be with a people who fight him. The Bedouin returned to his people, amazed, saying: "I have come to you from the best of people." (Agreed upon, and this wording is Al-Bukhari's/متفق عليه واللفظ للبخاري).

Fourth: Balancing the Use of Means with Sincere Trust in the Heart (رابعاً: الموازنة بين الأخذ بالأسباب والتوكل بالقلوب)

This Prophetic system summarizes the ideal spiritual and practical rule in facing life: "The obligation of taking material precautions with the hand, along with complete trust and certainty in the heart in the Creator of the causes alone."

Taking precautions—such as guarding, weapons, and fortifications—is a religious duty that does not contradict trust in Allah, but is of its very essence. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not cancel the guarding except after the arrival of the specific, miraculous divine text regarding his person to protect the message. As for the rest of the Ummah, they remain addressed by cosmic laws and commanded to exercise caution and exert material effort. Laziness and neglecting precautions under the pretext of "trust" is a blameworthy dependence and ignorance of religion.

The correct equation requires that a Muslim works in his life, call, and labor with all his might, planning and using material means as if he owns nothing else, yet believing in his heart and certainty that these means do not harm or benefit by themselves except by the permission of Allah Almighty. Thus, he remains connected to his Lord, brave and courageous, unshaken by storms and untroubled by the swords of adversaries as long as he stands by the command of Allah and follows His laws.

5. The Legislative Philosophy of Jihad: The Flexibility of Gradual Rulings According to the Balance of Power (5. الفلسفة التشريعية للجهاد: مرونة تدرج الأحكام تبعاً لميزان القوى)

The Islamic Sharia (الشريعة الإسلامية) is a realistic divine law that respects cosmic sunan (laws) and adopts a precise balance between benefits and harms. Therefore, its rulings did not descend all at once in major issues like war and fighting, but progressed gradually. This gradual legislation represents a fundamental school confirming the flexibility of Islamic rulings and their applicability to practical reality according to the balance of power, far from theoretical rigidity that does not respect the understanding of reality.

The legislative path of fighting in Islam was established through four successive historical and legislative phases:

Phase One: Restraining Hands and Beautiful Pardon (The Makkan Era) (المرحلة الأولى: كف الأيدي والصفح الجميل (العهد المكي))

In this phase, the Muslims were a weak minority in Makkah (مكة), living in a hostile environment lacking an organized political entity to protect them. The divine guidance came decisively to "restrain hands" (كف الأيدي) and completely abstain from any military confrontation or armed defense, limiting themselves to educational building, spiritual resilience, and establishing prayer, as the verse states:

{أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِينَ قِيلَ لَهُمْ كُفُّوا أَيْدِيَكُمْ وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَآتُوا الزَّكَاةَ}
"Have you not seen those who were told, 'Restrain your hands and establish prayer and give zakah'?" [An-Nisa: 77] (النساء: 77).

The Muslims used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to defend themselves against the torture they experienced, but he would reply to them with the awareness of a leadership committed to divine revelation, saying: "I have been commanded to forgive, so do not fight." (Narrated by Al-Nasai (النسائي) and Al-Hakim (الحاكم)).

The wisdom behind restraining hands in this phase was profound. Permission to fight in the environment of Makkah would have meant the complete eradication of the nascent group of believers. Furthermore, individual, unregulated fighting turns a movement into a series of assassinations and chaos, striping it of its moral message. The alternative was patience and pardon to train souls for sacrifice and discipline, as Allah says:

{فاصْفَحِ الصَّفْحَ الْجَمِيلَ}
"So overlook with gracious forgiveness." [Al-Hijr: 85] (الحجر: 85).

Phase Two: Permission to Defend (The Beginning of the Madinan Era) (المرحلة الثانية: الإذن بالدفاع (بداية العهد المدني))

After the migration and the establishment of an organized political entity for the Muslims in Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة), the balances changed. The Muslims now had a land, power, and a system to protect them. Here, legislation moved to a new phase, which was the "permission to defend" without fighting being mandatory. The verse was revealed:

{أُذِنَ لِلَّذِينَ يُقَاتَلُونَ بِأَنَّهُمْ ظُلِمُوا ۚ وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ نَصْرِهِمْ لَقَدِيرٌ * الَّذِينَ أُخْرِجُوا مِن دِيَارِهِم بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ إِلَّا أَن يَقُولُوا رَبُّنَا اللَّهُ}
"Permission [to fight] has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged. And indeed, Allah is competent to give them victory. [They are] those who have been expelled from their homes without right - only because they say, 'Our Lord is Allah'." [Al-Hajj: 39-40] (الحج: 39-40).

The use of the passive voice {أُذِنَ} ("permission has been given") indicates in legal terms permissibility and concession. Fighting here is a concession to repel injustice and recover usurped rights for whoever among the believers wishes; it did not yet rise to the level of an individual or collective obligation. It served as a psychological and legislative transition for the companions from the long period of restraining hands to the era of resistance and confrontation.

Phase Three: The Obligation of Fighting Aggressors (Defensive Warfare) (المرحلة الثالثة: فرضية قتال المعتدين (وجوب الدفاع))

As the power of the Islamic state consolidated and the harassment of adversaries continued along with their inciting of tribes against it, the ruling of Sharia rose from permissibility (permission) to the level of obligation and duty to repel aggression and protect the religion and homeland. The verse was revealed:

{وَقَاتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ الَّذِينَ يُقَاتَلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوا ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِي الْمُعْتَدِينَ}
"Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress. Indeed. Allah does not like transgressors." [Al-Baqarah: 190] (البقرة: 190).

And:

{كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِتَالُ وَهُوَ كُرْهٌ لَّكُمْ}
"Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you." [Al-Baqarah: 216] (البقرة: 216).

In this phase, fighting became an obligation to repel aggressors and face the armies that approached Al-Madinah (المدينة) or sought to stop the Da'wah by force. The rulings were formulated to restrict fighting to actual combatants, with a prohibition on attacking peaceful civilians, women, children, and the elderly ({وَلَا تَعْتَدُوا}—"but do not transgress").

Phase Four: Offensive Jihad and Removing Obstacles (The Phase of Comprehensive Empowerment) (المرحلة الرابعة: جهاد الطلب وإزالة العقبات (مرحلة التمكين الشامل))

After the Conquest of Makkah (فتح مكة), when people entered the religion of Allah in crowds and the absolute sovereignty of the Islamic state was established in the Arabian Peninsula, the final legislation was revealed to organize relations with the polytheistic political entities plotting against the Da'wah. This was the phase of removing physical barriers and tyrannical systems that stood between nations and hearing the message of Islam with freedom and safety, as Allah says:

{وَقَاتِلُوهُمْ حَتَّىٰ لَا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ وَيَكُونَ الدِّينُ لِلَّهِ}
"Fight them until there is no [more] fitnah (fitnah/trial) and [until] worship is [acknowledged to be] for Allah." [Al-Baqarah: 193] (البقرة: 193).

And He says in Surah At-Tawbah (سورة التوبة):

{فَإِذَا انسَلَخَ الْأَشْهُرُ الْحُرُمُ فَاقْتُلُوا الْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ وَخُذُوهُمْ وَاحْصُرُوهُمْ وَاقْعُدُوا لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍ}
"And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them and capture them and besiege them and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush." [At-Tawbah: 5] (التوبة: 5).

This is the phase of "offensive Jihad" (جهاد الطلب), where the Muslims did not wait for the enemy to attack their land, but rather initiated campaigns to secure the Da'wah and convey the word of Allah, while giving nations the choice between accepting Islam, paying the Jizyah (الجزية) while remaining on their religion under the protection of the Islamic state, or fighting the political entity preventing the Da'wah.

The Fundamental Lesson: Rulings are Continuous and Not Completely Abrogated (الدرس الأصولي المستفاد: أحكام قائمة لا تنسخ بالكلية)

Some commentators and scholars of Usool (الأصوليون) held that the verses of the final phase (the verse of the sword) abrogated all previous verses of pardon, peace, and restraining hands in the Makkan and early Madinan eras. However, rigorous scientific research by major scholars—such as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (شيخ الإسلام ابن تيمية), Imam Al-Zarkashi (الإمام الزركشي), and Ibn al-Qayyim (ابن القيم)—settled this issue by establishing an important fundamental rule: "These legislative phases were not abolished or abrogated in a way that invalidates acting upon them forever. Rather, they are established and continuous rulings; each phase is acted upon according to the reality of the Muslims in terms of weakness, strength, and empowerment."

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (شيخ الإسلام ابن تيمية) says in his book Al-Sarim al-Maslul (الصارم المسلول):

"Whoever among the believers is in a land where he is weak, or at a time when he is weak, let him act upon the verse of patience and overlooking those who offend Allah and His Messenger from among the People of the Book and the polytheists. As for those of power, they act upon the verse of fighting the leaders of disbelief who defame the religion."

Imam Al-Zarkashi (الإمام الزركشي) says in his book Al-Burhan fi Ulum al-Qur'an (البرهان في علوم القرآن):

"It is not abrogation, but rather it is of the deferred (المنسأ); meaning that each ruling is tied to a specific circumstance and state. If that circumstance ceases, the first ruling returns. The verses of patience and overlooking are commanded during weakness, and the verses of fighting are commanded during strength."

Applying this fundamental understanding to our contemporary reality protects the Ummah from two dangerous extremes:

  1. The Extreme of Helplessness and Defeatism (منزلق العجز والانهزامية): Which seeks to impose the rulings of weakness and patience (the Makkan era) as a permanent, absolute ruling even in times of capability, seeking to cancel the obligation of Jihad and defense of the Ummah.
  2. The Extreme of Recklessness and Haste (منزلق التهور والاندفاع الصبياني): Which is the more dangerous of the two, where some reckless groups seek to apply the rulings of the fourth phase (offensive Jihad and comprehensive confrontation) in a reality where Muslims are in the highest degrees of weakness and division. In doing so, they bring upon the Ummah and its societies slaughter, destruction, and blood, imagining that they are applying Sharia, while they are violating its gradual legislation and the practical Prophetic methodology that precisely respected the balance of power.

6. The Movement of Early Expeditions and Battles: The Strategy of Suffocating the Enemy's Economic Lifeline (6. حركة السرايا والغزوات الأولى: استراتيجية خنق شريان العدو الاقتصادي)

The beginnings of the Islamic military movement after settling in Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة) were not random, but were part of an integrated military and economic strategy mapped out by the Prophetic methodology to weaken the opponent and project the prestige of the new state. This movement was represented in sending out Sariyyahs (سرايا—expeditions in which the Prophet did not participate personally) and leading Ghazwahs (غزوات—campaigns led by the Prophet himself). Tracking these early campaigns reveals a deep geopolitical vision that used economic warfare as a means of protecting the national security of Al-Madinah (المدينة).

First: Historical Tracking of Early Expeditions and Battles (أولاً: التتبع التاريخي للسرايا والغزوات الأولى)

  • Sariyyah of Sayf al-Bahr (سرية سيف البحر) (Ramadan, 1 AH): The first military expedition, led by the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ), Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib (حمزة بن عبد المطلب رضي الله عنه), with thirty men from the Muhajirun (المهاجرون), to intercept a caravan of Quraysh (قريش) led by Abu Jahl (أبو جهل) with three hundred riders. The two sides met at the coast of the Red Sea (Sayf al-Bahr/سيف البحر), and fighting was about to break out had it not been for the mediation of Majdi ibn Amr al-Juhani (مجدي بن عمرو الجهني), who was an ally to both parties, so they departed without fighting.
  • Sariyyah of Rabigh (سرية رابغ) (Shawwal, 1 AH): Led by Ubaydah ibn al-Harith ibn al-Muttalib (عبيدة بن الحارث بن المطلب) with sixty men from the Muhajirun (المهاجرون). He met Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان) at the head of two hundred fighters at the valley of Rabigh (رابغ). No direct fighting occurred, but the two sides shot arrows at each other. In this expedition, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (سعد بن أبي وقاص رضي الله عنه) shot the first arrow shot in the cause of Islam.
  • Sariyyah of al-Kharrar (سرية الخَرَّار) (Dhu al-Qi'dah, 1 AH): Led by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (سعد بن أبي وقاص) with twenty men to intercept a caravan of Quraysh (قريش). They reached the area of Al-Kharrar (الخرار—near Al-Juhfah/الجحفة) and found that the caravan had passed the day before, so they returned without fighting.
  • Ghazwah of Waddan / al-Abwa (غزوة ودان / الأبواء) (Safar, 2 AH): The first campaign led by the Prophet (ﷺ) himself with seventy men from the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) to intercept a caravan of Quraysh (قريش). He did not encounter any plot, but he utilized the movement to conclude a mutual defense treaty with the tribe of Banu Damrah (بني ضمرة), who were allies of Majdi ibn Amr al-Juhani (مجدي بن عمرو الجهني). He stayed there for fifteen nights.
  • Ghazwah of Buwat (غزوة بواط) (Rabi' al-Awwal, 2 AH): The Prophet (ﷺ) went out with two hundred of the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) to intercept a massive commercial caravan of Quraysh (قريش) led by Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف), containing one hundred men and two thousand five hundred camels. He reached the area of Buwat (بواط—from the mountains of Juhaynah/جهينة), but the caravan had taken another route, so he returned without fighting.
  • Ghazwah of Safawan / First Badr (غزوة سفوان / بدر الأولى) (Rabi' al-Awwal, 2 AH): A forced military movement. The polytheist Kurz ibn Jabir al-Fihri (كرز بن جابر الفهري) raided the pastures of Al-Madinah (المدينة) with a light force and stole some livestock. The Prophet (ﷺ) went out with seventy of his companions to pursue him until he reached the valley of Safawan (سفوان—near Badr/بدر), but Kurz had already escaped. This campaign is called "the First Battle of Badr" (غزوة بدر الأولى).
  • Ghazwah of Dhu al-Ushayrah (غزوة ذي العُشيرة) (Jumada al-Ula, 2 AH): The Prophet (ﷺ) went out with two hundred of the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) to intercept the great caravan of Quraysh (قريش) heading to Ash-Sham (الشام) led by Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان). He reached the area of Dhu al-Ushayrah (ذي العشيرة—between Yanbu/ينبع and Al-Madinah/المدينة) and found that the caravan had passed a few days prior. However, he utilized the situation to conclude a peace treaty and alliance with the tribe of Banu Mudlij (بني مُدْلج).

Second: Lessons of the Early Movements (ثانياً: الدروس المستفادة من الحركية الأولى)

The attempts to intercept Quraysh's caravans raise a question about the moral and legal legitimacy of these operations. Legal investigation confirms that these campaigns were an application of the principle of "reciprocity and recovering usurped rights." The Muhajirun (المهاجرون) were forced out of Makkah (مكة), and Quraysh confiscated their homes, wealth, and trades without right, as the Qur'an states:

{الَّذِينَ أُخْرِجُوا مِن دِيَارِهِمْ وَأَمْوَالِهِمْ يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًا مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَرِضْوَانًا}
"[They are] for the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and [His] approval." [Al-Hashr: 8] (الحشر: 8).

Quraysh was using these confiscated funds to run trade caravans and finance military efforts against the Muslims. Thus, their wealth became part of the hostile military system, and targeting it was a strategic duty to paralyze the enemy's capability and secure the emerging state, as Allah says:

{إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنفِقُونَ أَمْوَالَهُمْ لِيَصُدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ ۚ فَسَيُنفِقُونَهَا ثُمَّ تَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ حَسْرَةً ثُمَّ يُغْلَبُونَ}
"Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. So they will spend it; then it will be for them a regret; then they will be overcome." [Al-Anfal: 36] (الأنفال: 36).

The failure of the Muslims to intercept Abu Sufyan's (أبو سفيان) caravan in the Ghazwah of Dhu al-Ushayrah (غزوة ذي العشيرة) carries a deep lesson in "contentment and trust in divine planning." The Muslims planned to intercept the caravan on its way to Ash-Sham (الشام) and exerted their efforts, but they missed it. By human standards, this failure was disappointing, but by the standards of gentle divine planning, missing it was the preparation for the decisive Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى).

Allah Almighty preserved this same caravan for them to intercept on its return from Ash-Sham (الشام). This became the reason for Quraysh to march out with all its military pride, so that Allah might establish a matter already ordained, breaking the power of polytheism and raising the banner of Islam, as He says:

{كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِتَالُ وَهُوَ كُرْهٌ لَّكُمْ ۖ وَعَسَىٰ أَن تَكْرَهُوا شَيْئًا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ ۖ وَعَسَىٰ أَن تُحِبُّوا شَيْئًا وَهُوَ شَرٌّ لَّكُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ}
"Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not." [Al-Baqarah: 216] (البقرة: 216).

These continuous campaigns reveal a physical and physical-endurance aspect in the personality of the Prophet (ﷺ). He personally led four military campaigns (Waddan, Buwat, Safawan, Dhu al-Ushayrah) in a matter of a few months (between Safar and Jumada al-Ula of the second year AH).

The Prophet (ﷺ) was fifty-five years old at the time—an age classified by the standards of his era and ours as advanced. Nevertheless, he traversed deserts and wilderness under the burning sun of the desert, riding or walking, enduring the hardships of the military field and strategic planning with physical and spiritual fitness. This continuous physical exertion directs a message to the Ummah on the necessity of "preserving strength and body." The Sharia, which urged the preparation of physical strength, made preserving health a recognized interest, so that a believer remains capable of giving, striving, and supporting his religion in all stages of his life, following the Prophetic ambition that was not deterred by advanced age from leading armies and establishing states.

7. The Expedition of "Nakhla": The Fiqh of Confronting Mistakes and Dismantling the Double Standards of Falsehood (7. سرية "نخلة": فقه مواجهة الأخطاء وتفكيك ازدواجية معايير الباطل)

The expedition of "Nakhla" (سرية نخلة), which occurred in the month of Rajab of the second year AH, is one of the most prominent historical and legislative stages in the Prophetic biography. It revealed the unique method of Islam in dealing with internal mistakes and correcting them with courage, while establishing rules in confronting the psychological and media war of adversaries and dismantling the double standards of falsehood. The circumstances of this expedition, starting from its precise intelligence organization to the Quranic commentary on it, offer a profound lesson in education and Islamic politics.

First: Organizational Details and the Tactical Dilemma (أولاً: التفاصيل التنظيمية والمعضلة الاجتهادية)

The Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abdullah ibn Jahsh (عبد الله بن جحش رضي الله عنه) at the head of eight (and in some narrations twelve) men from the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) on a highly secret and dangerous intelligence mission. To ensure complete secrecy, the Prophet (ﷺ) handed the leader of the expedition a closed letter and commanded him with strict security:

"Do not look into it until you have traveled for two days, then look into it and proceed to do what I have commanded you, and do not force any of your companions." (Narrated by Ibn Hisham (ابن هشام) and Al-Daraqutni (الدارقطني)).

Abdullah ibn Jahsh (عبد الله بن جحش) marched for two days, then opened the letter, and found in it:

"When you look into this letter of mine, proceed until you dismount at Nakhla (نخلة), between Makkah (مكة) and Al-Ta’if (الطائف), and lie in wait there for a caravan of Quraysh (قريش), and gather news of them for us."

The companions complied and dismounted at Nakhla (نخلة), observing the caravans of Quraysh. A commercial caravan of Quraysh passed by carrying raisins and leather, guarded by four men: Amr ibn al-Hadrami (عمرو بن الحضرمي), Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah (عثمان بن عبد الله بن المغيرة), his brother Nawfal (نوفل), and Al-Hakam ibn Kaysan (الحكم بن كيسان).

Here, the companions faced a complex "interpretative and tactical dilemma" (معضلة اجتهادية وتكتيكية). The caravan was passing on the last day of the month of Rajab (رجب), which is one of the Sacred Months (الأشهر الحُرُم) in which fighting was prohibited among the Arabs. The companions consulted and made an ijtihad (اجتهاد), saying: "If you leave them tonight, they will enter the Sanctuary (الحرم) and be protected from you, and if you kill them, you will have killed them in the Sacred Month."

The option to attack prevailed. Waqid ibn Abdullah al-Tamimi (واقد بن عبد الله التميمي) shot Amr ibn al-Hadrami (عمرو بن الحضرمي) with an arrow and killed him. They captured Uthman ibn Abdullah (عثمان بن عبد الله) and Al-Hakam ibn Kaysan (الحكم بن كيسان), while Nawfal ibn al-Mughirah (نوفل بن المغيرة) escaped back to Makkah. The companions drove the caravan and the two captives toward Al-Madinah (المدينة).

Second: The Firm Prophetic Stance and Correcting the Mistake (ثانياً: الموقف النبوي الصارم وتصويب الخطأ)

When the expedition reached Al-Madinah Al-Munawwarah (المدينة المنورة) with the spoils and the two captives, they were surprised by an angry and decisive Prophetic stance. The Prophet (ﷺ) refused to approve their ijtihad and their violation of the Sacred Months, saying to them with disapproval: "I did not command you to fight in the Sacred Month."

The Prophetic leadership did not accept justifying the mistake under the guise of "ijtihad" or "military benefit," nor did it flatter its companions because they belonged to the Muslim ranks. Rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) took strict practical measures to correct the violation:

  1. Suspending the Spoils (وقف الغنائم): The Prophet (ﷺ) halted the caravan and the two captives and did not take anything from them.
  2. Paying the Blood Money (أداء الدية): The Prophet (ﷺ) paid the blood money of the slain Amr ibn al-Hadrami (عمرو بن الحضرمي) from the treasury of the Muslims to his tribe in Makkah.
  3. Releasing the Captives (إخلاء الأسرى): He released the two captives (Uthman and Al-Hakam) as soon as the two companions who had lagged behind the expedition (Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas/سعد بن أبي وقاص and Utbah ibn Ghazwan/عتبة بن غزوان) returned safely.

Third: The Polytheistic Propaganda and the Decisive Quranic Reply (ثالثاً: البروباجندا الشركية والرد القرآني المفحم)

Quraysh and its allies from among the Jews and hypocrites exploited the incident for propaganda to sway public opinion and distort the image of the emerging Islamic entity. They launched an intense campaign among the tribes, proclaiming: "Muhammad has violated the Sacred Month, shed blood in it, taken wealth in it, and captured men in it."

This campaign caused concern within the Muslim ranks until divine revelation descended to put things in their proper perspective, adopting a powerful psychological and media methodology that dismantled the double standards of the polytheists, as stated in Surah Al-Baqarah (سورة البقرة):

{يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرَامِ قِتَالٍ فِيهِ ۖ قُلْ قِتَالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ ۖ وَصَدٌّ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَكُفْرٌ بِهِ وَالْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ وَإِخْرَاجُ أَهْلِهِ مِنْهُ أَكْبَرُ عِندَ اللَّهِ ۚ وَالْفِتْنَةُ أَكْبَرُ مِنَ الْقَتْلِ}
"They ask you about the sacred month - about fighting therein. Say, 'Fighting therein is great [sin], but averting [people] from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him and [preventing access to] al-Masjid al-Haram and the expulsion of its people therefrom are much greater [evil] in the sight of Allah. And fitnah is greater than killing'." [Al-Baqarah: 217] (البقرة: 217).

The divine reply relied on two primary pillars:

  1. Acknowledging the Mistake and Self-Honesty (الإقرار بالخطأ والصدق الذاتي): {قُلْ قِتَالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ} ("Say, fighting therein is a great sin"). Yes, fighting in the Sacred Month is a major sin and a violation of Allah's law, and we do not deny or justify it.
  2. Dismantling the Adversary's Standards and Highlighting Their Crimes (The Counterattack) (تفكيك معايير الخصم وإبراز جرائمه): The verses turned to the complaining party (Quraysh) to expose the abundance of their crimes and the falsehood of their moral crying. For those who practice averting people from the way of Allah, disbelieving in Him, preventing access to al-Masjid al-Haram, expelling its people unjustly (which is what Quraysh did to the Muslims in Makkah), and committing fitnah (polytheism and torturing believers to turn them back from monotheism)... have no moral right to speak of sanctity and Sacred Months. Your crimes {أَكْبَرُ عِندَ اللَّهِ} ("are much greater in the sight of Allah") than the mistake of the believers, and your fitnah {أَكْبَرُ مِنَ الْقَتْلِ} ("is greater than the killing") that occurred in the expedition.

Fourth: Lessons in Leadership and Confronting Psychological Warfare (رابعاً: دروس في القيادة ومواجهة الحرب النفسية)

The Nakhla expedition (سرية نخلة) establishes highly important educational and political rules:

  • Courage in Acknowledging and Correcting Mistakes (الشجاعة في الاعتراف بالخطأ وتصويبه): The Islamic methodology does not fear admitting the mistakes of its members; mistakes occur as long as humans make ijtihad. Flattery and justifying mistakes or crimes under the pretext of "supporting the ranks" or "preserving reputation" is an un-Islamic path. Acknowledging mistakes and returning material rights (such as blood money and releasing captives) is the source of moral strength for the Da'wah.
  • Rejecting Media Blackmail and Dismantling Double Standards (رفض الابتزاز الإعلامي وتفكيك ازدواجية الباطل): Falsehood always plays the game of "moral crying," ignoring its own major crimes and organized massacres, while focusing on an individual mistake or an unintentional transgression by the people of truth to make it the issue of the era. The Quranic methodology teaches us not to stand in a defensive, apologetic, fearful position in such situations. Rather, we acknowledge the mistake with courage, and then direct a direct counter-critique against falsehood to expose its shame and double standards, reminding people of its major crimes that it tries to make them forget while crying over ruins.

1. The Psychology of Response to Commands: The Trial of the "First Abrogation" as an Educational Sieve (1. سيكولوجية الاستجابة للأوامر: ابتلاء "النسخ الأول" كمصفاة تربوية)

The issue of "command and prohibition" holds a central position in the Islamic conception of shaping the human personality and preparing it to carry the message. The divine command is not merely a dry, legalistic obligation devoid of psychological dimensions; rather, it is a surgical scalpel that cuts deep into the human soul to stir its hidden aspects and test its level of detachment from self-interest and the illusion of an intellect independent of revelation.

This educational philosophy is manifested in its finest form during the event of the "changing of the Qibla" from Jerusalem (بيت المقدس) to the Holy Kaaba (الكعبة المشرفة) in Sha'ban (شعبان) of the second year of the Hijra (الهجرة). This event was not merely a geo-spiritual shift in the direction of prayer, but rather represented the first legislative shake-up in Islam through the gateway of the "First Abrogation." This made it a decisive educational sieve whose methodological effects remain active in the understanding of change and confronting trials.

First: The Psychological Dimensions of the "First Abrogation" and the Weight of the Legislative Shock (أولاً: الأبعاد النفسية لـ "النسخ الأول" وثقل الصدمة التشريعية)

According to psychological and social laws, human beings naturally incline toward familiarity and habit. Acts of worship acquire an additional sacred character in human consciousness when they are linked to temporal and spatial stability. Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem (بيت المقدس) throughout the Meccan era (thirteen years) and continued to do so in Medina (المدينة المنورة) for approximately sixteen or seventeen months, as established in the Sahihayn from the Hadith of Al-Bara bin Azib (البراء بن عازب), may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

"We prayed with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, toward Jerusalem (بيت المقدس) for sixteen or seventeen months, then we were turned toward the Kaaba (الكعبة)."

During this long period, the devotional structure of Muslims was formed around this geographical and spiritual direction, which was historically linked to the efforts of previous prophets, peace be upon them, and their monotheistic heritage. Because the soul grows accustomed to the familiar and finds sudden change difficult, the arrival of the command to change direction represented a genuine shock to the established mental and devotional system.

This psychological weight was doubled because this event was the "First Abrogation" experienced by the Muslim community. The Companions had not previously been accustomed to the reversal of an established ruling or the replacement of one obligation with another in the major pillars of worship, such as prayer. From this starting point, those lurking in wait for the call found wide loopholes to raise doubts and spread psychological disturbance within the ranks of the Muslims. The fronts of this psychological warfare were divided into three camps:

  • The Jewish Camp (المعسكر اليهودي): They focused on intellectual and foundational attacks to undermine the worship of Muslims, raising questions such as: "If your initial prayer toward Jerusalem (بيت المقدس) was correct, then you have abandoned the truth now and turned to falsehood. And if your current direction toward the Kaaba (الكعبة) is correct, then your prayers throughout those years were invalid, and your rewards and the rewards of those who died while praying toward the first Qibla have been lost."
  • The Polytheist Camp (المعسكر المشرك): They exploited the event politically and psychologically by claiming that Muhammad (محمد) had reneged on his Qibla and begun to return to the Qibla of his fathers and ancestors—the Kaaba (الكعبة)—which, according to their claims, meant he was close to abandoning his religion and returning to the pagan creed of his people.
  • The Hypocrite Camp (معسكر المنافقين): They used the event as a means to sow confusion and doubt, claiming that the leader could not settle on a decision, turning sometimes to the north and other times to the south without revelation or guidance.

In the face of this psychological and propaganda storm, steadfastness in obeying the command required a strength of certainty that transcended the limits of abstract rational logic to settle in the realms of absolute submission.

Second: The Mechanism of Divine Consolidation and the Philosophy of Repetition in the Qur'anic Text (ثانياً: آلية التثبيت الإلهي وفلسفة التكرار في النص القرآني)

This psychological shake-up necessitated a decisive and intensive Qur'anic intervention that did not stop at merely announcing the new ruling, but worked primarily on dismantling doubts and providing psychological support to the Muslims. This focus is prominent in the linguistic and methodological structure of the verses in Surah Al-Baqarah (سورة البقرة), where we find a striking repetition of the command to change direction in close succession:

  • The First Instance:
    {قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِي السَّمَاءِ ۖ فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةً تَرْضَاهَا ۚ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ...}
    "We have certainly seen the turning of your face, [O Muhammad], toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a Qibla with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram..." [Surah Al-Baqarah: 144] (البقرة: 144).
  • The Second Instance:
    {وَمِنْ حَيْثُ خَرَجْتَ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ ۖ وَإِنَّهُ لَلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ...}
    "And from wherever you go out [for prayer], turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord..." [Surah Al-Baqarah: 149] (البقرة: 149).
  • The Third Instance:
    {وَمِنْ حَيْثُ خَرَجْتَ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ ۚ وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ...}
    "And from wherever you go out [for prayer], turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you [believers] may be, turn your faces toward it..." [Surah Al-Baqarah: 150] (البقرة: 150).

Repetition in Qur'anic eloquence is not redundant; in this context, it is a security and educational tool used to achieve "psychological and legislative consolidation." The first instance came to explain the permission for change, taking into account the desire of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and pleasing him. The second instance came to link this transition to the absolute truth and revelation issuing from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to repel any suspicion of personal desire or self-reversal. The third instance came to generalize the ruling to all Muslims in every corner of the earth and under all circumstances, cutting off any interpretation or exception that skeptics might exploit.

These verses descended to eliminate the gray area in people's souls; it was either complete submission to the new command without hesitation, or turning back on one's heels. The definitive verse summarized the philosophy of this trial with the words of Allah Almighty:

{وَمَا جَعَلْنَا الْقِبْلَةَ الَّتِي كُنتَ عَلَيْهَا إِلَّا لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّن يَنقَلِبُ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ ۚ وَإِن كَانَتْ لَكَبِيرَةً إِلَّا عَلَى الَّذِينَ هَدَى اللَّهُ ۗ وَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمَانَكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنَّاسِ لَرَؤُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ}
"And We did not make the Qibla which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels. And indeed, it is difficult except for those whom Allah has guided. And never would Allah have caused you to lose your faith. Indeed Allah is, to the people, Kind and Merciful." [Surah Al-Baqarah: 143] (البقرة: 143).

Thus, it became clear that the purpose of the "First Abrogation" was not geographical, but was a process of sifting and sorting the ranks to extract pure servitude that does not hesitate in the face of changing obligations.

Third: The Methodological Paradox in Surah Al-Baqarah: From the Hesitation of the Children of Israel to the Compliance of the Companions (ثالثاً: المفارقة المنهجية في سورة البقرة: من تردد بني إسرائيل إلى امتثال الصحابة)

The structural genius of Surah Al-Baqarah (سورة البقرة) is evident in highlighting a massive methodological paradox comparing two human models in dealing with the divine command; one model left its people with humiliation and dispersion, while the other qualified its people for leadership and guidance of humanity:

The Surah was named "Al-Baqarah" (البقرة - The Cow) to immortalize the model of failure in responding. The verses [Surah Al-Baqarah: 67-71] show how the Children of Israel (بني إسرائيل) dealt with a simple and clear divine command to "slaughter a cow":

  1. Doubt and Accusations of Mockery: The beginning was confronting the prophet with accusations and skepticism: {قَالُوا أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُوًا ۖ قَالَ أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِنَ الْجَاهِلِينَ} (They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.").
  2. Requesting Details to Evade Execution: They resorted to the weapon of impossible questions to evade direct implementation: {قَالُوا ادْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ} (They said, "Call upon your Lord to make clear to us what it is."), then they asked about its color: {قَالُوا ادْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوْنُهَا} (They said, "Call upon your Lord to make clear to us what is its color."), and then they used similarity and ambiguity as an excuse: {قَالُوا ادْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ إِنَّ الْبَقَرَ تَشَابَهَ عَلَيْنَا} (They said, "Call upon your Lord to make clear to us what it is. Indeed, [all] cows look alike to us.").
  3. Heavy-hearted and Soulless Execution: After narrowing options upon themselves with highly rare details, they executed the command without willingness or love: {فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ} (So they slaughtered it, and they were near to not doing it.).

This model represents the "bane of philosophizing and arguing in the face of obligation," where the intellect is transformed from a tool for understanding and executing the command into a cover to justify evasion and maneuvering through questioning and intellectual evasion.

Immediately after reviewing the transgressions and hesitation of the Children of Israel (بني إسرائيل), the Surah transitions to present the scene of response in the new Muslim community through the event of the changing of the Qibla. This model was practically embodied in the incident narrated by Imam Al-Bukhari (الإمام البخاري) on the authority of Abdullah bin Umar (عبد الله بن عمر), may Allah be pleased with them both, who said:

"While the people were at Quba (قباء) offering the morning prayer, a man came to them and said: 'Some Qur'anic verses have been revealed to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, tonight, and he has been commanded to face the Kaaba (الكعبة), so face it.' Their faces were toward the Levant (الشام), so they turned around toward the Kaaba (الكعبة)."

In the narration of Al-Bara bin Azib (البراء بن عازب) in Sahih Muslim (صحيح مسلم), a man passed by some people while they were bowing in the afternoon (or noon) prayer toward Jerusalem (بيت المقدس), and he called out: "I testify by Allah that I have prayed with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, toward Mecca (مكة)," so they turned, just as they were, toward the House.

This scene represents the peak of ethical and methodological contrast and distinction:

  • They did not interrupt their prayer waiting for intellectual verification or the issuance of a written administrative decision.
  • They did not hold a consultative council during the prayer to ask: "How can we turn based on a single-narrator report? And what is the fate of our previous prayers?"
  • They turned 180 degrees while in bowing or standing positions, responding to the voice of the Commander immediately.

This rapid response crushed the temporal and mental distance between "hearing the command" and "acting upon it." While the Children of Israel (بني إسرائيل) spent days arguing and being obstinate over a cow, the Muslims spent a mere few seconds to completely turn their prayers from the far north to the far south.

Fourth: The Bane of "Intellectual Philosophizing" and the Relationship between Submission and Inheriting the Earth (رابعاً: آفة "الفلسفة الفكرية" وعلاقة التسليم باستخلاف الأرض)

This methodological contrast reveals a deep truth regarding the laws of succession and the building of nations: namely, that "sovereignty and empowerment are not granted by Allah to a nation that excels in philosophizing and arguing in the face of His commands." The historical fall of the Children of Israel (بني إسرائيل) and their removal from the leadership of humanity was not due to a lack of intelligence or reasoning, but was due to the sickness of hesitation and bypassing obligations with questions and intellectual maneuvers that empty the text of its spirit and content.

The "philosophy of obligation" dictates that the human intellect possesses full space for research and contemplation in understanding the wisdom of a legal ruling, but it does not possess the right to halt the execution of the ruling while waiting for that wisdom to be uncovered. The true believer hastens to act as soon as the command is issued, out of certainty in the wisdom of the Commander, Subhanahu wa Ta'ala, and in submission to His encompassing knowledge, and then seeks the subtleties and wisdoms of the legislation during or after the action. As for conditioning compliance upon abstract rational conviction, this is a deification of the intellect and making desire a judge over Allah, Glorified be He.

Therefore, Surah Al-Baqarah (سورة البقرة) came to establish this methodological boundary between the two nations. From the moment of immediate response in changing the Qibla, Allah Almighty announced the transfer of the leadership of the earth and the carrying of the trust of the message to this new nation, which summarized its motto of survival in two words: {سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا} (We hear and we obey). By this, the Muslim community transformed from a weak "quantity" into a qualified "quality" ready to establish strength and deterrence, preparing to fight the great battle of the criterion at Badr (بدر) with solid hearts and resolves that do not hesitate in the face of hardships.

2. The Jurisprudence of "Purification" and Preparing the Ranks Before Major Events (2. فقه "التصفية والتربية" وتهيئة الصفوف قبل الأحداث الكبرى)

Divine decrees do not move toward paths of empowerment and victory randomly or by temporal coincidence; rather, they are governed by constant laws and precise rules that prepare the psychological and human ground for the event before it occurs. In this context, the precise timing of changing the Qibla in the month of Sha'ban (شعبان) in the second year of the Hijra—just one month before the decisive Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) in Ramadan (رمضان) of the same year—stands out as one of the deepest models of divine planning to prepare and purify the Muslim rank before fighting fateful battles.

First: Allah's Constant Sunnah in Sifting and Distinguishing Before Empowerment (أولاً: سنة الله المطردة في الغربلة والتمهيز قبل التمكين)

The divine laws in building nations and states dictate that victory and empowerment are not granted to a rank in which the truthful is mixed with the pretender, or through which weak-hearted individuals and hypocrites can infiltrate decision-making positions and fields of confrontation. Victory is not merely a numerical mobilization; it is the ripe fruit of internal cohesion and ultimate spiritual and organizational solidity. From here, the Qur'an establishes a general law in dealing with believing groups:

{مَّا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيَذَرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَلَىٰ مَا أَنتُمْ عَلَيْهِ حَتَّىٰ يَمِيزَ الْخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ ۗ وَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُطْلِعَكُمْ عَلَى الْغَيْبِ وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَجْتَبِي مِن رُّسُلِهِ مَن يَشَاءُ...}
"Allah would not leave the believers in that [state] you are in until He distinguishes the evil from the good. And Allah would not reveal to you the [secrets of] the unseen, but Allah chooses of His messengers whom He wills." [Surah Ali 'Imran: 179] (آل عمران: 179).

The remaining of the Muslim rank in a state of mixing and ambiguity before major battles represents a strategic threat to the national and existential security of the emerging state. Because Allah, Glorified be He, does not disclose to humans the realities of the unseen, consciences, and what lies hidden in breasts, He made sudden trials and transitions the physical, worldly tools that force souls to reveal their reality and compel hypocrites and doubters to declare their positions clearly. Thus, the corrupt is distinguished from the good in the world of physical reality, not only in the world of the unseen and intentions.

Second: The Engineering of Legislative Timing: Why Sha'ban Before Ramadan? (ثانياً: هندسة التوقيت التشريعي: لماذا شعبان قبل رمضان؟)

The connection between the event of changing the Qibla in Sha'ban (شعبان) and the Battle of Badr (بدر) in Ramadan (رمضان) reveals extreme precision in the engineering of legislative and educational timing. If the Muslims had entered the Battle of Badr (بدر) while containing in their ranks those whose hearts shook during the changing of the Qibla, internal collapse during the fighting would have been inevitable.

The event of changing the Qibla functioned as an "earthquake" that disassembled fragile structures in the Muslim rank before the military confrontation:

  1. Forcing the Hesitant to Declare Their Identity: The hypocrites, Jews, and those in whose hearts was a disease used to display compliance with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, for social or political reasons in Medina (المدينة المنورة). When the command to change the Qibla arrived, these people could not tolerate this "sudden shift" which cut their connection with the Jews and restored prestige to the Kaaba (الكعبة). Consequently, they withdrew from following and raised doubts, leading to their automatic departure from the rank or their retreat to the margins.
  2. Achieving Complete Homogeneity Before the Encounter: The sifting process in Sha'ban (شعبان) resulted in a homogeneous, solid rank that did not hesitate in the face of obligation, nor did it debate divine commands with curiosity and argumentation. This homogeneity was the true guarantee against intelligence or psychological breaches during the Battle of Badr (بدر).
  3. Psychological Preparation for Major Military Shifts: The nation that possesses the psychological and educational flexibility to turn 180 degrees in its prayers immediately upon the issuance of a command is the nation qualified for sudden transitions in the battlefield from seeking the Caravan (العير - the easy target) to facing the Army (النفير - the heavily armed force). Whoever succeeded in the legislative trial of the Qibla was worthy of success in the military trial of Badr (بدر).

Third: The Danger of Mixed Ranks and the Law of Internal Collapse (Al-Khabal) (ثالثاً: خطورة الصفوف المختلطة وقانون الانهيار الداخلي (الخبال))

Islamic law emphasizes in its military teachings that a large mobilization combined with weak faith and loyalty represents a burden on the army, not a source of strength. The Qur'an clearly defines the catastrophic repercussions of unpurified groups going out to battle:

{لَوْ خَرَجُوا فِيكُم مَّا زَادُوكُمْ إِلَّا خَبَالًا وَلَأَوْضَعُوا خِلَالَكُمْ يَبْغُونَكُمُ الْفِتْنَةَ وَفِيكُمْ سَمَّاعُونَ لَهُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِالظَّالِمِينَ}
"Had they gone forth with you, they would not have increased you except in confusion, and they would have hurried about in your midst, seeking [to cause] you dissension. And among you are avid listeners to them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers." [Surah At-Tawbah: 47] (التوبة: 47).

The verse reveals three laws of internal collapse in the absence of prior purification and sifting:

  • Al-Khabal (الخبال): This is confusion in opinion and planning, and physical and psychological weakness that transfers contagiously from the discouragers to the rest of the soldiers.
  • Hurrying in the Midst of the Ranks (الإيضاع خلال الصفوف): This is the rapid movement among soldiers to transmit rumors, spread false news, and demoralize resolves, which disrupts the command structure of the army.
  • The Presence of Susceptibility to Respond ("And among you are avid listeners to them"): As long as educational purification is not complete, there will be a group of weak-faith individuals in the rank who will be influenced by those rumors and listen to the callers of dissension, transforming the army into a fragile entity easily penetrated and broken by the enemy.

Therefore, the divine purification of the Badr (بدر) rank through the trial of changing the Qibla was a mercy to the Muslims, protecting them from this internal "confusion" (khabal) which would have ruined the historical victory in Ramadan (رمضان).

Fourth: The Trial of Talut's River: The Historical Precedent for the Sifting Method (رابعاً: ابتلاء نهر طالوت: السابقة التاريخية لمنهجية الغربلة)

The event of changing the Qibla was not an unprecedented occurrence in the history of messages; rather, it was a repetition of consistent laws that applied to previous nations. The Qur'an presents us with a similar model in the story of Talut (طالوت) and his army before facing Jalut (جالوت) and his soldiers, where the "trial of the river" was the purifying tool equivalent to the trial of the Qibla:

{فَلَمَّا فَصَلَ طَالُوتُ بِالْجُنُودِ قَالَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكُم بِنَهَرٍ فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنْهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي وَمَن لَّمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي إِلَّا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ ۚ فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِّنْهُمْ...}
"And when Talut set out with the soldiers, he said, "Indeed, Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me, except one who takes [from it] in the hollow of his hand." But they drank from it, except a few of them..." [Surah Al-Baqarah: 249] (البقرة: 249).

The army of Talut (طالوت) was facing a formidable enemy, Jalut (جالوت), and the path was long and exhausting. The test came through something the soul most desperately desires in the desert: water. The law was strict: whoever drank was not part of the army qualified for victory, and whoever was patient and restrained himself was worthy of carrying the trust.

Just as the river of Talut (طالوت) revealed the failure of the majority and their falling before physical desires and familiarity, the changing of the Qibla revealed the failure of the hypocrites and followers of desire before the changing of rulings and strategic transformations. In the end, only a small believing group crossed the river with Talut (طالوت), but they were the group that achieved victory and defeated the tyrant: {كَم مِّن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ} (How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.). This was exactly the case at Badr (بدر); the Muslims crossed the trial of Sha'ban (شعبان) with pure, submissive hearts, entering Ramadan (رمضان) as the few who overcame the many by Allah’s permission.

Fifth: The Field Fruit in Badr: The Solidity of the Purified Rank (خامساً: الثمرة الميدانية في بدر: صلابة الصف المصفى)

The fruit of this comprehensive educational purification was clearly manifested during the actual encounter in the Battle of Badr (بدر). When the Muslims went out initially, they were not prepared for fighting; rather, they were seeking the unarmed caravan: {وَتَوَدُّونَ أَنَّ غَيْرَ ذَاتِ الشَّوْكَةِ تَكُونُ لَكُمْ} (and you wished that the one but armed [i.e., the caravan] should be yours). When the caravan escaped, and divine decree placed them before an inevitable confrontation with the army of Quraish (قريش) with all its equipment and numbers, no retreat, collapse, or rebellion occurred in the Muslim rank.

Yes, the Qur'an recorded the presence of a natural, human dislike of death and confrontation: {وَإِنَّ فَرِيقًا مِّنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لَكَارِهُونَ} (and indeed, a party among the believers were detesting it), but this natural dislike did not translate into disobedience, hesitation, or abandonment, as was the case with the Children of Israel (بني إسرائيل) with Moses (موسى), or the fallen soldiers of Talut's (طالوت) army at the river. Rather, the entire rank complied with utmost resolve to the prophetic command, and their leaders stood like mountains declaring absolute submission and marching with the leadership to the very end.

This field solidity at Badr (بدر) was the direct result of the education of Sha'ban (شعبان) and the changing of the Qibla. The hearts that had trained to commit to sudden divine commands by turning away from the Qibla they had been familiar with for years found no difficulty in complying with the sudden command to fight a battle for which they were not materially prepared. Thanks to this discipline and detachment, the nation deserved the descent of angelic support, inaugurating the first era of empowerment and sovereignty in its history.

3. The Geography of Military Demographics for the Battle of Badr and its Political Dimensions (3. جغرافية الديموغرافيا العسكرية لمعركة بدر وأبعادها السياسية)

The military demographics of armies in wars represent a decisive tool for understanding the balance of power, not only from a numerical and material perspective, but also from the political and constitutional perspective that governs the relationship of soldiers with the leadership. In the Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى), the composition of the Muslim army was not merely numbers recorded in biographies, but involved a major political and legislative dilemma that almost threatened the political existence of the nascent Islamic state in Medina (المدينة المنورة), were it not for the exceptional, historic stance of the chief of the Ansar (الأنصار) and leader of the Aws (الأوس), Sa'd bin Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ), may Allah be pleased with him.

First: Demographic Analysis of the Badr Army: Numbers and Their Social Significance (أولاً: التحليل الديموغرافي لجيش بدر: الأرقام ودلالتها الاجتماعية)

Approved historical accounts state that the number of the Muslim army at Badr (بدر) ranged between 313 and 317 fighters, with the most famous and established number in biography references being 314 fighters. When breaking down this number demographically, we find a clear imbalance between the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) and the Ansar (الأنصار) in favor of the latter:

  • The Muhajirun (المهاجرون): Their number reached only 82 fighters.
  • The Ansar (الأنصار): Their number reached 232 fighters (representing approximately 74% of the army's total strength).

Diving deeper into the tribal composition of the Ansar (الأنصار), we find a demographic variation reflecting the social structure of Medina (المدينة المنورة) at the time:

  • The Khazraj (الخزرج) Tribe: Represented by 170 fighters.
  • The Aws (الأوس) Tribe: Represented by 61 fighters.

These numbers reveal the following geopolitical facts:

  • The Ansari Majority: The solid core and striking numerical power of the army came from the people of Medina (الأنصار), while the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) represented the numerical minority.
  • Khazraj Superiority: The large number of the Khazraj (الخزرج) (170 fighters) reflects the demographic and political weight of this tribe in Yathrib (يثرب) compared to the Aws (الأوس). This was the tribe that, before the Hijra, aspired to crown Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul (عبد الله بن أبي بن سلول) as its king, which made securing and consolidating their full loyalty a highly sensitive and complex process from a security and political standpoint.

Second: The Constitutional Dilemma: The Geographical Limits of the "Second Pledge of Aqaba" (ثانياً: المعضلة الدستورية: الحدود الجغرافية لبيعة العقبة الثانية)

The political and constitutional dilemma of the Battle of Badr (بدر) lies in the founding document of the state: the "Second Pledge of Aqaba" (بيعة العقبة الثانية) which took place in Mecca (مكة) before the Hijra. This pledge was, in essence, a "local defensive treaty" bound by clear geographical limits. Its historical clauses, as agreed upon by historians, stated:

"You pledge allegiance to me to hear and obey... and to protect me from that which you protect your women and children from when I arrive to you [i.e., Medina]."

Under this constitutional contract, the Ansar (الأنصار) committed to protecting the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and defending the call and the state only within the walls of Medina (المدينة المنورة). The terms of the treaty did not include any military obligation to fight outside the borders of Yathrib (يثرب), or to enter preemptive offensive wars to retrieve the wealth of the Muhajirun (المهاجرون), or to fight Quraish's (قريش) armies in the far deserts away from their homes.

The Ansar’s (الأنصار) initial departure with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to intercept the caravan (العير) fell within non-combat economic activities that did not involve major military confrontation. The caravan was guarded by only forty men, and intercepting it was not considered a fundamental breach of the defensive nature of the pledge. However, when the caravan escaped, and the Muslims faced an inevitable confrontation with the fully armed army of Quraish (قريش) about 150 kilometers outside the borders of Medina (المدينة المنورة), the legislative and constitutional dilemma arose: Did the prophetic leadership have the right to obligate the Ansar (الأنصار) to fight a military battle outside the borders of the signed defensive treaty?

If the Ansar (الأنصار) had adhered to the literal and constitutional text of the Second Pledge of Aqaba, they could have said to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "O Messenger of Allah, our covenant with you is to protect you within our homes. Now that the army has appeared in the desert, return with us to Medina and we will fight them there." If that had happened, the Muslim army would have immediately shrunk to 82 fighters from the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) only, which would have meant certain military suicide and a crushing defeat ending the existence of the state in its infancy.

Third: The Strategy of Prophetic Shura and Respecting Treaties (ثالثاً: استراتيجية الشورى النبوية واحترام العهود)

The moral and constitutional commitment of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to covenants and treaties was manifested in his management of this political crisis. He did not use his absolute religious authority to force the Ansar (الأنصار) into fighting, nor did he issue a direct military command that exploited their social embarrassment; rather, he resorted to an "open shura strategy" to elicit their positions voluntarily and out of love.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, gathered the leaders of the army and consulted them, repeating a general phrase:

"Advise me, O people."

Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق), may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and spoke excellent words declaring loyalty and readiness to fight. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed for him and then repeated: "Advise me, O people." Umar bin Al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب), may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and spoke similarly to Abu Bakr (أبو بكر), and the Prophet prayed for him and repeated the same phrase. Then, Al-Miqdad bin Amr (المقداد بن عمرو), may Allah be pleased with him, stood up and spoke his historic words:

"O Messenger of Allah, go forward to what Allah has shown you, for we are with you. By Allah, we will not say to you as the Children of Israel (بني إسرائيل) said to Moses (موسى): {اذْهَبْ أَنتَ وَرَبُّكَ فَقَاتِلَا إِنَّا هَاهُنَا قَاعِدُونَ} (Go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are remaining right here sitting.) Rather, we say to you: Go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are with you, fighting..."

All three speakers were from the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) (the numerical minority in the army), to whom the rulings of absolute loyalty and migration applied; none of the Ansar (الأنصار) had spoken yet. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, listened, thanked them, and returned to repeating the same phrase: "Advise me, O people."

This repetition was a clear constitutional message captured by the chief of the Ansar (الأنصار) and leader of the Aws (الأوس), Sa'd bin Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ), may Allah be pleased with him, with his intelligence and political acumen.

Fourth: The Declaration of Sa'd bin Mu'adh: The Voluntary Constitutional Amendment (رابعاً: إعلان سعد بن معاذ: التعديل الدستوري الطوعي)

Sa'd bin Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ), may Allah be pleased with him, realized that the target of the consultation was the Ansar (الأنصار); because they represented the numerical majority, and because they were the holders of the geographically restricted defensive covenant. He stood up with the gravity of a leader representing his rank and speaking on behalf of his people, saying:

"It seems as if you mean us, O Messenger of Allah?"

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Yes."

Here, Sa'd bin Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ) delivered his historic document, which in the jurisprudence of Sharia politics is considered a "voluntary constitutional amendment" that shattered the geographical boundaries of the first pledge, establishing a new era of absolute loyalty based on love and belief:

"We have believed in you and testified to your truth, and we have witnessed that what you have brought is the truth, and we have given you our covenants and treaties to hear and obey. So go forward, O Messenger of Allah, to what you want, for we are with you. By Him Who sent you with the truth, if you presented this sea to us and plunged into it, we would plunge into it with you, not a single man of us would stay behind... Perhaps you fear that the Ansar (الأنصار) do not see it as their duty to aid you except in their homes. I speak on behalf of the Ansar (الأنصار) and answer for them: journey wherever you wish, connect the ropes of whomever you wish, cut the ropes of whomever you wish, take from our wealth what you wish, and give us what you wish. What you take from us is more beloved to us than what you leave... So march with us upon the blessing of Allah."

This declaration went beyond diplomatic maneuvering to formulate a new philosophy in the relationship between the nation and the leadership:

  1. Transitioning from Defense to Initiative: Sa'd bin Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ) voluntarily and out of love canceled the geographical condition of the Pledge of Aqaba, declaring the readiness of the Ansar (الأنصار) to fight anywhere specified by the leader, even if it meant crossing the sea or traversing the desert.
  2. Prioritizing the Public Interest Over Private Constitutional Rights: The Ansar (الأنصار) did not adhere to their "legal right" to abstain from fighting outside their homes; rather, they gave it up voluntarily, recognizing the gravity of the situation and the fateful nature of the battle.
  3. Integration and Full Delegation to the Leadership: The Ansar (الأنصار) delegated full authority to the prophetic leadership over wealth, political ties, and military decisions without any restriction or reservation, placing their resources entirely at the service of the general reform project.

Fifth: The Geopolitical Dimensions of the New Covenant (خامساً: الأبعاد الجيوسياسية للعهد الجديد)

The declaration of Sa'd bin Mu'adh (سعد بن معاذ) caused an immense positive wave in the Muslim camp. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, smiled, was pleased, and his face shone. The legislative and security anxieties dissipated, and he immediately ordered the march to meet the army, bringing glad tidings of victory, saying:

"March and have glad tidings, for Allah Almighty has promised me one of the two groups. By Allah, it is as if I am now looking at the death places of the people."

This voluntary constitutional amendment resulted in geopolitical dimensions that changed the course of history:

  • Establishing an Initiating Regional Power: Medina (المدينة المنورة) transformed from a "city-state" defending its narrow borders and turning inward, into a "mission-state" capable of protecting its national security in distant horizons and taking initiatives to thwart the plans of opponents before they reached its territory.
  • Complete Integration into the Crucible of Creed: The demographic and tribal differences between the Aws (الأوس) and the Khazraj (الخزرج) (whose blood from the War of Bu'ath [حرب بعاث] was still fresh in their memories) dissolved, and they merged with the Muhajirun (المهاجرون) into a single, homogeneous rank, expressed by the words of Allah Almighty: {وَالَّذِينَ تَبَوَّءُوا الدَّارَ وَالْإِيمَانَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ يُحِبُّونَ مَنْ هَاجَرَ إِلَيْهِمْ وَلَا يَجِدُونَ فِي صُدُورِهِمْ حَاجَةً مِّمَّا أُوتُوا وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ ۚ وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ}
    "And [also for] those who were settled in al-Madinah and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the greed of his soul - those are the successful." [Surah Al-Hashr: 9] (الحشر: 9).

The historical victory at Badr (بدر) could not have begun in the military field had it not begun first in the political and constitutional field, thanks to this detachment and great loyalty recorded by the Ansar (الأنصار); thus, they deserved to be immortalized by the Qur'an and praised for their support and sheltering of the call in all its difficult stages.

4. Intelligence Warfare and Analysis of Field Impact in the Desert (4. حرب الاستخبارات وتحليل الأثر الميداني في الصحراء)

Military intelligence is the lifeblood feeding strategic and field decisions in wars; for battle is, in essence, a conflict of information before it is a clash of swords and spears. In the harsh desert environment where the events of the Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) took place, every physical trace—no matter how small—possessed immense informational value that could turn the scale of victory and defeat. This battle presented an early pioneering model in "forensic tracking," logistical analysis, and military deduction, manifested in the intelligence acumen of Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان) on one hand, and the analytical prophetic genius in estimating the size of the enemy's army and identifying its leadership on the other.

First: Intelligence Anatomy of Abu Sufyan's Maneuver: "Forensic Tracking" in the Desert (أولاً: التشريح الاستخباري لمناورة أبي سفيان: "تقفي الأثر" في الصحراء)

Abu Sufyan bin Harb (أبو سفيان bin حرب) was not merely a merchant leading a caravan; he was a strategic mind fully aware of the security dangers threatening Mecca’s (مكة) commercial lifeline. When returning with the major caravan from the Levant (الشام), he realized that the Muslims were lying in wait; thus, he took highly vigilant preemptive security measures, including sending scouts, constantly questioning travelers, and changing accustomed routes.

Abu Sufyan’s (أبو سفيان) intelligence genius was demonstrated in the famous incident upon his arrival at the wells of Badr (بدر). He immediately asked Majdi bin Amr Al-Juhani (مجدي بن عمرو الجهني) (who resided in that area) if he had seen anyone suspicious. Majdi answered with the certainty of a simple Bedouin:

"I did not see anyone I disapproved of, except that I saw two riders who knelt their mounts at this hill, then filled their water-skin, and left."

Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان) did not stop at this passing answer; a cautious leader does not build decisions on assumptions, but verifies physical evidence himself. He immediately went to the spot where the two riders (who were the scouts of the Muslims: Basbas bin Amr [بسبس بن عمرو] and Adiy bin Abi Al-Zaghba [عدي بن أبي الزغباء], whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had sent to gather news) had knelt their camels.

Here, the details of "forensic and environmental tracking" emerged. Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان) crumbled the camel dung (روث الإبل) and examined it carefully with his hand, finding date stones inside. Thanks to his precise knowledge of the agricultural geography of the Hejaz (الحجاز), he recognized the quality and structure of the stones, crying out immediately:

"By Allah, this is the fodder of Yathrib (يثرب) [i.e., the dates of Medina]!"

This physical analysis led him to a precise strategic deduction:

  1. The camels that knelt here were fed on Medina dates, which meant the two riders were scouts from Medina (يثرب).
  2. The presence of Yathrib (يثرب) scouts at the wells of Badr (بدر) meant that the Medina army was lying in wait for the caravan and was very close to this site.
  3. Keeping the caravan on its traditional route meant falling completely into the tight trap of the Muslims.

Based on these decisive intelligence findings, Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان) made a rapid decision to save the caravan; he abandoned the road of Badr (بدر) to the right and shifted the direction of movement sharply toward the coast (the shore of the Red Sea) to the west, racing against time to escape with Mecca's (مكة) economic wealth from the grasp of the Muslims.

Second: Interrogation of the Water-Bearers and Prophetic Deductive Intelligence (ثانياً: استجواب السقاة والذكاء الاستدلالي النبوي)

On the other side, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was managing an integrated intelligence operations room to gather information on the caravan's path and the enemy's movements. When the Muslims descended near Badr (بدر), the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, sent an advanced reconnaissance detachment led by Ali bin Abi Talib (علي بن أبي طالب), Al-Zubayr bin Al-Awwam (الزبير بن العوام), and Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas (سعد بن أبي وقاص), may Allah be pleased with them, to gather news at the wells of Badr (بدر).

The detachment succeeded in capturing two boys who were fetching water for the Quraish (قريش) camp: Aslam (أسلم), the slave of Bani Al-Hajjaj (بني الحجاج), and Yasar (يسار), the slave of Bani Al-As bin Sa'id (بني العاص بن سعيد). When they returned with them to the Muslim camp, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was standing in prayer. The Companions began questioning the boys to find the location of the caravan and Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان).

Here, what is known in military psychology as "cognitive bias" became apparent. The Companions desperately desired the caravan (العير) to avoid facing the army (النفير). When the boys said, "We are from the army of Quraish (النفير)," the Companions beat them to force them to lie and say, "We belong to Abu Sufyan (العير)." When they beat them, they said, "We belong to Abu Sufyan," and when they left them, they said, "We are from the Quraish army."

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, noticed this methodological flaw in the interrogation while in his prayer. When he finished, he corrected the situation for the Companions, establishing the foundations of "objective interrogation" that seeks physical truth rather than what souls desire, saying with disapproval:

"When they tell you the truth, you beat them, and when they lie to you, you leave them! By Allah, they spoke the truth; they belong to Quraish (قريش)."

Third: Prophetic Logistic Analysis to Calculate the Enemy's Human Strength (ثالثاً: التحليل اللوجستي النبوي لحساب القوة البشرية للعدو)

After correcting the interrogation method, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, personally undertook the intelligence questioning of the two boys, presenting an astonishing historical model of how to estimate the enemy's human strength through indirect logistical analysis.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked them: "Tell me about Quraish (قريش)?" They said: "By Allah, they are behind this hill at the furthest bank." He asked them about the number: "How many are they?" They said: "Many." He asked them for the precise number: "What is their number?" They said: "We do not know."

Here, the intelligence genius emerged. When the boys failed to provide a "direct numerical piece of information" (as ordinary servants do not usually know the total numbers of armies), the questioning did not stop. Instead, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, shifted the question to the logistical and supply material governing the life of the army—namely, "daily food consumption"—asking them:

"How many camels do they slaughter each day?"

They replied: "Nine one day, and ten the next."

Upon receiving this logistical figure, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, conducted a rapid calculation and deduction based on his deep knowledge of meat consumption rates among fighters. It is strategically known in the desert that one camel suffices to feed approximately one hundred fighters for a full day. Thus, he deduced with extreme accuracy:

"The people are between nine hundred and a thousand."

This estimate was remarkably accurate and objective. It was later proven that the army of Quraish (قريش) that attended the Battle of Badr (بدر) numbered approximately 950 fighters, a figure located precisely in the middle of the range between nine hundred and a thousand deduced by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from the number of daily slaughters. This method represents a foundation in modern military sciences for estimating the size of hostile forces by monitoring their supply lines and logistical consumption rates.
