"O mother of Harithah, indeed there are gardens in Paradise, and your son has attained Al-Firdaus Al-A'la (الفردوس الأعلى — the Highest Paradise)."

This certainty relieved his mother's grief and proved that the young Companions martyred at Badr ascended to the highest levels of Paradise through the sincerity of their intentions and high ambition.

6. An Educational and Behavioral Pause: The Cubs of Badr Facing Digital Isolation and Virtual Reality

The epic of "The Cubs of Badr" presents us with a decisive educational and psychological comparison between the faith-driven youth model and the contemporary reality of today's youth:

Point of Comparison The Cubs of Badr (Faith-driven Field Model) Youth of Today (Digital Isolation Model)
Meaning and Existential Purpose A grand cause lived out, and a divine message for which life is sacrificed. Existential disorientation and a continuous search for quick "dopamine" hits.
Management of Energy and Abilities Transforming deprivation into scientific achievement (Zayd (زيد) learning a language in 17 days). Consuming energy in following platforms and consumerist behaviors.
Psychological and Physical Resilience Legendary capacity to endure pain to pursue the goal (Mu'adh (معاذ) severing his dangling arm). Psychological fragility, severe pressure, and anxiety in the face of minor daily crises.
Relationship with Reality Awareness of duty and direct responsibility on the ground. Immersion in virtual reality and isolation from the real issues of the Ummah.

The Educational Message to the Ummah:
The lesson of "The Cubs of Badr" proves that building a generation capable of change is not accomplished through procrastination or marginalizing the youth's capabilities under the pretext of "young age." Rather, it begins with:

  1. Instilling Grand Causes: Connecting the hearts of youths to pleasing Allah, supporting His religion, and serving the issues of their Ummah.
  2. Investing and Directing Passion: Just as the door of knowledge and intelligence was opened to Zayd ibn Thabit (زيد بن ثابت) when he was prevented from fighting, the frontiers of science, technology, media, and languages must be opened for youth to direct their energy and serve their faith.
  3. Rescuing the Generation from Digital Isolation: Shifting youth from passive consumers of digital platforms and virtual solutions to active influencers who leave a real impact on their society and Ummah.

Element 3: The Doctrine of Loyalty and Disavowal (Al-Wala' wa-l-Bara') and Stripping Away Ignorant Kinship Ties (العنصر الثالث: عقيدة الولاء والبراء وتجريد أواصر القرابة الجاهلية)

The Great Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) was not merely a military confrontation to settle a field dispute; it was "Yawm al-Furqan" (يوم الفرقان — The Day of Criterion) that redefined the concept of identity and human relationships in history. On that day, pre-Islamic tribal ties were severed, and blood and lineage bonds fell away to make room for a single bond above all material anchors: the bond of faith and creed. The Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — placed the doctrine of "Al-Wala' wa-l-Bara'" (الولاء والبراء — Loyalty and Disavowal) on the critical test of practical execution, proving that true brotherhood is the brotherhood of religion and Tawheed (التوحيد — Monotheism), and that spiritual enmity is stripped of all tribal favoritism when truth collides with falsehood.

1. Fighting Relatives at Badr .. Severing Pre-Islamic Ties for the Sake of Monotheism

Arab society before Islam was based on absolute fanaticism for tribe and lineage under the slogan "Help your brother, whether he is the oppressor or the oppressed" in its pre-Islamic sense. But Badr came to make a historical break with this concept. The Muslim found himself on the battlefield facing his father, uncle, brother, or cousin who had chosen to stand in the ranks of shirk (شرك — polytheism) and aggression against the Islamic state.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) — may Allah be pleased with him — embodied absolute devotion to faith on the day of Badr. When he met his maternal uncle, Al-'As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah (العاص بن هشام بن المغيرة) (brother of Abu Jahl — أبو جهل), in the battlefield, neither his lineage nor womb ties deterred him from facing him; rather, he initiated combat and killed him with his own hand.

'Umar (عمر) — may Allah be pleased with him — took pride in this stance and made it a declaration of the correct faith concept, saying to those around him:

"I did not kill my uncle because he was my uncle; rather, I killed disbelief in him."

'Umar (عمر) wanted to send a message to all Muslims that protecting religion and Tawheed takes precedence over all emotional considerations, and that material kinship dissolves when it becomes a barrier between a servant and his Lord.

The custodian of this Ummah, Abu 'Ubaydah 'Amir ibn al-Jarrah (أبو عبيدة عامر بن الجراح) — may Allah be pleased with him — recorded one of the most intense stance of faith in human history. His father (Al-Jarrah — الجراح) was fighting in the ranks of the polytheists on the day of Badr.

Abu 'Ubaydah (أبو عبيدة) tried to avoid encountering his father on the field out of natural filial respect; whenever he saw him approaching, he turned away and moved out of his path. However, the polytheist father insisted on pursuing his son, blocking his paths in the field to fight him. When the father's insistence grew and paths of avoidance closed — with religion on one side of the scale and polytheist fatherhood on the other — Abu 'Ubaydah (أبو عبيدة) advanced with decisive conviction and fought his father until he killed him.

Scholars of Tafsir and Seerah (such as Ibn Kathir — ابن كثير, Al-Qurtubi — القرطبي, and Al-Baghawi — البغوي) agreed that this event and the stances of the Companions at Badr were the reason for the revelation of the decisive verse from Surah Al-Mujadilah (سورة المجادلة) to immortalize this steadfastness of faith:

{لَّا تَجِدُ قَوْمًا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ يُوَادُّونَ مَنْ حَادَّ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَوْ كَانُوا آبَاءَهُمْ أَوْ أَبْنَاءَهُمْ أَوْ إِخْوَانَهُمْ أَوْ عَشِيرَتَهُمْ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ كَتَبَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْإِيمَانَ وَأَيَّدَهُم بِرُوحٍ مِّنْهُ...}
"You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their manner of kinship. Those — He has decreed within their hearts faith and supported them with a spirit from Him" [Surah Al-Mujadilah: 22] (المجادلة: 22).

This doctrine was demonstrated clearly in the stance of Mus'ab ibn 'Umair (مصعب بن عمير) — may Allah be pleased with him — after the battle ended. He passed by a group of Ansar (الأنصار) holding a polytheist captive, who happened to be his full brother, Abu 'Aziz ibn 'Umair (أبو عزيز بن عمير).

Mus'ab (مصعب) saw his brother tied up in the hands of the Ansar soldier, Abu al-Yasar Ka'b ibn 'Amr (أبو اليسر كعب بن عمرو). Neither lineage tenderness nor pre-Islamic brotherly emotion overtook him; instead, he turned to the Ansar soldier and said clearly:

"Bind his hands tightly, for his mother is a woman of wealth; perhaps she will ransom him from you with abundant wealth!"

His brother Abu 'Aziz (أبو عزيز) was astonished and condemned this seemingly harsh stance, saying to Mus'ab (مصعب) reproachfully: "O my brother, is this your recommendation regarding me?!" The historic response came from Mus'ab ibn 'Umair (مصعب بن عمير) to define the new standard of brotherhood:

"He (the Muslim Ansar) is my brother, not you!"

Mus'ab (مصعب) established a firm faith principle through this stance: that the bond connecting a Muslim to his Muslim brother — even if a stranger in blood — is stronger and firmer than the bond of blood with a polytheist brother.

2. Prophetic Care and Humanity .. Solacing Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah (أبو حذيفة بن عتبة)

Despite strict firmness in applying the doctrine of Loyalty and Disavowal, Islam did not negate natural human compassion; rather, it presented the highest model in managing emotions and comforting hearts. This moral peak is evident in the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم) stance with the noble Companion Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah (أبو حذيفة بن عتبة) — may Allah be pleased with him — after the battle ended.

'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah (عتبة بن ربيعة) (father of Abu Hudhayfah — أبو حذيفة) was one of the senior leaders of Quraish (قريش), and he was killed in the duel at the beginning of the battle. When the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) ordered that the bodies of the slain polytheists be dragged to be buried in the pit (Qalib — القليب) of Badr, they passed by the body of 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah (عتبة بن ربيعة) being dragged to the well.

Abu Hudhayfah (أبو حذيفة) was looking at his father's body being dragged, and the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) noticed a shade of grief, gloom, and emotional change on Abu Hudhayfah's (أبو حذيفة) face. The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) did not pass over this stance casually, nor did he accuse him of weak faith or doubt in creed. Instead, he approached him with the mercy and gentle care of prophetic leadership, asking him softly:

"O Abu Hudhayfah, perhaps something has affected you regarding the matter of your father?"

The answer of Abu Hudhayfah (أبو حذيفة) — may Allah be pleased with him — revealed a sophisticated understanding that distinguished between "the grief of natural compassion over one's fate" and "doubt in faith and truth." He said with sincere conviction:

"No, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah! I have not doubted my father nor his death. However, I knew my father to possess wisdom, forbearance, and virtue, and I used to hope that these would guide him to Islam. So when I saw what befell him, and remembered the disbelief upon which he died after what I had hoped for him, that grieved me."

Abu Hudhayfah (أبو حذيفة) clarified that he did not grieve over his father being killed in the cause of Allah, nor did he doubt that he deserved this end. Rather, he grieved because his polytheist father — despite his intellect, forbearance, and virtue among the Arabs — did not benefit from his intellect and died upon disbelief, deprived of the guidance of Islam that he had wished for him.

When the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) heard this truthfulness and elevated human devotion from Abu Hudhayfah (أبو حذيفة):

"The Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) prayed for good for him and spoke kindly to him." (Narrated by Ibn Hisham — ابن هشام, Al-Hakim in Al-Mustadrak — المستدرك, and Al-Bayhaqi in Dalail al-Nubuwwah — دلائل النبوة).

Summary of Spiritual Balance in the Prophetic Methodology:
This element presents a complete picture of the unique balance in Islamic law, combining firmness of principle with tenderness of humanity:

  1. Firmness of Faith in Collisions of Truth and Falsehood: No room for compromise or tribal favoritism on the field; religion reigns supreme (as demonstrated by 'Umar — عمر, Abu 'Ubaydah — أبو عبيدة, and Mus'ab — مصعب).
  2. Natural Mercy and Emotional Care: Deep Prophetic understanding that allows space for natural grief over fathers and relatives who died upon polytheism, supporting Companions psychologically and comforting them without compromising faith principles.
  3. Forming the New Society: Rebuilding the Ummah upon Tawheed and faith equality, so that all Muslims become one hand against others, undivided by lineage and ununited by pre-Islamic tribalism.

Element 4: Echoes of Defeat in Makkah and Victory in Madinah (العنصر الرابع: صدى الهزيمة في مكة والفتح في المدينة)

The results of the Great Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) were not merely a shift in the military landscape of the Badr battlefield; rather, they caused a geostrategic and psychological earthquake whose immediate effects extended to the two major poles of the Arabian Peninsula: Makkah (مكة المكرمة) (the stronghold of polytheism and capital of tyranny) and Madinah (المدينة المنورة) (the nascent capital of Islam). While astonishment, disgrace, and fear hovered over Makkah after its elite leaders were eradicated, Madinah was living a unique emotional epic where tears of human grief over the death of the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم) daughter blended with Takbeers (تكبيرات) of joy and celebration over the first Divine victory.

1. Echoes of Defeat in Makkah .. The Shock and the Fall of Pride

Quraish (قريش) lived in a state of psychological shock and self-denial following the battle; its leaders had not calculated that their magnificent army would return broken, and that the heads of disbelief would be severed within hours at the hands of the oppressed group they had driven out yesterday.

The first person to bring news of the defeat to Makkah was Al-Haysaman ibn 'Abdullah al-Khuza'i (الحيصمان بن عبد الله الخزاعي). People met him eagerly, asking for news, so he began listing the dead without introduction: "Killed was 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah (عتبة بن ربيعة), Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah (شيبة بن ربيعة), Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham (أبو الحكم بن هشام) (Abu Jahl — أبو جهل), Umayyah ibn Khalaf (أمية بن خلف), Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad (زمعة بن الأسود)..."

These names caused immense shock in Makkah, so much so that Safwan ibn Umayyah (صفوان بن أمية) (who was sitting in the Hijr — الحِجر) could not comprehend the magnitude of the calamity. He thought the man had lost his mind, saying to those around him with arrogant denial:

"By Allah, this man does not know what he is saying! Ask him about me, for if he is sane, he will remember me!"

They turned to Al-Haysaman (الحيصمان) and asked him: "What happened to Safwan ibn Umayyah (صفوان بن أمية)?" Al-Haysaman (الحيصمان) pointed directly toward Safwan (صفوان) and said:

"There he is, sitting in the Hijr! By Allah, I saw his father and brother when they were killed!"

At that moment, Quraish (قريش) realized the magnitude of the disaster, and fear spread through its homes. Due to the severity of the shock and fear of showing vulnerability in front of Muslims, Quraish issued a firm decree prohibiting mourning and weeping for the slain, and forbidding complaints, so that Muhammad (محمد) and his companions would not rejoice at their grief, and so that the morale of those remaining would not break.

Abu Lahab ('Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib — أبو لهب، عبد العزى بن عبد المطلب) had stayed behind from Badr, sending Al-'As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah (العاص بن هشام بن المغيرة) in his place in exchange for a debt owed to him. He was anxiously waiting for news in Makkah.

Historical narrations record (as in Sirat Ibn Hisham — سيرة ابن هشام, Dalail al-Nubuwwah by Al-Bayhaqi — دلائل النبوة للبيهقي, and Al-Mustadrak by Al-Hakim — مستدرك الحاكم) that Abu Lahab (أبو لهب) was sitting in a dome near Zamzam (زمزم). Sitting nearby was Abu Rafi' (أبو رافع) (freed slave of Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib — العباس بن عبد المطلب, who was concealing his Islam), shaping arrows, and with them was Umm al-Fadl Lubabah bint al-Harith (أم الفضل لبابة بنت الحارث) (wife of Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib — العباس بن عبد المطلب, who was also concealing her Islam).

Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (أبو سفيان بن الحارث بن عبد المطلب) arrived returning from Badr. Abu Lahab (أبو لهب) sat by him and asked eagerly: "Tell me, how went the matter of the people?" Abu Sufyan (أبو سفيان) replied with deep regret:

"By Allah, as soon as we met the people, we turned our backs to them; they killed us as they wished, and captured us as they wished! By Allah, despite that, I do not blame the people. We encountered white men on piebald horses between heaven and earth; by Allah, nothing stood against them, nor could anything withstand them!"

Abu Rafi' (أبو رافع) could not contain his joy at the mention of the angels, so he raised his head and said with spontaneous conviction:

"By Allah, those were the angels!"

Abu Lahab (أبو لهب) flew into a rage and struck Abu Rafi' (أبو رافع) severely, then lifted him and slammed him to the ground, kneeling on him and beating him because he was a servant.

Here, Umm al-Fadl (أم الفضل) stepped up with faith-driven courage and rare bravery. She grabbed a large wooden pillar from the tent structures and struck Abu Lahab (أبو لهب) on his head, inflicting a severe, deep wound that caused his blood to flow, saying to him with dignity:

"Do you treat him as weak because his master is absent?!"

Abu Lahab (أبو لهب) left humiliated and broken. He lived for only seven days after this blow, whereupon Allah afflicted him with a malignant and contagious disease known to Arabs as "Al-'Adasah" (العَدَسَة — a malignant plague-like malignant tumor that spreads through the body and hastens death).

Abu Lahab (أبو لهب) died a shameful death, and his corpse stank so severely that his sons left him for three days out of fear of infection and the foul odor. When people from Quraish reproached them, saying: "Are you not ashamed to leave your father rotting in his house without burying him?", they dug a trench for him from a distance, then pushed his body with sticks and long pieces of wood until they dropped him into the trench, throwing stones over him from afar until he was covered.

This disgraceful end was a Divine fulfillment and confirmation of what was revealed regarding him in the Holy Quran years before his death:

{تَبَّتْ يَدَا أَبِي لَهَبٍ وَتَبَّ * مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ * سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ}
"May the hands of Abu Lahab be ruined, and ruined is he * His wealth will not avail him or that which he gained * He will [enter to] burn in a Fire of [blazing] flame" [Surah Al-Masad: 1-3] (المسد: 1-3).

2. Echoes of Victory in Madinah .. Joy of Victory Blended with Grief

On the other side, Madinah (المدينة المنورة) was awaiting news from the battlefield with anxious hearts and raised hands in supplication. As soon as the battle concluded with Allah's victory, the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) sent two heralds to deliver news of the conquest to the people of Madinah to boost morale and spread reassurance.

The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) sent two heralds:

  • Zayd ibn Harithah (زيد بن حارثة) — may Allah be pleased with him — (riding the Prophet's camel "Al-Qaswa'" — القصواء) to the people of the lower area of Madinah ('Awali al-Madinah — عوالي المدينة).
  • 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah (عبد الله بن رواحة) — may Allah be pleased with him — to the people of the upper area of Madinah ('Aliyat al-Madinah — عالية المدينة).

Hypocrites and Jews in Madinah had tried to spread rumors prior to their arrival, falsely spreading: "Muhammad has been killed, and this is his camel ridden by Zayd, who does not know what he is saying out of terror!"

However, 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah (عبد الله بن رواحة) and Zayd ibn Harithah (زيد بن حارثة) entered Madinah shouting at the top of their voices with the names of the slain leaders of Makkah, confirming the safety of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) and the Muslims. Madinah shook with Takbeer (التكبير), Tahleel (التهليل), and celebration, and the faces of believers shone with the joy of this conquest that established the pillars of the nascent state.

Amidst this overwhelming joy over strategic victory, a shade of human grief fell over the Prophetic household and close Companions: the passing of Ruqayyah (رقية) — may Allah be pleased with her (daughter of the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) and wife of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan — عثمان بن عفان).

Authentic narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari (صحيح البخاري) state that Ruqayyah (رقية) was severely ill prior to the army's departure to Badr. The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) commanded her husband 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (عثمان بن عفان) and his adopted brother Usamah ibn Zaid (أسامة بن زيد) to remain in Madinah to care for her, saying to 'Uthman (عثمان):

"Indeed, you have the reward of a man who attended Badr and his share of the booty."

Ruqayyah's (رقية) soul passed to her Creator just before the heralds arrived. Usamah ibn Zaid (أسامة بن زيد) — may Allah be pleased with him — describes this moment mixed with tears and joy, saying:

"Zayd ibn Harithah (زيد بن حارثة) came to us with the glad tidings while we were leveling the earth over Ruqayyah (رقية), the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم)."

Madinah experienced conflicting and elevated emotions during those hours:

  • Grief with human compassion: over the departure of the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم) daughter.
  • Joy with spiritual pride: over the victory of Tawheed and the eradication of polytheist leaders.

This timing taught the Companions and the Ummah an educational lesson: that joy over a general victory for faith and state does not negate human compassion for the departed, and that personal grief does not prevent praising Allah and rejoicing in the victory of truth and empowerment for the Muslim nation.

Element 5: Jurisprudence of Healing Hearts After Victory (Surah Al-Anfal and Educational Link) (العنصر الخامس: فقه علاج القلوب بعد النصر)

The real battle at Badr did not end with the conclusion of field combat and the flight of polytheist remnants; rather, another battle began that was no less fierce or important: "the battle of reforming souls and healing hearts." A swift military victory and the sudden shift from a state of oppressed, deprived people to victorious gainers carries within it psychological and strategic afflictions that can compromise the cohesion of the Muslim rank. Thus, Surah Al-Anfal (سورة الأنفال) was revealed as an "educational and psychological manual" dissecting the repercussions of victory and treating the ailments that might creep into souls following triumph, reconnecting material gain with faith and confirming that purity of heart and unity of rank are more precious to Allah than all earthly gains.

1. Dispute Over the Distribution of Booty and Division into Three Groups

The Great Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) was the first major military encounter fought by Muslims that yielded vast spoils and military assets. Detailed rulings regarding war booty (Anfal — الأنفال) had not yet been revealed in Islamic jurisprudence; in previous nations, spoils were forbidden, and a fire would descend from the sky to consume them.

When the war laid down its burdens, Muslims found themselves before abundant spoils. The Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — divided on the field into three tactical groups based on their assigned duties:

  1. The First Group (The Pursuers): Set out to chase fleeing polytheists to prevent them from regrouping, capturing their leaders, and breaking their strength in the desert.
  2. The Second Group (The Gatherers of Spoils): Focused on the enemy camp, collecting weapons, equipment, camels, and assets left on the battlefield.
  3. The Third Group (The Guards): Surrounded the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) and guarded the command center (Al-'Arish — العريش), fearing that the enemy might launch a surprise counter-attack.

When the men gathered in the evening, material gain caused a human disagreement among these three groups. Each faction claimed it was most entitled to these spoils:

  • Those who gathered the spoils said: "We contained and collected them, so no one else has a share in them!"
  • Those who pursued the enemy said: "You are not more entitled to them than us; we repelled the enemy and defeated them, and had it not been for us, you would not have obtained them!"
  • Those who guarded the leadership said: "You are not more entitled to them than us; we feared the enemy might attack the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم), so we occupied ourselves with guarding him, so you are no more entitled to them than us!"

Imam Ahmad (أحمد) in his Musnad (مسند), Al-Tirmidhi (الترمذي), and Abu Dawud (أبو داود) narrated with an authentic chain on the authority of the noble Companion 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit (عبادة بن الصامت) — may Allah be pleased with him — that he documented this incident with total honesty and self-awareness:

"It was revealed regarding us, the companions of Badr, when we disputed over the spoils and our conduct worsened regarding them. So Allah stripped them from our hands and placed them with the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم), so the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) distributed them equally among the Muslims."

2. The Quranic Lesson in Surah Al-Anfal and Treating the Afflictions of Victory

This disagreement among the Companions was not a departure from faith; rather, it was a Divine test and a transient human reaction to worldly material wealth tested by the soldiers for the first time after years of poverty and oppression in Makkah and Madinah. Divine intervention came through the opening verses of Surah Al-Anfal (سورة الأنفال) to establish fundamental and educational remedies for the afflictions of victory.

The first curative step was resolving the dispute by stripping ownership of spoils from all groups and returning authority over them entirely to the True Sovereign and the Prophetic leadership:

{يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الْأَنفَالِ ۖ قُلِ الْأَنفَالُ لِلَّهِ وَالرَّسُولِ ۖ فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَصْلِحُوا ذَاتَ بَيْنِكُمْ ۖ وَأَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ}
"They ask you, [O Muhammad], concerning the spoils of war. Say, 'The spoils are for Allah and the Messenger.' So fear Allah and amend that which is between you and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you should be believers" [Surah Al-Anfal: 1] (الأنفال: 1).

The verse declared that these spoils were not an earned right for any faction based on combat effort; rather, they were a favor from Allah and His Messenger. The goal was to remove the root of division and rivalry, returning the soldiers to pure intention: that their fighting was for Allah and in His cause, not for transient gain.

The verse immediately followed with three interrelated educational commands prioritized over receiving wealth:

  1. Taqwa (God-consciousness): {So fear Allah}; by invoking His awareness and spiritual consciousness that produced the victory.
  2. Reconciliation: {And amend that which is between you}; by repairing relationships, pardoning one another, and removing grudges caused by material disputes, because purity of hearts is more obligatory than acquiring spoils.
  3. Absolute Obedience: {And obey Allah and His Messenger}; by fully submitting to whatever Allah and His Messenger decree regarding these assets.

One of the greatest afflictions of victory is for soldiers to forget Allah's help and attribute success to themselves, their bravery, or weapons. Thus, the Quranic text in the Surah addressed pride and vanity with decisive words:

{فَلَمْ تَقْتُلُوهُمْ وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ قَتَلَهُمْ ۚ وَمَا رَمَيْتَ إِذْ رَمَيْتَ وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ رَمَىٰ ۚ وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا...}
"And you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them. And you threw not when you threw, but it was Allah who threw that He might test the believers with a good test" [Surah Al-Anfal: 17] (الأنفال: 17).

The battle — according to the Quranic account — was not decided by their swords or spears, but by Divine support, angels, tranquility, and cosmic decrees; their role was merely providing available human effort.

To prevent soldiers from becoming arrogant in victory, the Surah reminded them of their initial psychological state before departing Madinah, when some disliked engagement, argued about fighting, and desired the easy commercial caravan instead of military confrontation:

{كَمَا أَخْرَجَكَ رَبُّكَ مِن بَيْتِكَ بِالْحَقِّ وَإِنَّ فَرِيقًا مِّنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لَكَارِهُونَ * يُجَادِلُونَكَ فِي الْحَقِّ بَعْدَمَا تَبَيَّنَ كَأَنَّمَا يُسَاقُونَ إِلَى الْمَوْتِ وَهُمْ يَنظُرُونَ * وَإِذْ يَعِدُكُمُ اللَّهُ إِحْدَى الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ أَنَّهَا لَكُمْ وَتَوَدُّونَ أَنَّ غَيْرَ ذَاتِ الشَّوْكَةِ تَكُونُ لَكُمْ...}
"[It is] just as when your Lord brought you out of your home in truth, while indeed, a party among the believers were disagreeable * Arguing with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as if they were being driven to death while they were looking on * [Remember] when Allah promised you one of the two groups that it would be yours, and you wished that the one of no war-power would be yours" [Surah Al-Anfal: 5-7] (الأنفال: 5-7).

This direct reminder revealed to the Companions that Divine decree was what led them to conquest despite their initial hesitation, and that Allah's wisdom crafted the glory, so no one who disliked fighting yesterday had the right to dispute over spoils today.

The Surah concluded this educational treatment by returning to define the spiritual and heart-centered characteristics of the faith-driven personality seeking the Hereafter:

{إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَإِذَا تُلِيَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتُهُ زَادَتْهُمْ إِيمَانًا وَعَلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ يَتَوَكَّلُونَ * الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلَاةَ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ * أُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ حَقًّا...}
"The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts become fearful, and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith; and upon their Lord they rely * The ones who establish prayer and from what We have provided them, they spend * Those are the believers, truly" [Surah Al-Anfal: 2-4] (الأنفال: 2-4).

Result and Educational Dimension for the Ummah:
After Surah Al-Anfal fulfilled its role in purifying hearts from vanity and dispute, and after sacrifice and Taqwa were established as permanent standards, Allah returned the spoils to the Muslims through an equal and fair distribution. The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) equalized all three groups (those who gathered, pursued, and guarded), even allocating shares for those who stayed behind due to valid excuses (such as 'Uthman ibn 'Affan — عثمان بن عفان and Abu Lubabah — أبو لبابة).

Badr and Surah Al-Anfal proved to the Ummah throughout history that "purity of hearts and cohesion of ranks" is the primary strategic asset, and that victory, if not guarded by Taqwa, preference for the Hereafter, and forgiveness, will be consumed by worldly afflictions and destroyed by internal disputes.

Element 6: Managing the Captives File and Prophetic Consultation (Shura) (العنصر السادس: إدارة ملف الأسارى والشورى النبوية)

Handling the file of polytheist captives following the Battle of Badr represented a foundational milestone in Islamic humanitarian and legal history. The Prophetic leadership established the first rules of international humanitarian law governing war outcomes and captives' fates. This file demonstrated leadership wisdom in distinguishing between "war criminals" who deserved direct punishment for crimes against humanity and "regular captives" with whom consultation (Shura — الشورى) and ransom were pursued. Badr presented an unprecedented model in prioritizing "literacy and education" over collecting money, alongside a human model of Prophetic loyalty to the memory of Khadijah (خديجة) — may Allah be pleased with her.

1. Executing War Criminals (Applying International Criminal Justice)

Islamic law did not deal with Badr's captives through generalization. The Prophetic leadership distinguished between those who joined Badr as regular soldiers and those classified as "top figures in inciting polytheism and orchestrating torture and aggression against the Call," referred to in modern terms as "war criminals."

Thus, the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) issued a decree excluding two Quraish leaders and executing them in justice before reaching Madinah:

Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith (النضر بن الحارث) was the head of the intellectual and media campaign against Islam in Makkah. He used to travel to Persia, learn legends of its kings (such as Rustam and Esfandiyar), and return to Makkah to sit behind the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) when he spoke, telling people: "By Allah, I tell better stories than him; come, I will tell you the stories of kings." He was also among the fiercest in inciting harm against the weak. Al-Nadr (النضر) was executed in punishment at Al-Safra' (الصفراء) by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (علي بن أبي طالب) — may Allah be pleased with him.

'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ait (عقبة بن أبي معيط) possessed the most severe criminal record of direct physical assault against the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم). He was the one who placed the camel intestines and dirt on the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم) back while he was prostrating at the Ka'bah (الكعبة), and he choked him with his cloak so intensely that he almost killed him, had Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق) not intervened. 'Uqbah (عقبة) was executed in punishment at 'Irq al-Dhubyah (عِرق الظُّبْية) by 'Asim ibn Thabit (عاصم بن ثابت) (or 'Ali ibn Abi Talib — علي بن أبي طالب). When 'Uqbah (عقبة) cried out in terror before his death: "Who will care for the children, O Muhammad?", the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) answered him with the words of just retribution: "The Fire."

This exception proved that Islam rejects "impunity for criminals" who stained their hands with the blood of the oppressed and tortured people for ideological and tyrannical reasons.

2. The School of Shura for Remaining Captives (Between Mercy and Firmness)

After settling the file of war criminals, around seventy captives from the general polytheist army remained in Muslim hands. Because a definitive Quranic text regarding captives had not yet been revealed, the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) activated the principle of "Shura" (consultation) to derive the best decision for the Ummah and state interest.

It is established in Sahih Muslim (صحيح مسلم) on the authority of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas (عبد الله بن عباس) — may Allah be pleased with them both — that the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) consulted Abu Bakr (أبو بكر), 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب), and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (علي بن أبي طالب) — may Allah be pleased with them — on the day of Badr regarding the captives:

Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) spoke with compassion and missionary vision:
"O Prophet of Allah, they are our cousins and kin. I believe we should accept a ransom from them, which will give us strength against the disbelievers, and perhaps Allah will guide them to Islam." Abu Bakr (أبو بكر) looked at the immediate financial benefit (strengthening the nascent state's economy) and future missionary prospects (hoping for their guidance so their offspring would support Islam).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) spoke with uncompromising conviction and intent to solidify strength:
"No, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah! I do not hold the opinion of Abu Bakr. Rather, I hold that you enable us to strike their necks! Enable 'Ali (علي) to execute 'Aqil (عقيل) (his brother), and enable me to execute so-and-so (a relative of 'Umar); for these are the leaders and champions of disbelief!" 'Umar (عمر) believed that the first battle in the state's history required decisive field dominance to shatter polytheist hopes of underestimating Muslims, empowering every Muslim to execute his relative to eliminate remaining tribal favoritism.

The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) inclined toward the opinion of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (أبو بكر الصديق) out of mercy and hope for their guidance, accepting financial ransom from the captives.

The Quran gently reproved the Muslim camp for choosing "worldly gain and temporary financial benefit" (ransom) in the first major battle, rather than focusing on breaking the enemy's military power and securing the state's strategic existence:

{مَا كَانَ لِنَبِيٍّ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُ أَسْرَىٰ حَتَّىٰ يُثْخِنَ فِي الْأَرْضِ ۚ تُرِيدُونَ عَرَضَ الدُّنْيَا وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ الْآخِرَةَ ۗ وَاللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ * لَّوْلَا كِتَابٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ سَبَقَ لَمَسَّكُمْ فِيمَا أَخَذْتُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ * فَكُلُوا مِمَّا غَنِمْتُمْ حَلَالًا طَيِّبًا...}
"It is not for a Prophet to have captives [of war] until he inflict a defeat [upon the enemy] in the land. You desire the commodities of this world, but Allah desires [for you] the Hereafter. And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise * If not for a decree from Allah that preceded, you would have been touched for what you took by a great punishment * So consume what you have taken of war booty [as being] lawful and good" [Surah Al-Anfal: 67-69] (الأنفال: 67-69).

The verses clarified that the reproof was not for committing a sin, but for leaving the most complete and firm choice for state interest at that crucial historical moment. Nevertheless, the Quran validated the ransom decision and made spoils lawful and good for Muslims.

3. Financial and Educational Ransom (Establishing Human Capital Investment)

The genius of Prophetic management of the ransom file manifested in considering the financial and social conditions of captives, transforming the file from a "financial transaction" into a "developmental project for building human capacity."

Ransom amounts were determined according to the financial capability of the captive and his family:

  • The Wealthy: Four thousand dirhams to three thousand dirhams.
  • The Middle Class: Two thousand dirhams to one thousand dirhams.
  • The Poor and Indigent: The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) granted freedom to some without payment due to poverty, on condition that they would not return to fight him (such as Abu 'Azzah al-Jumahi — أبو عزة الجمحي).

For impoverished captives who possessed no money but could read and write, the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) set an exceptional condition representing the first literacy initiative in Islamic history:

Imam Ahmad (أحمد) in his Musnad and Ibn Sa'd (ابن سعد) in Al-Tabaqat (الطبقات) narrated with a good chain:

"He set the ransom for the people of Badr from four thousand to one thousand dirhams. Whoever had no ransom but could write was given ten boys from Madinah to teach them reading and writing. Once they mastered it, that was his ransom."

The Prophetic leadership preferred spreading knowledge and literacy among Madinah's youth over acquiring money, confirming that knowledge and education are core pillars for building a strategic nation. Among those who learned reading and writing through this ransom was Zayd ibn Thabit (زيد بن ثابت) — may Allah be pleased with him.

4. A Story of Loyalty and Tenderness (Khadijah's Necklace and the Ransom of Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' — أبو العاص بن الربيع)

The ransom file witnessed one of the most tender human stances combining official leadership ethics with personal Prophetic loyalty.

Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' (أبو العاص بن الربيع) (husband of Zainab — زينب, the eldest daughter of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم), and nephew of Mother of the Believers Khadijah — خديجة) was among the polytheist captives at Badr. Zainab (زينب) was still residing in Makkah upon her Islam.

When Makkans sent funds to ransom their captives, Zainab (زينب) sent money to ransom her husband Abu al-'As (أبو العاص), including in the ransom a "gold necklace" that her mother Khadijah (خديجة) — may Allah be pleased with her — had gifted her on her wedding day.

It is established in Sunan Abi Dawud (سنن أبي داود), Musnad Ahmad (مسند أحمد), and Al-Mustadrak (المستدرك) on the authority of Mother of the Believers 'Aishah (عائشة) — may Allah be pleased with her — that she said:

"When the people of Makkah sent funds to ransom their captives, Zainab (زينب) sent funds to ransom Abu al-'As (أبو العاص), sending among it a necklace that belonged to Khadijah (خديجة) which she had given her upon her marriage to Abu al-'As. When the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) saw it, he felt immense tenderness for her!"

Upon seeing the necklace, the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) remembered Khadijah (خديجة), her early sacrifices, and maternal love for her daughter Zainab (زينب), and his heart swelled with loyalty. However, he did not exploit his executive authority to free his son-in-law and return the necklace through an absolute decision, because spoils were a collective right of the army. Instead, he used the etiquette of seeking permission from the Companions, saying to them with gentleness and humility:

"If you see fit to release her captive for her and return to her what is hers, then do so."

The Companions — may Allah be pleased with them — responded immediately to this Prophetic affection and loyalty, saying with joy:

"Yes, O Messenger of Allah, most willingly!"

They returned Zainab's (زينب) wealth and necklace to her and released Abu al-'As (أبو العاص). The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) stipulated a personal and security condition upon him: that he allow Zainab (زينب) to migrate to Madinah. Abu al-'As (أبو العاص) fulfilled his promise and sent her to Madinah, before later accepting Islam, whereupon the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) reunited him with his wife Zainab (زينب).

Element 7: Faith-Based Intelligence Penetration (The Story of 'Umair ibn Wahb's Conversion to Islam) (العنصر السابع: الاختراق الاستخباراتي الإيماني - قصة إسلام عمير بن وهب)

The military and political repercussions of Badr presented unique scenes revealing dimensions of Divine support and preventive security awareness for the nascent Islamic state. Prominent among these scenes was the conversion to Islam of 'Umair ibn Wahb al-Jumahi (عمير بن وهب الجمحي), the Quraish knight nicknamed in pre-Islamic times as "the Satan of Quraish" (شيطان قريش) due to his fierce hostility and severity in harming Muslims in Makkah. An intelligence assassination plot — in which swords were poisoned and details arranged in absolute secrecy — turned into a prophetic miracle and a testament to soul transformation, establishing an educational principle for the Ummah: that the light of guidance can penetrate the darkest hearts, and no one should be despaired of receiving guidance regardless of their past evil.

1. The Secret Plot in Al-Hijr (Planning Executive Assassination)

Following the defeat suffered by Quraish at Badr and the death of its leaders, Makkah lived in a state of rage and deep resentment. Under these conditions, 'Umair ibn Wahb al-Jumahi (عمير بن وهب الجمحي) sat with his friend Safwan ibn Umayyah (صفوان بن أمية) (whose father Umayyah ibn Khalaf — أمية بن خلف and brother 'Ali — علي were killed at Badr) in the Hijr (الحِجر) beside the Ka'bah, discussing the casualties of the well (Qalib — القليب) and Quraish's calamity.

Safwan (صفوان) said with regret: "By Allah, there is no good in life after them!" 'Umair ibn Wahb (عمير بن وهب) — who sought revenge and whose son Wahb ibn 'Umair (وهب بن عمير) was a captive in Muslim hands in Madinah — seized the moment and said:

"You spoke the truth, by Allah! By Allah, were it not for a debt I owe with no means to pay, and a family I fear will be destitute after me, I would ride to Muhammad (محمد) and kill him! I have an excuse to go to them: my son is a captive in their hands."

Safwan ibn Umayyah (صفوان بن أمية) seized this strategic opportunity and offered 'Umair (عمير) a complete financial and social deal to fund the operation:

"Your debt is upon me to pay, and your family shall be with my family to support as long as they live; nothing shall expand for me while failing them!"

The agreement was struck between the two parties in absolute secrecy with no third party present in the Sanctuary. 'Umair (عمير) ordered his sword to be sharpened and soaked in deadly poison, then set out disguised toward Madinah under the cover of negotiating with Muslims to release his captive son.

2. The Acumen of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) and Preventive Security Awareness

Upon arriving in Madinah, 'Umair ibn Wahb (عمير بن وهب) made his mount kneel at the door of the Prophet's Mosque while wearing his poisoned sword. At that time, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) — may Allah be pleased with him — was sitting with a group of Companions talking about Allah's favors at Badr and what He had shown them regarding their enemy.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (عمر بن الخطاب) noticed 'Umair's (عمير) entry with sharp security intuition. He saw him wearing his sword and was not deceived by his ostensible excuse, saying to his companions with firm intelligence observation:

"This dog, the enemy of Allah, 'Umair ibn Wahb (عمير بن وهب)! By Allah, he has come for nothing but evil! He is the one who incited conflict against us and estimated our numbers for the enemy on the day of Badr!"

'Umar (عمر) entered upon the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) immediately and alerted him to the direct threat: "O Prophet of Allah, this enemy of Allah, 'Umair ibn Wahb (عمير بن وهب), has come wearing his sword!" The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) commanded him to secure his entry: "Bring him in to me."

'Umar (عمر) executed an extraordinary preventive security measure; he grabbed the belt of 'Umair's (عمير) sword around his neck and restrained him by it (gaining complete physical control over his sword belt), then said to men from the Ansar (الأنصار): "Enter upon the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) and sit near him, and guard him against this evil man, for he is not to be trusted!" He then brought him in to the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) while holding him tightly.

3. The Prophetic Miracle and Unveiling the Unseen Secret

When the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) saw him with 'Umar (عمر) holding his sword belt, he displayed the calm of leadership assured of Allah's protection, saying to 'Umar (عمر):

"Release him, O 'Umar. Come closer, O 'Umair."

'Umair (عمير) approached, attempting to disguise his intent using pre-Islamic customs, saying: "An'imu Sabahan" (انعموا صباحاً — "Good morning", the pre-Islamic greeting). The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) replied with the faith-based greeting of peace:

"Allah has honored us with a greeting better than your greeting, O 'Umair: As-Salam (السلام), the greeting of the people of Paradise."

Then the following tactical dialogue took place:

  • The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم): "What brought you, O 'Umair?"
  • 'Umair (deceptively): "I came regarding this captive in your hands, so treat him well."
  • The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم): "Then what is the matter with the sword around your neck?"
  • 'Umair (evasively): "May Allah curse these swords! Did they avail us anything on the day of Badr? I merely forgot it on my neck."
  • The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم): "Tell me the truth, what did you come for?"
  • 'Umair: "I came for nothing other than that!"

At this point, the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) unveiled the secret plot in its exact verbatim details as arranged in the Makkan Sanctuary, revealed through Divine revelation; he said to him:

"Rather, you and Safwan ibn Umayyah (صفوان بن أمية) sat in the Hijr (الحِجر) and mentioned the casualties of the well from Quraish (قريش). Then you said: 'Were it not for a debt I owe and a family I have, I would go out and kill Muhammad!' So Safwan (صفوان) took upon himself your debt and your family on condition that you kill me for him! But Allah stands between you and that!"

4. 'Umair's Conversion to Islam and Transformation into an Inviter to Faith

'Umair ibn Wahb (عمير بن وهب) was struck with shock and awe that shook his entire being; the conversation had occurred between him and Safwan (صفوان) in secret within the walls of the Hijr (الحطيم), with no third person present to convey news. He knew with absolute certainty that this news could only be disclosed through Divine revelation from heaven.

Allah caused his tongue to declare the testimony of Truth immediately:

"I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah! O Messenger of Allah, we used to belie you regarding the news of heaven and revelation that descended upon you. But this was a matter where no one was present except Safwan (صفوان) and myself! By Allah, I know that none brought this to you except Allah. Praise be to Allah Who guided me to Islam and drove me along this path!"

The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) and the Muslims rejoiced in his conversion, and the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) issued an immediate educational and pastoral directive to the Companions:

"Teach your brother his religion, recite the Quran to him, and release his captive for him."

Meanwhile, Safwan ibn Umayyah (صفوان بن أمية) was walking through the streets of Makkah arrogantly boasting and promising Quraish good news soon, saying to them: "Rejoice over an event coming in a few days that will make you forget Badr!" He kept asking riders about 'Umair (عمير), until a rider arrived and informed him of 'Umair ibn Wahb's (عمير بن وهب) conversion to Islam! Safwan (صفوان) was devastated and swore never to speak to 'Umair (عمير) again or benefit him in any way.

As for 'Umair (عمير) — may Allah be pleased with him — he asked the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم) permission to return to Makkah as a caller to Islam to wash away his past in disbelief, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, I exerted myself in extinguishing Allah's light, and I would love for you to permit me to go to Makkah to call them to Allah, His Messenger, and Islam; perhaps Allah will guide them." The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) permitted him, so he returned to Makkah alone, and many people of Makkah accepted Islam through his hands due to his conviction and steadfastness.

5. Educational Lessons from the Conversion of "The Satan of Quraish"

The story of 'Umair ibn Wahb's (عمير بن وهب) conversion contained a package of timeless educational lessons addressing Islamic work across ages:

  1. Never Despairing of Anyone's Guidance: No matter how severe a person's rebellion, criminality, or hostility to faith (even if nicknamed "the Satan of Quraish"), hearts are between two fingers of the Most Merciful, turning them as He wills. No one has the right to deem a person permanently excluded from Allah's mercy.
  2. The Power of Truth to Penetrate Hearts and Redirect Energies: Just as 'Umair (عمير) was a force in polytheism, he transformed through faith into a force in calling to Islam. Islam does not negate human capacities; rather, it redirects and refines them in service of Truth.
  3. Integration of Security Caution with Prophetic Mercy: The stance demonstrates balance in the Islamic personality; 'Umar's (عمر) security awareness, precaution, searching, and restraint did not contradict the Prophet's (صلى الله عليه وسلم) broadmindedness, mercy, and granting of safety to the opponent once his sincerity became clear.
  4. Infallibility of Prophethood and Confirmation of Revelation: The disclosure of the secret conversation represented tangible proof of the truth of Prophethood and Divine revelation, establishing 'Umair's (عمير) faith upon intellectual and emotional conviction.

General Conclusion of the Article (الخاتمة العامة للمقالة)

With this Seventh Element, the pillars of this comprehensive historical and intellectual study of "The Events and Repercussions of the Great Battle of Badr" (أحداث وتداعيات معركة بدر الكبرى) are completed. Through its seven axes, the study has revealed an integrated model for building the first generation, combining:

  • Outstanding field heroism,
  • The high ambition of youth,
  • Firmness in the doctrine of Loyalty and Disavowal (Al-Wala' wa-l-Bara' — الولاء والبراء),
  • Strategic awareness of the repercussions of victory and defeat,
  • The jurisprudence of healing souls and purifying intentions,
  • Humanitarian justice in managing international files such as captives, and
  • Firm faith reinforced by signs of Prophethood.

This ensures that Badr remains truly "Yawm al-Furqan" (يوم الفرقان — The Day of Criterion) and the greatest foundational milestone in the history of the Islamic nation.

Element 1: The Shift in Strategic Balance After Badr .. The Collapse of Illusions and the Formation of a New Political Landscape (العنصر الأول: انقلاب الموازين الاستراتيجية بعد بدر .. سقوط أوهام السقوط وتشكّل المشهد السياسي الجديد)

The Great Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر الكبرى) was not a mere passing military engagement on the fringes of the Hijaz (الحجاز); rather, it was a geopolitical turning point that split history into two distinct eras: pre-Badr and post-Badr. If the "Day of Criterion" (يوم الفرقان — Yawm al-Furqan) differentiated dogmatically between truth and falsehood, on the strategic level it triggered a colossal earthquake that shattered all predictive analyses constructed by the hostile forces lurking around the nascent Islamic State in Medina (المدينة المنورة — Al-Madinah al-Munawwarah).

1. The Collapse of the "Inevitable Defeat" Hypothesis and Recalibration of Regional Calculations

Prior to Badr (بدر), the prevailing perspective among all factions across the Arabian Peninsula (جزيرة العرب — Jazirat al-'Arab)—whether Quraysh (قريش) in Mecca (مكة — Makkah), nomadic Bedouin tribes roaming the desert, the Jews of Yathrib (يثرب — Yathrib), or internal waverers—rested on a single, fixed premise: "The survival of the Islamic State is impossible."

Detached political analysis dictated that Muhammad (محمد — صلى الله عليه وسلم) and his companions were merely an exiled, vulnerable group that had taken refuge in an agricultural oasis, completely incapable of withstanding the centralized hegemony of Quraysh (قريش)—a power possessing religious preeminence, economic depth sustained via the winter and summer trade caravans, and expansive military alliances with the tribes of Kinana (كنانة) and the desert Bedouins (الأعراب — Al-A'rab).

Based on this materialist assessment, various factions adopted the posture of a "cautious spectator." Their prevailing policy was one of appeasement and accommodation, avoiding direct and costly confrontation with the Muslims. Their internal conviction was that the matter would last no more than "a year or two," after which the swords of Quraysh (قريش) would eradicate this call, settling the score without requiring others to shed a single drop of blood.

However, the outcome of Badr (بدر) delivered a deafening shock:

  • A faithful contingent of no more than 314 fighters, meagerly equipped (two horsemen and seventy camels), confronted a heavily armored army of approximately one thousand warriors and one hundred horsemen.
  • The outcome: A decisive, overwhelming victory within mere hours; seventy of the senior tyrants and historic chieftains of Quraysh (قريش) were slain (such as Abu Jahl — أبو جهل, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah — عتبة بن ربيعة, and Umayyah ibn Khalaf — أمية بن خلف), another seventy captured, and the remainder routed in disarray and disgrace.

This seismic triumph dismantled all prior estimations. Every dweller of the Arabian Peninsula was compelled—willingly or grudgingly—to reset their calculations from scratch. Medina (المدينة) was no longer an asylum for refugees; it had emerged as an "intimidating regional power" whose reactions were feared and whose military confrontation was deeply dreaded by surrounding tribes.

2. The Reaction of Regional and Local Powers to the New Reality

This outcome forged a new reality that forced various factions to adopt shifting postures characterized by confusion and hasty adaptation:

  • The Nomadic Bedouin Tribes Surrounding Medina: Those nomadic tribes (such as Banu Sulaym — بنو سليم, Ghatafan — غطفان, Banu Tha'labah — بنو ثعلبة, and Muharib — محارب) that had lived off brigandage, plundering caravans, and preying upon settled towns, were struck with bewilderment and terror. They no longer viewed Medina (المدينة) as easy prey; rather, they sensed an existential threat from this ascendant Islamic force that had asserted control over the Syrian trade route and shattered the prestige of the Meccan aristocracy.
  • The Schemers Within Medina (The Nucleus of the Hypocrite Movement): Notable leaders who had not embraced Islam—foremost among them Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (عبد الله بن أبيّ بن سلول)—found themselves backed into a critical corner. The Muslim camp was no longer a fragile element that could be marginalized or overthrown; it was now the actual ruling authority. This forced them to pivot their strategy from blatant opposition to covert infiltration, outwardly feigning acceptance of the fait accompli.

3. The Explosion of Jewish Rancor and Envy: From Cold Truce to Overt Hostility

The Jewish factions of Medina (Banu Qaynuqa' — بنو قينقاع, Banu al-Nadir — بنو النضير, and Banu Qurayzah — بنو قريظة) were the most profoundly affected and shocked by the results of Badr (بدر). This manifested in a radical shift in their engagement with the Islamic State:

  • The Nature of the Initial Covenant (The Constitution of Medina — وثيقة المدينة / صحيفة المدينة): Following the Hijrah (الهجرة), the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) concluded a precise constitutional charter with the Jews. It guaranteed the freedom of their religion and wealth, mandated peaceful coexistence, mutual defense of Yathrib (يثرب), and non-aggression. The Jews accepted this treaty as a "tactical armistice" and a cautious maneuver, believing the conflict would soon culminate in the defeat of the Muslims by Quraysh (قريش) without requiring them to break the pact themselves.
  • The Evaporation of Illusions and Igniting of Resentment: When the news of Badr (بدر) arrived bearing a clear victory for the Muslims, the Jews of Yathrib (يثرب) lost their composure. The battle extinguished their hopes of eliminating the Muslims through a third party. Crucially, the victory struck a fatal blow to Jewish religious pride. For centuries, they had assumed an air of superiority over the unlettered Arabs of Medina (المدينة), prophesying the imminent arrival of a prophet from the Children of Israel whom they would follow to vanquish the Arabs like 'Ad (عاد) and Iram (إرم). Suddenly, the Prophet emerged from the heart of the Arabs, triumphant, establishing a state that captivated hearts and unified the tribes of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج)—the very tribes whose mutual bloodshed and wars had long sustained Jewish economic and political hegemony.
  • Transitioning to Direct Confrontation and Subversion: At this juncture, the Jewish factions could no longer exercise self-restraint or adhere to the terms of the charter. Jewish conduct shifted from a cold truce to blatant hostility, venting malice and envy, and striving to dismantle the Muslims' internal cohesion. Conspiracies surfaced in Medina (المدينة) along multiple tracks: rekindling pre-Islamic tribalism among the Ansar (الأنصار), imposing economic and commercial blockades, and sowing doctrinal doubt—all serving as preludes to openly abrogating their treaties, as subsequently manifested by Banu Qaynuqa' (بنو قينقاع).

Badr (بدر) inaugurated a new phase wherein the Prophetic leadership was not merely confronting an external, identifiable enemy in Mecca (مكة), but was compelled to navigate a complex, multi-front struggle against internal fifth columns (النفاق — Nifaq) and Jewish deceit lurking within fortresses and marketplaces.

Element 2: The Genesis of Hypocrisy in Medina .. The Internal Fifth Column and the Unmasking of Traitors (العنصر الثاني: نشأة ظاهرة النفاق في المدينة .. طابور الخيانة الداخلي وسقوط الأقنعة)

The ramifications of the Great Battle of Badr (بدر) were not confined to redrawing the military balance of power across the Arabian Peninsula; their profoundest impact penetrated the social and psychological fabric of Medinan society. The triumph at Badr (بدر) gave birth to an unprecedented doctrinal and security crisis absent throughout the entire Meccan period: the emergence of the "Hypocrite Faction" (طائفة النفاق — Ta'ifat al-Nifaq) and the founding of an internal fifth column that corroded the community from within, posing a peril that often surpassed that of the declared external adversary.

1. The Involuntary Inversion .. Hypocrisy Born from the Womb of Victory

Throughout the thirteen years of the Meccan era, Islam never knew the phenomenon of hypocrisy (النفاق — Nifaq). There was no human incentive for an individual to claim faith while concealing disbelief; embracing Islam then meant torture, social boycotts, loss of protection, and constant fear. Faith in Mecca (مكة) was a losing transaction by material measures, undertaken only by the sincere and detached.

Even after the migration to Medina (المدينة) and prior to Badr (بدر), the polytheists of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) maintained open rejection or detached indifference without needing dissimulation, presuming the Islamic State would neither endure nor gain ascendancy.

However, once the dust of Badr (بدر) settled, bringing news of a crushing Muslim victory and the slaughter of the polytheist aristocracy of Quraysh (قريش), Islam in Medina (المدينة) transformed within moments from a vulnerable movement seeking sanctuary into an absolute governing authority and triumphant power.

Here, the hostile schemers faced only two choices:

  1. Remain in open polytheism, enduring political and social isolation, and potential legal accountability.
  2. Outwardly profess Islam as a "protective shield" to spare their blood, safeguard their wealth, and preserve their social standing, while enjoying the civil rights afforded by Islamic governance.

This faction chose the second path: they displayed Islam begrudgingly while harboring disbelief, bitterness, and spite, marking the birth of organized hypocrisy in the history of the Ummah.

2. Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (عبد الله بن أبيّ بن سلول) .. The Complex of the "Stolen Crown" and Legacy of Prestige

This movement was spearheaded by a man representing the quintessential archetype of hypocrisy in history: Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (عبد الله بن أبيّ بن سلول), the chieftain of Al-Khazraj (الخزرج).

  • The Complex of the Stolen Crown: To comprehend Ibn Salul's (ابن سلول) motives, one must recall the historical backdrop of Medina (المدينة) prior to the Hijrah. The Battle of Bu'ath (حرب بُعاث) had decimated both Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) and wiped out their senior leaders. Abdullah ibn Ubayy (عبد الله بن أبيّ) was an honored, obeyed nobleman who abstained from fighting at Bu'ath (بُعاث). Consequently, both factions agreed upon him, threading beads to fashion a crown to coronate him as the "King" of Yathrib (يثرب). As they stood on the verge of his coronation, the dawn of the Prophetic Migration broke; the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) entered Medina (المدينة), and the people rallied around him, abandoning Ibn Salul (ابن سلول). A permanent psychological trauma and historical grievance settled deep within his soul; he viewed Muhammad (صلى الله عليه وسلم) as having robbed him of an assured kingdom and a coronation ready to take place.
  • The Outward Profession of Islam and the Survival Strategy: Following Badr (بدر), Ibn Salul (ابن سلول) recognized that open resistance had become impossible. He uttered his famous, bitter remark to his partisans: "This is a matter that has definitively materialized," and outwardly declared his Islam immediately.
  • The Deception of "Social Prestige" and the Patient Strategy of Exposure: The Prophetic leadership faced a profoundly intricate psychological and social dilemma in dealing with Ibn Salul (ابن سلول). The Muslim masses—particularly his own tribe, Al-Khazraj (الخزرج)—long maintained a favorable opinion of him. They regarded him as a wise elder and historical chieftain whom they could not conceive would lie, betray, or dissimulate. Hence, it was unwise to precipitate a direct confrontation through an immediate purge. Rather, the Prophetic leadership employed "patient, sound political governance" (السياسة الشرعية — Al-Siyasah al-Shar'iyyah), allowing successive practical situations to unmask him gradually. His own deeds exposed his treachery to the public until society achieved complete conviction regarding his status as the arch-hypocrite, without triggering tribal civil strife.

3. The Danger of Concealed Enmity: Distinguishing Jews from Hypocrites

Medina (المدينة) was rife with diverse currents of adversaries, but contrasting the hostility of the Jews with that of the hypocrites revealed an essential divergence in threat profiles:

  • The Nature of Jewish Hostility (Overt Enmity): Due to their ethnic chauvinism and psychological disposition, the Jews could not sustain complete religious dissimulation for long. Their inherent superiority complex drove them to voice open opposition and insolence in marketplaces and public councils. This overt hostility—despite its malice—was easier to monitor, guard against, and counter directly from a security standpoint.
  • The Nature of the Hypocrites' Enmity (Covert, Infiltrated Hostility): Conversely, Ibn Salul's (ابن سلول) retinue and dozens of embedded hypocrites donned the mantle of Islam. They stood in the front rows of the mosque during prayer, attended consultative councils, and convened secret meetings in their homes to coordinate subversion. Their lethal danger lay in executing psychological and ideological warfare under the guise of "sincere counsel and concern for the public interest."

The hypocrite does not approach you with a drawn sword; he approaches in the guise of an affectionate, sympathetic brother, dampening resolve, whispering doubts, and instilling terror: "Where are you going? Quraysh cannot be vanquished; you are casting yourselves into ruin. Remain in your homes and protect your livelihoods."

The Noble Quran captured this tactical malice and the vulnerability that could afflict some believers upon hearing it:

{لَوْ خَرَجُوا فِيكُم مَّا زَادُوكُمْ إِلَّا خَبَالًا وَلَأَوْضَعُوا خِلَالَكُمْ يَبْغُونَكُمُ الْفِتْنَةَ وَفِيكُمْ سَمَّاعُونَ لَهُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِالظَّالِمِينَ}
"Had they gone forth with you, they would not have increased you except in confusion, and they would have hurried about in your midst, seeking to cause you discord. And among you are avid listeners to them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers" [Surah At-Tawbah: 47] (التوبة: 47).

That is: there exist within your ranks pure, naive hearts easily deceived by their facade and former prestige, listening to them and believing their poisoned warnings cloaked in counsel.

4. The Eschatological Retribution: The Secret of the "Lowest Depths of the Fire"

Confronting this exceptional treachery that fractures internal trust, decisive divine judgment declared the true gravity of hypocrisy:

{إِنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ مِنَ النَّارِ وَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُمْ نَصِيرًا}
"Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire—and never will you find for them a helper" [Surah An-Nisa: 145] (النساء: 145).

The hypocrites were not relegated to the lowest abyss of Hell—beneath idolaters, Jews, and Christians—arbitrarily, but because their damage to Islam is far more heinous:

  1. Breach of Trust: The disbeliever fights you chest-to-chest, whereas the hypocrite stabs you in the back after you entrusted him with your sanctuary and secrets.
  2. Fracturing the Ummah's Cohesion: An external enemy unites the community against him, whereas the internal hypocrite fractures ranks, disseminates sedition, demoralizes spirit, and tears apart social bonds from within.

Thus, Medina (المدينة) after Badr (بدر) transformed into a complex operational theater wherein Muslims had to master distinguishing substance from appearance, recognizing that while the victory at Badr (بدر) broke the sword of the external foe, it awoke poisoned daggers lurking within their own city walls.

Element 3: The Intrigue of Shas ibn Qays and the Policy of "Divide and Rule" .. A Blaze Averted by Prophetic Intervention (العنصر الثالث: مكيدة شاس بن قيس وسياسة "فرّق تسد" .. كاد أن يشتعل الحريق لولا الغوث النبوي)

Following the epic triumph at Badr (بدر), the adversaries in Medina (المدينة) lacked the courage and capability to confront the Islamic State on an open battlefield. Consequently, Jewish malice resorted to its historically favored weapon: "psychological warfare, stoking internal strife, and applying the doctrine of 'divide and rule'." The conspiracy orchestrated by the Jewish rabbi Shas ibn Qays (شاس بن قيس) served as an alarm bell, exposing the profound cunning aimed at the unity of the Muslim ranks, and the fragility of the human construct whenever deprived of divine guidance and vigilant leadership.

1. The Spectacle of Fraternal Harmony that Disturbed the Adversaries

For long centuries preceding the Hijrah, Yathrib (يثرب) was the arena of an exhaustive civil war between ancestral brothers: Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج). The Jews capitalized on this enmity for decades, instigating one clan against the other and financing their wars through usury and arms sales to guarantee both factions remained in a state of permanent attrition, securing Jewish economic and political dominance over the oasis. The climax of these catastrophic wars was the Battle of Bu'ath (حرب بُعاث) — a bloody engagement that decimated the leadership of both sides and left deep, unhealed scars in their hearts.

Yet, Islam wrought the miracle that all the wealth and arbitrations of the pre-Islamic era failed to accomplish. The moment the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) settled in Medina (المدينة), vendettas dissolved, grudges vanished, and bitter enemies transformed into loving brothers competing in sacrifice and altruism. Concerning them, the divine declaration was revealed:

{وَأَلَّفَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِهِمْ ۚ لَوْ أَنفَقْتَ مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًا مَّا أَلَّفْتَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِهِمْ وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ أَلَّفَ بَيْنَهُمْ}
"And He brought together their hearts. If you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have brought their hearts together; but Allah brought them together" [Surah Al-Anfal: 63] (الأنفال: 63).

This scene—the men and youth of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) seated together in a single assembly characterized by affection and camaraderie, crowned by the glory of Badr (بدر)—struck the adversaries like a thunderbolt. They realized that the cohesion of this body behind the Prophetic leadership meant the absolute termination of their historical influence across the region.

2. Engineering Sedition: Covert Malice Through Historic Grievances

An elderly Jewish man named Shas ibn Qays (شاس بن قيس) passed by this assembly. He was deeply entrenched in disbelief, burning with hatred, enmity, and envy toward the Muslims. Witnessing the unity and affection of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) after their long-standing estrangement, he was consumed by indignation and remarked bitterly: "The leaders of the children of Qaylah (Banu Qaylah — بنو قيلة, referring to Al-Aws and Al-Khazraj) have united in this land! By God, we have no place with them if their leadership remains united!"

Shas ibn Qays (شاس بن قيس) did not enter the gathering himself to insult or fight, knowing that overt aggression would unite them against him. Instead, he resorted to the "psychological engineering of sedition" by engaging a local proxy:

  • Recruiting the Instrument: He secured an articulate, clever Jewish youth versed in Arabic poetry and historical battle lore, providing him with financial incentives.
  • Structuring the Operational Plan: He instructed him to sit among the members of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) in their assembly, engaging them courteously. Once they grew comfortable, he was to subtly introduce the memory of the Day of Bu'ath (يوم بُعاث) and preceding conflicts, reciting the partisan poetry composed by both factions satirizing one another, boasting over the killing of ancestors, and gloating over the victims' blood.

3. The Resurgence of Tribalism: When Vigilance Lapses

The youth executed the plan with precision. He sat with the group, gained their confidence, and dropped the venomous words under the guise of recalling classic literature and history. As he recited the poetry of Bu'ath (بُعاث), dormant remnants of pre-Islamic tribalism (الجاهلية — Al-Jahiliyyah), suppressed only by their recent entry into Islam, were rekindled.

The Dramatic Escalation of the Fitnah:

  1. Verbal Skirmishing: It began with recollections: "We did such-and-such to you on that day... and we killed so-and-so among you on that day."
  2. Igniting Pride and Blood Lust: Discussion rapidly descended into prideful boastfulness and rage. An Awsite stated: "Rather, it was we who slew your leaders!" A Khazrajite replied: "Nay, we humiliated you and triumphed over you!"
  3. Evoking Personal Blood Vengeance: Each party recalled the blood of fathers, uncles, and brothers shed at Bu'ath (بُعاث).
  4. Declaration of War: Two prominent leaders sprang forward—Aws ibn Qayzi (أوس بن قيظي) from Al-Aws and Jabbar ibn Sakhr (جبار بن صخر) from Al-Khazraj. They insulted one another, until one shouted: "If you wish, we shall rekindle the war right now!" (رددناها الآن جذعة). The other replied: "We accept! Your rendezvous is at Al-Zahirah (Al-Harrah — الحرة outside Medina)! To arms! To arms!" (السلاحَ السلاح!).

Within minutes, all harmony evaporated. Both sides departed in fury, summoning their respective tribes, raising weapons, and marching to Al-Harrah (الحرة) to ignite a catastrophic civil war within the capital of Islam.

4. Decisive Prophetic Intervention: Rapid Extinguishment of the Fire

The dire news reached the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم). In that critical moment, the brilliance of Prophetic leadership manifested:

  • Immediate Initiative: The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) did not hesitate for a moment, nor did he dispatch delegations of conciliation. He rushed personally to the scene of the dispute before a single drop of blood could be shed; for once ignited, civil strife becomes uncontrollable.
  • Tactical Composition of the Entourage: He took with him a group of the Emigrants (المهاجرون — Al-Muhajirun)—the completely neutral party in this equation, possessing no stake in historical conflicts between Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج)—to serve as a human barrier and an objective voice of truth.

The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) stood between the two battle lines and proclaimed in a voice that shook the field:

«يَا مَعْشَرَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ! اللهَ اللهَ! أَبِدَعْوَى الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ وَأَنَا بَيْنَ أَظْهُرِكُمْ؟! بَعْدَ أَنْ هَدَاكُمُ اللهُ لِلإِسْلامِ، وَأَكْرَمَكُمْ بِهِ، وَقَطَعَ بِهِ عَنْكُمْ أَمْرَ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ، وَاسْتَنْقَذَكُمْ بِهِ مِنَ الْكُفْرِ، وَأَلَّفَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِكُمْ؟! تَرْجِعُونَ إِلَى مَا كُنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ كُفَّاراً؟!»
"O gathering of Muslims! Remember Allah, remember Allah! Do you resort to the calls of Jahiliyyah while I am among you?! After Allah guided you to Islam, honored you by it, severed from you the affairs of Jahiliyyah, rescued you from disbelief, and joined your hearts together?! Will you return to the disbelief you were upon?!"

5. Awakening, Contrition, and Fraternal Embrace

The words of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) fell upon their heated tempers like ice water, instantly quenching the fires of rage:

  • Lifting the Veil: The Companions recognized the precipice of ruin they had almost tumbled over. They recalled how they had been on the brink of a pit of Fire, how Allah delivered them through Muhammad (صلى الله عليه وسلم), and how their hearts had been united after bitter division.
  • Identifying the Source of Subversion: In a moment of renewed faith, they realized this instigation was a satanic manipulation and a sinister plot engineered by their enemy Shas ibn Qays (شاس بن قيس) and the Jewish schemers to tear down their state.
  • The Final Scene: The men threw down their weapons, weeping profusely in repentance and shame before the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم). Men of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) rushed to embrace one another in tears and compassion, shaking hands, and returning with the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) in absolute obedience. Allah dismantled their enemy's plot, and revealed concerning this event:

{يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِن تُطِيعُوا فَرِيقًا مِّنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ يَرُدُّوكُم بَعْدَ إِيمَانِكُمْ كَافِرِينَ * وَكَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ وَأَنتُمْ تُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْكُمْ آيَاتُ اللَّهِ وَفِيكُمْ رَسُولُهُ ۗ وَمَن يَعْتَصِم بِاللَّهِ فَقَدْ هُدِيَ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ}
"O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will turn you back, after your belief, into disbelievers. And how could you disbelieve while to you are recited the verses of Allah and among you is His Messenger? And whoever holds firmly to Allah has indeed been guided to a straight path" [Surah Ali 'Imran: 100-101] (آل عمران: 100-101).

This incident proved that the Ummah's unity is the guarantor of its survival. When the enemy fails to defeat it on the battlefield, he weaponizes history, prideful lineage, and tribalism so that it dismantles its own home from within.

Element 4: The Jurisprudence of the "Call of Jahiliyyah" .. Between Legitimate Naming, Blameworthy Partisanship, and the Plot to Fragment the Ummah (العنصر الرابع: فقه "دعوى الجاهلية" .. بين التسميات المشروعة والتحزب المذموم ومؤامرة تفتيت الأمة)

The anger of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) upon hearing the partisan rallying cries of Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج) was not an emotional outburst, but a foundational stance aimed at uprooting a lethal pathogen capable of leveling the community's edifice. When he delivered his warning: «Do you resort to the call of Jahiliyyah while I am among you?!» and reiterated on another occasion: «Leave it, for it is putrid», he opened a vital door of doctrinal and political discernment, distinguishing sharply between "legitimate descriptive designation" and "blameworthy tribal/partisan chauvinism."

1. Deconstructing the Prophetic Term: The Significance of "Putrid" (مُنْتِنَة — Muntinah)

This incident recurred twice in the Prophetic biography:

  1. The first time: During the plot of Shas ibn Qays (شاس بن قيس) between Al-Aws (الأوس) and Al-Khazraj (الخزرج).
  2. The second time: On the Day of Al-Muraysi' (يوم المريسيع — Ghazwat Bani al-Mustaliq — غزوة بني المصطلق), when an Emigrant (Muhājir) scuffled with an Ansāri, prompting the former to shout: "O Emigrants!" (يا للمهاجرين) and the latter: "O Ansar!" (يا للأنصار). The Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) emerged enraged and said:

    «مَا بَالُ دَعْوَى الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ؟! دَعُوهَا فَإِنَّهَا مُنْتِنَةٌ»
    "What is this call of Jahiliyyah?! Leave it, for it is putrid."

The use of the term "putrid" (مُنتنة — muntinah) is a profound Prophetic metaphor of precise psychological insight. Fanaticism for race, tribe, party, or nationalism is akin to a rotting carcass buried in the soil; if disturbed, it emanates foul odors of death and decay. It is a psychological and moral regression that drags man from the lofty realm of Islamic brotherhood back into the swamp of primal, animalistic tribalism.

2. Jurisprudential Delineation: Is the Prohibition in the "Name" or the "Chauvinism"?

Many fall into a grave methodological error by assuming the Prophetic prohibition applies to merely adopting any identifier other than "Muslim," citing the literal wording of the verse: {He named you Muslims} [Surah Al-Hajj: 78] (الحج: 78). The Prophetic methodology reveals the precise reality:

  • The Continuation of Legitimate Designations: Did the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وسلم) abolish the titles Al-Muhajirun (المهاجرون) and Al-Ansar (الأنصار) after these incidents? Did he erase tribal names such as Al-Aws (الأوس), Al-Khazraj (الخزرج), and Quraysh (قريش)? Absolutely not. The Noble Quran immortalized and praised these very names:

    {وَالسَّابِقُونَ الْأَوَّلُونَ مِنَ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنصَارِ وَالَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُم بِإِحْسَانٍ رَّضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ}
    "And the first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Ansar and those who followed them with good conduct—Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him" [Surah At-Tawbah: 100] (التوبة: 100).

The legal ratio (العلة — al-'illah) does not lie in the mere "name" or "description"; rather, it lies in the consequences and functional reality of that designation:
